```ember
    Deferred = 1

enum Shape:
    Circle(radius: f32)
    Rect(w: f32, h: f32)
    Empty

    fn area() -> f32:
        return match this:
            Circle(r) => 3.14159 * r * r
            Rect(w, h) => w * h
            Empty => 0.0
```

* `[ENM-2]` A `match` on an enum MUST be exhaustive (`E2090` lists the missing variants); `_` covers
  the rest.
* `[ENM-3]` A unit-only enum is `Copy`, `Eq`, `Ord` (declaration order), `Hash` and `Debug`
  automatically, converts to its representation with `as`, and converts back with
  `Mode.from_repr(x) -> Option[Mode]`.
* `[ENM-4]` A payload enum is `Copy` only by `@derive(Copy)` with every payload `Copy`; `[STR-5]`'s
  implicit derives apply to it.

## V.5 Classes

```ember
open class Script:
    let entity: int
    pub(read) enabled: bool = true

    fn init(entity: int):
        this.entity = entity

    virtual fn on_update(dt: f32):
        pass

class Door(Script):
    angle: f32 = 0.0

    override fn on_update(dt: f32):
        this.angle = min(this.angle + 90.0 * dt, 90.0)
```

* `[CLS-1]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A class object lives in its own heap block with
  the header of `[OBJ-1]`, except as `[OPT-1]` permits; the block comes from the built-in memory
  manager, or from the instance the line that makes the object names with `using`
  (`Enemy(hp=5) using current`, `[ALC-1]`). `Name(args)` allocates, runs the constructor and gives the
  object to the place it is stored in, its one owner: a class object has one owner unless a line says
  `shares` (`[OWN-1]`, `[RC-1]`), and `=` from a whole name hands it over (`[OWN-3]`). `owns` on a class
  type is `E2114` ("a `Player` object always lives in its own block; remove `owns`: `p: Player`").
* `[CLS-2]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `fn init(…)` is the
  constructor; it sets the fields of the object it builds through `this`, with no word. Before any
  `init` body runs, every field default of the class and of its bases is evaluated and stored. Every
  field without a default MUST then be set on every path before `this` is used as a whole (`E2100`):
  `this` is used as a whole when it is passed, stored, returned or captured, when a link or an owner of
  it is made (`weakref this`, `shares this`), and by a call of a method whose body lets `this` out in
  any of those ways, which the compiler works out from that body (`[EFF-24]`). Before then `init` may
  call a method of its object once every field that method's body reads is set: after
  `this.renderer = r`, `this.assets = this.load_assets()` is allowed when `load_assets` reads only
  `this.renderer`, and is `E2100` when it reads a field not yet set ("`init` calls `load_assets()` (line
  6), which reads `this.assets` (its line 14), and `assets` is set only on line 7; give it a value
  first: write `this.assets = []` above line 6"); a method that lets `this` out is called only after
  every field is set ("`enrol` keeps a link to the player (`ROSTER.push(weakref this)`, its line 2), and
  `name` is set only on line 9; set every field first: move line 6 below line 9"). A `return` from
  `init`, like the end of its body, hands the object to its caller, so every such field is set on that
  path too. `owns this` on `init` is `E2108` ("`init` builds the object, so it cannot take it over;
  write `fn init(name: String):`"). Several constructors are written as `static fn`s that call
  `Self(…)`.
* `[CLS-3]` A class with no `init` and no base class gets a memberwise constructor as a struct does.
* `[CLS-10]` *(new in 0.9.9)* A derived class with no `init` gets its base's constructor: `Door(entity)`
  evaluates `Door`'s field defaults and then runs `Script.init(entity)`. A derived class with a field
  that has no default MUST declare an `init` (`E2101`).
* `[CLS-4]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A class is final unless declared `open` or `abstract`. Methods are
  non-virtual unless `virtual`; replacing one requires `override`; overriding a non-virtual method is
  `E2110`. A method named like an inherited one replaces it (ODR-028): over a virtual method without
  `override` it is `E2111`, and over a non-virtual one it is `E2110`, `override` or not; `init`, `drop`
  and `static fn`s are each class's own. An `override` is itself virtual, so a further subclass may
  override it again. `virtual` in a class that cannot be subclassed (neither `open` nor `abstract`) is
  `E2112` ("`Door` cannot be subclassed, so `virtual` on `on_update` changes nothing; to let subclasses
  replace it write `open class Door:`, or remove `virtual`"). A call through a `virtual` method counts
  what every override the program has changes, worked out from their bodies (`[DSP-5]`), so nothing is
  written about what an override changes. A derived `init` MUST call `super.init(…)` exactly once
  (`[CLS-11]`). Fields cannot be overridden. Base fields are laid out first; there is at most one base.
* `[CLS-11]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* Construction is two-phase. In a derived `init`, the code before
  `super.init(…)` MUST set every field the class itself declares without a default, and MUST NOT
  read an inherited field or use `this` as a whole; the code after it may do anything (`E2102`,
  naming the field or the use). So when any method runs, even a `virtual` method called from a base
  `init`, every field of the object holds a value.
* `[CLS-5]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Interface calls on a class object are dispatched statically unless
  the object is a `dyn` value.
* `[CLS-6]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Destruction runs the derived `drop`, then the base's, then ends the
  fields in reverse declaration order, then frees the block once no `weakref` link to it remains
  (`[OBJ-3]`). The object is ended before its `drop` runs (`[WK-3]`).
* `[CLS-7]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **`this` in a class method.** Inside a class
  method `this` is the object the method was called on, for the whole call. What a method does to it is
  worked out from its body, and `this` is never the only name of its object (`[EXC-15]`): a method whose
  body changes `this` may change it and is not called through a name that only reads it (`E3023`), and
  one whose body neither changes nor ends anything of `this` only reads it. Giving `this` another object
  in a class method is `E2103` ("`this = Node()` cannot replace the `Node` object `reset` was called
  on; set its fields instead: `this.v = 0`"); a function that gives a caller's place another object
  takes it as a `ref mut` parameter (`[FN-9]`) (ODR-072). A method changes its object through `this`
  with no word: `mut this` is `E0113` and `mut self` `E1010`, each with the help `fn reset():`.
* `[CLS-7a]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Inside `drop`, `this` MUST NOT be stored anywhere that outlives the
  call, and no owner of it is made (`shares this`, `thread_shared this`): the object has already ended
  (`E3016`, `[OBJ-5]`). A `drop`'s first line is `fn drop():`; it changes its object as a given
  (`[DRP-1]`).
* `[CLS-9]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A `let` field is set only in `init` (`E2104`).
* `[CLS-9a]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* After `init`, nothing is changed through a `let` field, for every
  type: a number or struct field never changes, a list field is never added to, and a class-object
  field is never pointed at another object nor its object changed through it (`E2104`: "`items` is
  `let`: it is set in `init` and never changed after; to add to it, write the field without `let`:
  `items: Array[int]`"). Other owners of a `shares` object change it as `shares` allows (`[RC-7]`);
  `let` speaks only of the field it is written on.
* `[CLS-12]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **`@cached`.** `@cached` above a method with no parameters keeps the
  method's result after the first call, and gives it again until a change, through any name, of a
  field the method's body reads clears it (`[EFF-27]`). A `Copy` result is returned by value, any other
  as a `ref T` view into the kept value, which clearing it ends (a later use is `E3060`). On an object
  several threads reach, the kept result is filled once under a once-flag. It costs one flag test per
  call and one store per change of a field the body reads. `@cached` is `E2117`, each message giving
  the `@cached` line to remove: on a method with parameters ("`@cached` keeps one result, and `radius`
  takes `scale`; remove `@cached` (line 2), or keep the results in a field: `radii: Map[f64, f64]`");
  on one whose body changes anything ("a cached method keeps one result, so it only reads, and `radius`
  changes `this.verts` (its line 4); remove `@cached` (line 2)"); and on one whose body reads a
  `shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared`, `weakref`, `sharedref mut` or `Cell` field, or a field other
  threads change under a lock, whose changes need not pass through its object ("`radius` reads `verts`,
  which other threads change under `lock`; a kept result could be stale; remove `@cached` (line 18)").
  For a method that reads a value its other owners may change: E2117 ("`radius` reads `mesh`, which its other owners may change without `Mesh` seeing it, so a kept result could be stale; remove `@cached` (line 13)").

## V.6 Interfaces and `extend`

```ember
pub interface Shape2D:
    fn area() -> float
    fn describe() -> String:
        return f"shape with area {this.area():.2f}"

struct Square:
    side: float

extend Square implements Shape2D:
    fn area() -> float:
        return this.side * this.side
```

* `[IFC-1]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* `extend T:` without `implements` adds inherent methods to `T`; it is
  legal in any module of `T`'s package.
* `[IFC-2]` Adding inherent methods to a type from another package is `E2120`; use an interface or a
  wrapper type.
* `[IFC-3]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* `interface Ord: Eq` requires implementers of `Ord` to implement `Eq`. So a bound brings
  its parents: `T: IndexMut[int]` provides `Index[int]`'s methods too, and a binding it writes
  (`Output = f32`) names the parent's associated type (ODR-042).
* `[IFC-4]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* Interfaces may declare associated types and constants, not statics.
  An associated type may carry bounds (`type Real: Float`), and a type implementing the interface
  states it (`type Real = f64`) with a value that meets them (`E2040` if it is missing or does not).
  `T.Name` names the associated type `Name` of a type parameter `T` whose bound declares it: inside
  the generic body it has what its declared bounds provide, and each call takes it from what the
  argument's type states (ODR-038). An `extend` block that implements several interfaces states an
  associated type once, for each of them that declares it (`extend i32 implements Add, Sub: type
  Output = i32`). `Name = T` inside an interface's brackets is written only in a bound (`T: Add[Output
  = T]`), and is `E2020` in an `implements` list. A bound that leaves an associated type unsaid
  (`T: Add`) makes `a + b` a `T.Output`, which only a signature naming it (`-> T.Output`) can hold
  (`E2040` otherwise) (ODR-040). An interface may give an associated type a **default** (`type Out =
  Self`): an implementation that does not state it takes the default, read with `Self` as the
  implementing type, and the default must meet the associated type's bounds (`E2040`). A default is
  not an equality: a bound `T: I` leaves `T.Out` abstract whatever the default says, and a default
  method body sees `Out` as itself, never as its default, since an implementation may override it
  (ODR-049). A default that leads back to itself, directly or through other defaults, is `E2043`.
* `[IFC-5]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Interface values say who owns them.** `owns dyn I` is a value of some
  type implementing `I`, held alone in a block of its own; `shares dyn I` and `shares mut dyn I` are one
  of several owners of such a value, reading it or changing it too; `dyn I` as a parameter's type is a
  read-only view (`ref mut v: dyn I` may change it). A bare interface name used as a type is `E2173`
  ("`Shape` is an interface, so `Array[Shape]` does not say who owns the shapes; say who owns them:
  write `shapes: Array[owns dyn Shape]` in place of line 19 (the list is their only owner), and
  `scene = Scene(shapes=[owns Square(side=2)])` in place of line 22"). A generic method whose type
  parameter is only the type of a `ref` or `ref mut` parameter gets one entry for `dyn` use; an
  interface whose generic method returns or stores its type parameter is not usable as `dyn` (`E2050`,
  `[TYP-22]`: "`Inspect` cannot be used as `dyn Inspect`: `make` returns its `V`, and a `dyn` value has
  one entry per method; take the visitor in instead of returning it, `[V: Visitor]` above
  `fn make(ref mut v: V)`, or keep each list's own type with a type parameter instead of
  `dyn Inspect`: `[I: Inspect]` above `fn walk(xs: Array[I]) -> int:`"). A value of an interface type
  is tested for its kind with `is` and cast with `cast x as T` (`[DSP-4]`, `[DSP-6]`). What a `dyn`
  value's methods change is worked out from every value the program makes into that type (`[EFF-2]`).
* `[IFC-6]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Bounds of a generic function.** A function that is not `pub` may leave
  its type parameters' bounds unwritten: they are worked out from its body, and a method that no
  interface in scope declares is `E2072` ("`T` has no `weight`: no interface in scope declares
  `fn weight`; declare one, `interface Weighed:` with `fn weight() -> int`, and write
  `struct Crate implements Weighed:` for the type `heaviest` is given; the bound follows"). A `pub`
  function writes them (`[MOD-9]`): a missing one is `E2040`, one message, on the first line of the
  body that needs a bound the function does not write, giving every bound the body needs ("`total` is
  `pub`, so its bound is written: write `[T: Add[T, Output = T]]` in place of `[T]` above
  `pub fn total(a: T, b: T) -> T:`").

## V.7 Constants and statics

* `const NAME: T = e` is a compile-time constant, inlined at each use; `e` MUST be evaluable at compile
  time (Part XIV). Written without `: T` and with an untyped numeric literal as `e`, it is untyped
  (ODR-037): each use is that literal and takes its type as the literal would there (`[TYP-23]`),
  `int` or `float` where nothing fixes it. `T` MUST be `Copy`, `StrView`, a `bytes` literal type, or a fixed array of those
  (`E2130` otherwise, whose help suggests a `static`). A `const` in the body of a `struct`, `enum`,
  `class` or `extend` block belongs to the type: it is named `T.NAME`, or `Self.NAME` inside the
  type, and is private to its module unless `pub` (`[MOD-2]`). Constants may name one another in
  any order; one whose value depends on itself is `E6001`, and a panic while one is evaluated is
  `E6004` (`[CT-7]`) (ODR-045).
* `[STA-1]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `static NAME: T = e` is one value per program
  with a stable address, and it never changes; shared state that changes goes through an `Atomic`,
  `Mutex`, `RwLock` or `Once` in it. An assignment to it (`HOOK = v` in a function) is `E3023`, whose
  help names `static mut HOOK` or another name for a local; it never makes a local that hides the
  `static`. `T` MUST be `ThreadShared` (`E7002`). `static mut NAME: T = e` is a
  module variable that may change, written with no `unsafe`: a function changes it by its name, with no
  word (Python's `global` is `E0100`: "`global` is Python's; in Ember a function changes a module
  variable by its name, with no word: remove line 9"), and what a function changes is worked out from
  its code (`[EFF-24]`). It is reached only by the main thread and its scoped tasks unless it is
  `guarded by` a `static` `Lock` (`static mut LOG: Array[String] guarded by LOG_LOCK = []`); another
  thread that reaches it otherwise is `E7012` (Part XI). A statement at module level outside the entry file (where statements
  form the implicit `main`, `[FN-8]`) that would give a module variable a value is `E0100`, whose help gives the declaration ("`FRAME = 0` is a statement, and
  a module holds declarations; for a module variable that may change write
  `static mut FRAME: int = 0`"). A foreign `static mut` (declared in an `extern` block) is reached only
  inside `unsafe` (`[UNS-1]`). A foreign static read only in `unsafe` need not be `ThreadShared`: the
  programmer answers for sharing it between threads; one read without `unsafe` under
  `@ffi(immutable)` (`[FFI-10]`) must be (ODR-163).
* `[STA-3]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A static whose initialiser can be evaluated at
  compile time is placed in the image with no initialisation code, except a `static mut` whose value
  owns heap memory, which its functions may grow or free: that value is built on first access, never in
  read-only memory (`[CT-5]`). Any other initialiser runs **once**, on first access, exactly once even
  under concurrent first access; the first access blocks until it completes. A panic during
  initialisation aborts. An initialiser that reaches its own static is `static initialisation cycle`, a
  panic naming the chain.

```ember
from std.sync import Mutex

static GREETING: StrView = "hello"
static REGISTRY: Mutex[Map[String, int]] = Mutex({})
static mut FRAME: int = 0

fn tick():
    FRAME += 1
```

* `[STA-2]` There is no static-initialisation-order problem: statics are initialised at compile time
  or on first access, never by a global constructor.

## V.8 Attributes

* `[ATT-1]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* An attribute that is neither in the table below nor a visible
  `@attribute` struct (`[RFL-3]`) is `E0104`; one that Ember no longer has is `E0104` with the one to
  write (`@sync`: "`@sync` is gone: a class needs no mark to be shared between threads; remove `@sync`",
  and the value says `thread_shared`, each field that changes `guarded by` or `Atomic`;
  `@static_safe`: `@no_alias_checks`; `@fp(contract)`: `@fp(allow_fma)`; `@borrows(p)`: `from p` after
  the result type, `[LT-1a]`; `@component`: any type is a component, with no mark (Part XII); `@no_runtime_checks`: no switch turns a safety check off, `[UNS-11]`). An
  attribute on a declaration it does not apply to is `E0104` naming the positions it does apply to.
* `[ATT-4]` One attribute per line.
  A module attribute uses a `#! module` directive (`[GRM-37]`). Its effect and any item-level
  override follow the attribute's own rule: overflow uses `[TYP-8]`, deterministic applies to
  every function without opt-out (`[DET-8]`), and reload attributes retain `[HR-25]`'s item priority.
* `[ATT-6]` *(new in 0.9.9)* Every attribute in the table has exactly the effect its rule gives. An implementation that
  has not built an attribute's effect rejects the attribute with `E0900` (`[PHIL-12]`); it never
  accepts and ignores it.
* `[ATT-2]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A statement may carry only `@parallel`, `@unroll`, `@simd` and `@allow`; the first three
  only on a `for` statement (`E0108`).

| Attribute | Applies to | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `@derive(A, …)`, `@no_derive(A, …)` | struct, enum, class | `[STR-5]`, `[DRV-1]` |
| `@layout(c)`, `@packed`, `@align(N)` | struct, enum | `[LAY-2]` |
| `@repr(T)` | enum | `[LAY-2]` |
| `@gpu_layout(std140\|std430\|scalar)` | struct | Annex D |
| `@noalloc`, `@nosync`, `@noblock`, `@noio`, `@nolock`, `@nopanic(explicit)`, `@no_alias_checks`, `@deterministic`, `@realtime` | fn, interface method, and a `type` line naming a function type (`@noalloc` above `type Handler = fn()`, `[EFF-2]`); `@deterministic` also module | Part X |
| `@overflow(panic\|wrap\|saturate)` | fn, module | `[TYP-8]` |
| `@fastmath`, `@fp(allow_fma)` | fn | `[TYP-9]` |
| `@inline`, `@noinline`, `@cold`, `@hot` | fn | `[CG-C-3a]` |
| `@simd`, `@simd(assert)`, `@parallel(…)`, `@unroll(N)` | `for` statement | Part XII |
| `@must_use` | fn, type | `[ERR-5]` |
| `@deprecated(since, note)` | any item | `[VER-3]` |
| `@unsafe(export("symbol"))`, `@unsafe(export_table("Name", protocol=N))` (the plain `@export(...)` and `@export_table(...)` are `E3100`) | fn, static; struct | `[FFI-26]` |
| `@ffi(…)` | extern item, overlay item | Part XVI |
| `@test`, `@bench`, `@should_panic` | fn | `[TST-3]` |
| `@view` | struct, enum | `[TYP-34]` (optional; checked: `E2030` on a type that holds no view) |
| `@cached` | method with no parameters | `[CLS-12]` |
| `@reflect` | type | `[RFL-2]` |
| `@safety("…")` | unsafe fn | `[UNS-7]` |
| `@must_drop` | struct, class | `[THR-6]` |
| `@allow(code, …)` | any item or statement | suppresses the named `W`/`L` diagnostics |
| `@non_exhaustive` | enum | `[FFI-8]` |
| `@soa(flatten)` | field | Part XII |

| `@reloadable`, `@noreload`, `@renamed_from("n")`, `@reinit_on_reload`, `@allow_reload_terminate` | see Annex B | Annex B |
| `@prelude` | module (standard library only) | `[MOD-5]` |

`(explicit)`), `@allocator(Name)`, `@gpu`.

# Part VI — Expressions and Statements

## VI.1 Evaluation order

* `[EXP-1]` Operands, arguments, and the elements of tuple, list, map and set literals are evaluated
  left to right, completely, before the operation or call. Named arguments are evaluated in the order
  written.
* `[EXP-2]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* An assignment evaluates its right side first, into a temporary if it
  has several elements, then the target places, then stores left to right. `a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]`
  swaps. An augmented assignment `a[i] += x` evaluates `x`, then the place once, then reads, operates
  and writes.
* `[EXP-3]` `and` and `or` short-circuit. `x if c else y` evaluates `c` and then exactly one branch. A
  comparison chain stops at the first false link (`[GRM-25]`).
* `[EXP-4]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A temporary created while evaluating an
  expression statement is dropped at the end of that statement, in reverse order of creation, unless a
  view made from it is still to be used: it then lives until the last use of every view made from it,
  lists of views included (`word = line.to_lower().trim()` keeps the lowered string until `word`'s last
  use), and a view of it that would outlive it is refused (`[BRW-19]`, `E3063`). A temporary created
  while evaluating the **condition** of an `if`, `elif` or `while` is dropped before the chosen block
  runs, unless the condition names what it holds (`exists as`, a kind test, a pattern) and the name
  refers to it, in which case it lives to the end of that block only — never into an `elif` or `else`.
  A temporary bound by `with` lives to the end of the `with` block; one created by a `for` iterable
  lives to the end of the loop.

## VI.2 Places, values and hand-overs

A **place** denotes memory: a local, a field of a place, an element of a place, an enum variant's
payload, the place a `ref` or `ref mut` view names, the value an `owns` field holds, a field of a class
object, a `static`. A call whose result type is `ref T` or `ref mut T` is a place too
(`first(ref mut xs) += 1`, `counts.entry(k).or_default() += 1`, `[LT-1]`). Everything else is a value.

* `[EXP-5]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A change, a `ref mut` name and a hand-over require a place;
  `f(x).y = 1` is `E2140` unless `f` returns `ref mut`. A method that may change its object, called on a
  temporary that ends with the line, is `E2140` too when that change is the call's only effect, since
  the change would be lost (`enemy_at(es, 0).heal()`, `[BRW-19]`); a call whose result is used stays
  allowed (`line.split(" ").next()`).
* `[EXP-6]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A whole name of a type that is not `Copy`, used as a value (given with
  `=`, given to an `owns` parameter, returned, captured with `owns`), is **handed over**: it ends, and is
  uninitialised until it is given a value again (`[OWN-3]`); `owns` hands over a name of every type,
  numbers included (`[OWN-9]`). A part of a struct value is handed over on its own, and neither the part
  nor the struct used whole is used until the part has a new value (`E3040`, `[OWN-11]`). Handing over
  a field of a type with `drop` is `E3010`; an element of an array, `Array` or `Span` is `E3011` (use
  `mem.take`, `mem.replace`, `mem.swap`, `pop`, `remove`); a field of a class object, which other names
  may reach and would see the hole, and anything reached through a name that does not own it, are
  `E3013` (`[OWN-11]`).

## VI.3 Operators and literals

| Expression | Meaning | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `a + b`, `a - b`, `a * b` | arithmetic | overflow panics (`[TYP-8]`) |
| `a / b` | true division | floats only; integers are `E2240` (`[TYP-28]`) |
| `a // b`, `a % b` | floor division and modulo | Python meaning |
| `a ** b` | power | `[TYP-30]` |
| `a == b`, `a != b` | `Eq` | built in for scalars |
| `a < b` etc. | comparison | scalars built in, in generic code too (a float's is IEEE, `[TYP-37]`); other types through `Ord.cmp`; chains (`[GRM-25]`) |
| `x in c`, `x not in c` | `c.contains(x)` | `Contains` (`[STD-8]`) |
| `a is b`, `a is not b` | the same object | class objects and views (`[EXP-9]`) |
| `x is None`, `x is not None` | option test | `Option` (`[EXP-9]`) |
| `x is T`, `if x is T as name:` | kind test | a value of an interface or base-class type (`[EXP-9]`, `[DSP-4]`) |
| `a[i]` | `Index` / `IndexMut` / `IndexSet` | read; written in place; `a[i] = v` per `[STD-17]` |
| `a[i..j]`, `a[..j]`, `a[i..]` | slice | `Span`/`MutSpan`/`StrView`, bounds-checked |
| `a?.f`, `a?.m()` | optional chaining | on `Option`: `None` propagates (`[EXP-10]`) |
| `e?` | early return | on `Option` or `Result` (`[ERR-2]`) |
| `x as T` | conversion | `[TYP-6]` |
| `cast x as T` | downcast | stops the program if `x` is not a `T` (`[DSP-6]`) |
| `copy of x` | a copy of your own | by the type's `Clone` (`[OWN-8]`) |
| `owns x`, `shares x`, `shares mut x`, `thread_shared x`, `weakref x`, `sharedref mut x`, `ref x`, `ref mut x` | the words before a value | `[OWN-13]` |
| `f"…{e}…"` | formatting | allocates a `String`; `E4001` in `@noalloc` (use `format_to`) |
| `[a, b]`, `{k: v}`, `{a, b}` | collection literals | `[TYP-38]` |

* `[EXP-9]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `a is b` tests whether two class
  objects (or two views) are the same object, by comparing addresses. `x is None` and `x is not None`
  test an `Option` for absence and presence. Before a type name `is` asks for a kind: `x is T` is a
  `bool` that says whether `x`, a value of an interface type (`dyn I`, `owns dyn I`, `shares dyn I`) or
  of a base class, is a `T`, and `if x is T as name:` names it there (`[GRM-45]`, `[DSP-4]`); each is one
  type-id compare. A kind test that always passes is `E2036`, and one that can never pass, of a type
  that does not implement the interface or derive from the base class, is `E2037` (`[DSP-4]`). Any other
  operand of `is` is `E2150`, whose help names `==`.
* `[EXP-10]` *(new in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Optional chaining.** `a?.f` and `a?.m[T](…)` take an `Option`
  (or a view of one; anything else is `E2020`): `None` when `a` is `None`, and otherwise the
  field or the method's result of the value inside, wrapped in `Some`, unless it is an `Option`
  itself, which is then the result (a chain is one `Option`, never an `Option` of an `Option`), or
  nothing, which is then what the chain is. `a` is read as `[GRM-13]` reads a place it does not
  hand over: a `Copy` value inside is copied and any other viewed, so a field that is not `Copy` comes
  as a view (`p?.name` is an `Option[ref String]`) and `a` keeps its value; from a temporary it is
  handed over (ODR-107).
* `[TYP-38]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Collection literals.**
  * A list literal `[a, b, c]` has the type its context expects: `Array[T]` (allocates), `[T; N]` (no
    allocation) or `Span[T]` (a view of a temporary fixed array). With no context it is `Array[T]`.
    `[v; N]` is always the fixed array of `N` copies of `v`. A list literal is never a `Set`: in a
    `Set` position it is `E2020`, whose help is `{a, b}`.
  * A map literal `{k: v, …}` is a `Map[K, V]` (insertion-ordered, `[STD-11]`); a set literal
    `{a, …}` is a `Set[T]`. A repeated key keeps its first position and its last value, as Python's
    `dict` does; `{1, 1}` is `{1}`. With no context a text key, value or element is a `String`, since
    a map written with no type owns its text; it holds `StrView` only where the program says so
    (`labels: Map[StrView, int]`, `[STD-11]`).
  * `[]` and `{}` need their element type from the context or from later uses in the function
    (`[TYP-23]`); left open, they are `E2060`.
  * Every element converts to the element type by `[TYP-5]`, so `["ann", "bob"]` in an
    `Array[String]` position is two `String`s, and in an `Array[StrView]` position is two static
    `StrView`s. An element for a list of `owns` values is made with `owns` (`[owns Circle(r=1.0)]`,
    `[OWN-10]`).
  * A literal that allocates carries `Alloc`; in a `@noalloc` function it is `E4001`, whose help names
    the fixed-array form. A generator expression (`[GRM-38]`) is not a collection and never allocates.
    A literal followed by `using m` takes its memory from the memory manager's instance `m`
    (`[0.0, 1.0] using current`, `[ALC-1]`).

```ember
fn main():
    counts: Map[String, int] = {}
    for word in "the cat and the hat".split(" "):
        counts[word] = counts.get_or(word, 0) + 1
    squares = [n * n for n in 0..10 if n % 2 == 0]
    seen = {"ann", "bob"}
    if "ann" in seen and 0 <= squares[1] < 10:
        println(counts, squares)
```

## VI.4 Control flow

* `[CTL-0]` The condition of `if`, `elif`, `while` and a match guard MUST be a `bool`; there is no
  truthiness. `E2035` carries a type-directed fix-it: `not xs.is_empty()` for a container or string,
  `x is not None` for an `Option`, `x != 0` for a number.
* `[CTL-1]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `for names in e:` walks:
  * a place `e` whose type is `Iterable`: calls `e.iter()`; each loop name is a read-only view of the
    element it is on, and what it reads does not change while it is used (`[BRW-1]`);
    `for ref mut x in e:` names the element so that it may change it, the only name for it while it
    is used;
  * `for x in owns e:`, or a value `e` (a temporary) whose type is `IntoIterator`: hands `e` over, and
    each element to the loop's name;
  * an `Iterator` value: calls `next` until `None`.
  `Array`, `[T; N]`, `Span`, `MutSpan`, `Set`, `Map`, ranges and generators are iterable; a `Map`
  yields its keys, as Python's `dict` does, and with two names its keys and values (`for k, v in m:`,
  as `m.items()` gives them; `for k, ref mut v in m:` may change each value; `m.values()` the values),
  and `for k in owns m:` hands its keys over, ending the values (`into_items()` keeps both); a `String`
  or `StrView` yields its `char`s. A loop's names follow the comma rule
  (`for ref mut pos, ref vel in q:`; a name with no word after one with a word is `E0116`,
  `[OWN-13]`). A plain loop name changes
  nothing: `for v in xs.iter_mut(): v += 1` is `E3023`, whose help gives `for ref mut v in xs:`.
* `[CTL-2]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* While a `for` loop walks a collection, nothing changes it but the
  loop's own handle on the item it is on, whatever the change and through whatever name or call
  (`[BRW-18]`): `xs[0] = 5` inside `for x in xs:` is `E3020`, whose help gives `for ref mut x in xs:`
  and `x = 5`, and a collection that must gain or lose items does so after the loop (`retain`,
  `extend`, a list of the program's own). A counting loop `for i in 0..xs.len():` does not walk `xs`: it
  may write its elements and add to it, but a removal is `E3020`; a `while` loop that tests its position
  against the current length at every step may add and remove.
* `[CTL-3]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* `a..b` (`Range`), `a..=b` (`RangeInclusive`) and `a..` (`RangeFrom`) over integers are
  iterable and compile to a counted loop with no iterator object. `a..=MAX` terminates after `MAX`;
  `a..` has no end: it gives its type's maximum, and the value after it is an overflow (`[TYP-8]`),
  found when the loop or the iterator asks for it. A range is a
  value (ODR-027): `Range[T]`, `RangeInclusive[T]`, `RangeFrom[T]` and `RangeTo[T]` (`..b`) are
  prelude structs with public bounds, `start` and `end` (a `RangeFrom` has only `start`, a `RangeTo`
  only `end`), and are `Copy` when `T` is. A `for` over a range value counts over a copy of its
  bounds, so the range is unchanged and can be iterated again, as Python's `range` can.
* `[CTL-3b]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* Iteration over ranges, `Span`, `MutSpan`, `Array`, `[T; N]`, `SoA`
  columns, and `enumerate`, `zip`, `take`, `skip`, `step_by`, `copy_each` and `rev` composed over them,
  MUST compile to an induction-variable loop over base pointers and lengths, with no iterator object in
  memory and no call per element, independent of the host C compiler's optimiser. `step_by(k)` becomes
  the increment `k` (a `k` that is not a positive constant is checked once before the loop). An
  `enumerate` numbers in the type the known-numbers rule gives it (`[STD-19]`), which holds every
  number it can give, so the loop computes each number with no check: over a range of 64-bit
  numbers the compiler knows nothing of, an `i128`. The loop has a copy that computes numbers wider
  than 64 bits as `int`s, taken after one test before it when every number fits one, and computes
  them in their own type otherwise (G8-4 decision C); the numbers are the same either way.
  `tests/conformance/CTL-3b/` asserts it on the emitted C.
* `[CTL-4]` The `else` of `while` or `for` runs when the loop ends without `break`.
* `[CTL-5]` A `match` tests arms top to bottom; the first that matches runs; a guard is evaluated after
  binding; the arms MUST be exhaustive (`E2090`); an unreachable arm is `W2091`.
* `[CTL-6]` `with a = e1, b = e2:` binds `a` and `b` for the block and drops them in reverse order when
  it ends. `with e:` keeps the temporary alive for the block (a guard).
* `[CTL-7]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `defer:` registers a block to run when the enclosing block exits, last registered first.
  It may refer to locals declared before it, which it uses as they are when it runs; they are not
  dropped before it. It cannot `return`, `break` or `continue` (`E2160`).
* `[CTL-8]` On every exit from a block, its `defer` blocks run first and then its locals are dropped in
  reverse declaration order.
* `[CTL-9]` `pass` does nothing; an empty block is written `pass`.
* `[CTL-10]` *(new in 0.9.9)* **Names assigned in every branch.** In an `if`/`elif`/`else` that has an `else`, or an
  exhaustive `match` statement, a name that is not in scope before the statement and is declared (by
  `x = e`) in **every** arm that completes normally, at the **same type**, is declared in the enclosing
  block and is initialised after the statement. An arm that ends in `return`, `break`, `continue` or a
  panic does not need to declare it. Different types in different arms are `E2230`, naming each arm.
* `[CTL-11]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Headers that name what they test.** An `if` or `while` header that
  opens an `Option` or a `weakref` link (`if cam.target exists as p:`, `while cur.parent exists as p:`,
  `[GRM-44]`), and an `if` or `elif` header that tests a value's kind (`if s is Circle as c:`,
  `[DSP-4]`), run their block as those rules say, and the name they declare is in scope in that block
  only, never in an `elif` or `else`: `else:` runs when the link or `Option` holds nothing, or when the
  value is not of that kind. The name keeps its place for the whole block (`[BRW-14]`): a plain one
  only reads, and `exists as copy of v` is a copy of the program's own.

```ember
fn describe(n: int) -> String:
    if n < 0:
        kind = "negative"
    elif n == 0:
        kind = "zero"
    else:
        kind = "positive"
    return f"{n} is {kind}"
```

## VI.5 Lambdas and function values

```ember
fn apply_twice(f: fn(int) -> int, x: int) -> int:
    return f(f(x))

fn make_adder(n: int) -> fn(int) -> int:
    return fn(x: int) copy of n => x + n

struct Button:
    label: String
    on_click: fn()

fn main():
    step = 3
    println(apply_twice(fn(x) => x + step, 1))
    add5 = make_adder(5)
    b = Button(label="ok", on_click=fn() => println("clicked"))
    b.on_click()
    println(add5(1))
```

* `[CLO-1]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A named function, a lambda and a local function each have a type of
  their own (ODR-278), which implements its callable type; one that keeps no state is a value of size
  zero. Given to a type parameter (`[CLO-14]`) it keeps that type, and a call through it is direct;
  wherever a callable type is written (`[CLO-3]`) it becomes a **function value** of that type
  (`[CLO-10]`). Where two different functions meet in one place (`if c: f = a else: f = b`, a second
  assignment, a conditional's two branches, a collection's elements), the place has the callable type
  both convert to. A local holding a function that keeps no state is not captured: a lambda that uses
  it keeps nothing for it (`[CLO-2]`), since giving it the same function again changes nothing.
* `[CLO-2]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **What a function captures is written after its
  brackets.** A name a lambda or a local function uses from the function that made it is the **real
  variable**, that very variable and not a copy, unless a capture word after its brackets names it:
  `fn() copy of a, owns b, shares c, shares mut d, thread_shared e, weakref f, ref g:`. Each word means
  what it means before a value (`[OWN-13]`): `copy of` a copy of its own; `owns` handed over, for every
  type, numbers included (after `fn() owns count`, the function that made the lambda no longer uses
  `count`, `E3040`, and the lambda uses it under the same name); `shares`, `shares mut` and
  `thread_shared` one more owner; `weakref` a link; `ref` a read-only view of what the name views at
  that moment, for a loop's name the element of that round. So `b.on_click(fn(): score += 1)` changes
  the real `score`, and `b.on_click(fn() copy of score: println(score))` keeps a copy of its own. What a
  function captured with a word, and what that owns alone, is its own state (`[CLO-10]`); a real
  variable stays at its own address, and the function only borrows it (`[CLO-4]`). A place that holds
  the function value counts as reaching every real variable it uses, and a call that may run it as a
  change of each one it changes (`[BRW-11]`, `[CLO-17]`). `ref mut` is not a
  capture word (`E0120`: "remove `ref mut x`: without a word the function already uses the real `x`,
  and may change it: `fn(): x += 1`"); a captured name with no word after one with a word is `E0116`
  ("`copy of` here belongs to `name` only; say what the function does with `score`:
  `fn() copy of name, copy of score:`, or leave `score` out to use the real `score`"); `with` before the
  capture words is `E0100` ("a function's captures follow its brackets with no `with`: write
  `fn() copy of score:`"); `owned fn` is `E1010` and `owns fn` `E0109`, each naming the words to write
  on each captured name (`fn() owns name, copy of score:`).
* `[CLO-3]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **A callable type is one
  type wherever it is written.** `fn(A) -> R` as the type of a parameter, a field, a local, a result,
  a collection's element or a `static` is a function value of that type (`[CLO-10]`), filled from a
  named function (`fn log_click():` is a `fn()`), a local function or a lambda; one that captures
  nothing, or holds only its own state, may be stored anywhere a value may, and one that uses real
  variables may not outlive them (`[CLO-4]`). A parameter of callable type receives a function value
  and calls through it; a function that should get each function it is given as its own copy, called
  directly, takes it as a type parameter (`[CLO-14]`). A long callable type is named once with `type`
  (`type Handler = fn()`, then `handlers: Array[Handler] = []` and `fn on_click(owns f: Handler):`).
  `extern "C" fn(A) -> R` is a C function pointer: functions that capture nothing only. Converting a
  stored function value to one reads its C entry without handing it over; a value holding state has
  none, and the conversion panics (ODR-102).
* `[CLO-14]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A callable type may be written as a type parameter's
  bound, on the line above the function: `[F: fn(int) -> int]` above `fn apply(f: F, x: int) -> int:`.

  `apply`, and the call through `f` is direct and may be inlined, as C++'s `template <typename F>` and

## VI.5a Generators

A **generator** is a function whose body runs step by step, producing values with `yield`. It is
Python's generator, and it is also how Ember writes frame-spanning gameplay sequences.

```ember
gen fn countdown(n: int) -> Generator[int]:
    i = n
    while i > 0:
        yield i
        i -= 1

gen fn evens(xs: Span[int]) -> Generator[int]:
    for x in xs:
        if x % 2 == 0:
            yield x

fn main():
    for t in countdown(3):
        println(t)
    data = [1, 2, 3, 4]
    total = evens(data).sum()
    println(total)
```

* `[CORO-1]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* A `gen fn` declares a generator. Calling it runs none of its body; it
  returns the generator's **frame**, a value holding the parameters and suspended state. The declared
  return type is `Generator[Y]` or `Generator[Y, R]`, where `Y` is the type of each yielded value and
  `R` (default `void`) the type of the final `return` value.
* `[CORO-2]` `yield e` suspends the generator and produces `e`. `yield` outside a `gen fn` is `E2220`.
  A `gen fn` with no `yield` is accepted and produces `L2004`.
* `[CORO-3]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `Generator[Y, R]` in a signature names the function's own frame type
  opaquely, as `some Iterator[Item = Y]` would: each `gen fn` has a distinct, sized frame type, which is
  not `Copy`, that implements `Iterator[Item = Y]`. `next()` resumes the body to the next `yield`
  (returning `Some(y)`) or to its end (returning `None`, after which `result() -> Option[R]` gives the
  returned value). Calling `next()` after the end returns `None` again. Generators of different
  functions are kept together as `owns dyn Iterator[Item = Y]`. `yield` as an expression has type
  `void`.
* `[CORO-4]` The compiler rewrites the body into a state machine over the frame: locals live across a
  `yield` become frame fields, others stay on the stack. No run-time machinery exists beyond the frame.
* `[CORO-5]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **A generator allocates nothing.** The frame's size is a compile-time constant; it is an
  ordinary value, handed over by `=`, that may live in a local, a field, an `Array` or an arena. It is
  held `owns dyn` only to store generators of different functions together. A `gen fn` carries `Alloc`
  only if its body does.
* `[CORO-6]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A view **into the generator's own frame** (a view
  of one of its own locals) may not be held across a `yield`: moving the suspended frame would leave it
  pointing where the local was (`E2221`: "`r` (line 3) points into this generator's own frame, which may
  move while it is suspended at the `yield` on line 4; use `n` itself: remove line 3 and write
  `yield n` instead of line 5"). A `for` over a list, string, map or set whose body yields walks by
  position: after each resume it reads the collection again from where it lives now (the frame, or the
  object's field) and checks the position against its current length, so it holds no address across the
  suspension and the frame may move (`for s in buf: yield copy of s` over the generator's own `buf`
  compiles). Views that came in as parameters, or are made from them, may be held across `yield`; the
  frame is then a view of what they view, as a returned view would be (`[LT-1]`). `evens` above is such
  a generator.
* `[CORO-7]` Dropping a suspended generator drops exactly the locals live at its suspension point, in
  reverse declaration order.
* `[CORO-8]` A generator's effect set is the union over its whole body; contracts apply to it as to any
  function.
* `[CORO-9]` A frame never points into itself in Safe code; `unsafe` code that builds one states it in
  `@safety`.
* `[CORO-10]` A `gen fn` may not be `extern`, `@export`ed or passed to C (`E2222`).
* `[CORO-12]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A `gen fn` **method of a class** has `this`, and its frame is a
  view of the object (`[CORO-14]`): the object does not end while the generator will still be used, and
  the body changes the object as any method's body does (`[EXC-15]`).
* `[CORO-14]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **A generator is a walk of what it views.** A generator's frame is a view
  a call gave (`[LT-1]`): a method's points into its object, and `from` narrows it
  (`gen fn replay() -> Generator[int] from log:`). While it will still be used, the collection it walks
  does not change, however the generator walks it, by position included (`E3020`, `[BRW-18]`:
  "`d.log.push("open")` (line 3) changes `d.log`, which `g` walks (`g = d.replay()`, line 1), and `g`
  is used again on line 4; push after `g`'s last use: move `d.log.push("open")` below line 4"); any
  other change of what its view points into is `E3021` (`d.angle = 90.0` while `g` will still be used),
  unless `from` narrows the view to the field it walks.
* `[CORO-13]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A `yield` while a `@must_drop` value (`[THR-6]`) is live is `E2231`: a
  suspended generator may never be resumed, so the value's `drop`, on which a safety guarantee
  depends, would wait as long as the frame is kept (a `thread.scope()` whose tasks use the generator's
  parameters). A scope that closes before the next `yield` is unaffected.
* `[CORO-11]` `std.coroutine` builds gameplay sequencing on generators with no further compiler
  support: `Scheduler` resumes a set of `Generator[Wait]` once per frame and drops the finished ones;
  `wait(seconds)`, `wait_frames(n)` and `wait_until(pred)` produce `Wait` values.

```ember
from std.coroutine import Wait, wait

class Door:
    open_angle: float = 0.0

    gen fn swing_open() -> Generator[Wait]:
        yield wait(0.5)
        for _ in 0..60:
            this.open_angle += 1.5
            yield Wait.NextFrame
```

## VI.6 Assertions and panics

* `assert(cond)`, `assert(cond, msg)`, `assert_eq(a, b)`, `assert_ne(a, b)` are checked in every
  profile; `debug_assert(…)` only in `debug`, and it MUST NOT have side effects that change a program's
  result (`W2016` if its argument calls a function with effects other than `Panic`).
* `panic(msg)`, `todo()`, `unreachable()` have type `Never`.
* `[PAN-1]` A panic prints `panic at <file>:<line>:<col>: <message>` (and a backtrace outside
  `release`) to standard error and calls `abort()`. There is no unwinding in this version; `defer`
  blocks and destructors do not run on panic.
* `[PAN-2]` Formatting a panic message allocates only for an f-string; `panic("literal")` and
  `panic(some_str)` are `@noalloc`.
* `[PAN-3]` A panic inside a `drop` that runs while the process is already panicking aborts at once.
---

# Part VII — Ownership and Views

This Part specifies ownership and **views** for every type: structs, enums, collections, strings and
class objects alike. A value has one owner unless a line says otherwise; a name that points into a
place someone else owns is a view, and what a view may do is said by the word in front of it. Everything
in this Part is checked when compiling: nothing here runs while the program runs except a value's own
clean-up. How a class object is laid out, how `shares` owners are counted and how `weakref` links work
is Part VIII.

## VII.1 Terms

These words are used with these meanings throughout the specification.

- **owner**: the one place (a local, a field, a list element, a temporary, a `static`) that ends a value
  when it ends. A value made shared has several owners (`shares`, `[RC-1]`).
- **handed over**: the giver's name ends and the receiver becomes the owner, for every type, numbers
  included, wherever a line hands a value over (`snapshot = items`; an argument for an `owns`
  parameter; `return a`; a function's capture `owns count`; `[OWN-3]`, `[OWN-9]`).
- **copy**: a new value equal to the old one; nothing done to one is seen through the other. `copy of`
  copies the thing itself, never the link it is written before (`[OWN-8]`).
- **`Copy` type**: a type whose `=` makes such a copy bit for bit: the numbers, `bool`, `ref T`,
  `Span[T]`, `StrView`, and structs made only of these. Class objects, `shares` values, `weakref` and
  `sharedref mut` links, `ref mut` views and `MutSpan`s are not `Copy`.
- **place**: where a value lives: a local, a field, a list element, an enum variant's payload.
- **part**: a field (`p.name`), an element (`enemies[0]`), or a payload (`State.Walking(path)`).
- **view**: a name or value that points into a place someone else owns and may not outlive it:
  `ref T`, `ref mut T`, `sharedref mut T`, `Span[T]`, `MutSpan[T]`, `StrView`, a plain parameter, a
  plain loop or pattern name, a name opened with `exists as` (not `exists as copy of`, which is a copy
  of your own) or named by a kind test (`is T as`), a name a function captured with `ref`, a name for a
  part. A **read-only view** is every view except `ref mut T`, `sharedref mut T` and a `MutSpan[T]`
  held by a `ref mut` name. A **kept view** is a view stored in a struct or a list.
- **into X**: a view points into X when it points at X or at anything X owns, all the way down (X's
  fields, the elements of X's lists, X's `owns` parts). It does not go through links: what a link
  reaches is another object.
- **link**: a field or value that names an object it does not own alone: `weakref T` (does not keep the
  object alive), `shares T`, `shares mut T` and `thread_shared T` (one of several owners), and
  `sharedref mut T` (a view several holders may share, `[LT-46]`).
- **position**: a view of a list element that finds the element again at each use (`[BRW-16]`).
- **reshape**: a change that can free or move memory: replacing a value that owns memory; `push`,
  `pop`, `insert`, `remove`, `clear`, `sort`, `retain`, `extend` on a list, map, set or string;
  changing an enum's variant; ending an object's last owner. Writing a number or a `bool` is not a
  reshape. A reshape moves or frees only what it may move or free: adding to a list (`push`, `extend`)
  may move its buffer and every value stored inline in it, but not a class object, which lives in its
  own block and is not moved when the list grows.
- **ended**: an object is ended the moment its last owner lets it go, before its `drop` runs
  (`[WK-3]`); ending it counts as a call of its `drop` (`[DRP-8]`).
- **summary**: what the compiler works out from a function's code, with no word written (`[EFF-1]`):
  what it may change, read and end, and through which calls (the chain of calls a message names); which
  elements of a list it touches; which of its view parameters, `this` included, it uses after a line
  that may end or move what they view; and what it reaches by other names while a `ref mut` parameter
  of it is used. Across a package's edge it is recorded in the package's interface file (`[EFF-4]`).

## VII.2 Ownership

* `[OWN-1]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Every value has exactly one owner: a local, a field of an owned value,
  an element of an owned collection, a temporary, or a `static`, unless a line makes it shared
  (`shares x`, `thread_shared x`, `[RC-1]`). This holds for every type: a class object has one owner,
  as a struct value does.
* `[OWN-2]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A value is **dropped** (ended) when its owner goes out of scope (block
  end, reverse declaration order), when its owner is overwritten, or at the end of the statement that
  created it as a temporary. Dropping runs the value's `drop` method, if any, then drops its fields in
  reverse declaration order. A value always ends with its clean-up: nothing ends an owner without
  running it, and there is no `mem.forget` (`[OWN-6]`); a value given to C is handed over to it
  (`[OWN-12]`).
* `[OWN-3]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **`=` with a whole name hands it over.** `b = a`, where `a` is a whole
  name that owns a value whose type is not `Copy`, hands `a` over: `a` ends. Using it afterwards,
  whether it is read, handed over again or viewed (a method call, `print`), is `E3040`, labelled at the
  hand-over and at the use, and the message names both ways out: "`items` was handed over to
  `snapshot` on line 3 and is used on line 4; to keep both, write `snapshot = copy of items` (a copy of
  your own) or `snapshot = shares items` (two owners of one list)". Where `a` is itself a view (a plain
  parameter, a loop, pattern or opened name, a local holding a view), `b = a` makes `b` a read-only view
  of what `a` views, and `ref` may say so (`cur = ref p`); a view hands nothing over. For a `Copy` type
  `=` copies. A value handed over on only some paths is tracked with a hidden drop flag; a hand-over
  on some paths is legal, and a use a hand-over may have reached is `E3040` too.
* `[OWN-4]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A loop body that hands over a value declared outside the loop is
  `E3040`, unless every path gives it a value again before the next round.
* `[OWN-5]` Assigning to a place that holds a live value evaluates the new value, then drops the old
  one, then stores the new one. `Cell.set` stores first and drops after (`[CELL-1]`); `MaybeUninit.write`
  stores without dropping (`[ARN-8]`). These three orders are distinct and none generalises the others.
* `[OWN-6]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `mem.take(ref mut place: T) -> T` (leaves
  `Default`), `mem.replace(ref mut place: T, owns new: T) -> T`, `mem.swap(ref mut a: T, ref mut b: T)`
  and `mem.drop(owns x: T)` (ends `x` now: the name given to it ends, for every type, numbers included,
  as for every `owns` parameter, and a later use is `E3040`, ODR-065) are the operations that take
  values out of places a hand-over may not otherwise leave empty. A call writes `ref mut` before an
  argument the callee may change (`[FN-2a]`): `mem.take(ref mut this.items)`. There is no
  `mem.forget`: it is `E1010`, "`mem.forget` is gone: a value always ends with its clean-up; to give
  the widget to a C function that keeps it, hand it to a parameter its declaration says it takes
  (`widget_take(first)`), or, inside `unsafe:`, give it `first.into_raw()`".
* `[OWN-9]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **`owns` hands over, for every type, numbers included.** An argument for
  an `owns` parameter is handed over with no word: `f(n)` ends `n` when `f` takes `owns x: int`, and
  `f(copy of n)` keeps the caller's own. `return a` hands `a` over too. A number given with `=` is
  copied, so `b = owns n` is how `=` hands a number over: `n` ends there, and a later use is `E3040`.
  `owns` is not written before a name whose place already hands the value over, nor before `fn`
  (`E0109`: "`e.mesh = m` already hands `m` over; remove `owns`"; "`b = a` already hands `a` over; remove
  `owns`"; "`owns fn` does not say what the function takes or copies; name it on each captured name:
  `fn() owns report:`").
* `[OWN-10]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **`owns` on the line that makes a value for a place that owns it
  alone.** An `owns` field, an `Option[owns T]` and a list of `owns` values each hold their value in a
  block of its own, and the line that makes a value for such a place says `owns`, at first and later:
  `e = Entity(mesh=owns Mesh(points=[0.0]))`; `boss = Enemy(hp=500, mesh=owns Mesh(points=[0.0, 1.0])
  using current)` (`[ALC-1]`); `t = Tree(value=1, left=Some(owns Tree(value=2)))` for
  `left: Option[owns Tree]`; `r.pools.push(owns IntPool(items=[1, 2]))` for
  `pools: Array[owns dyn Pool]`; `e.mesh = owns Mesh(points=[1.0, 2.0])`, which frees the old mesh. The
  line without it is `E2123` ("`mesh` owns its mesh; say so where it is made:
  `mesh=owns Mesh(points=[0.0, 1.0]) using current`"; "`left` holds its tree in a block of its own; say
  so where it is made: `left=Some(owns Tree(value=2))`"). `owns` is also written where the default is
  a view, before a `for` loop's or a `match`'s source (`for x in owns xs:`, `match owns e:`), which then
  hands the value over. `owns` before a class type, whose object always lives in its own block, is
  `E2114` ("a `Player` object always lives in its own block; remove `owns`: `p: Player`").
* `[OWN-11]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **A part handed over on its own.** A part of a struct value stored
  somewhere else (`push`, `return`, a field, an `owns` argument) is handed over on its own: for a struct
  value `p`, `names.push(p.name)` moves `p`'s name into the list, and `p.hp` stays usable; `p.name`,
  and `p` used whole, are `E3040` until `p.name` is given a new value (`p.name = String("")`): "`p.name`
  was handed over to `names` on line 4; give it a new value first, or keep a copy:
  `names.push(copy of p.name)`". A field of a class object is not handed out this way, since other names
  may reach the object and would see the hole (`E3013`: "`q` is a `Player` object, which other names
  may reach, so `q.name` cannot be taken out and leave a hole; take it and leave a value in its place:
  `names.push(mem.take(ref mut q.name))`"). A hand-over out of a name or place that does not own the
  value is `E3013` too: "`v.push(template)` would hand over the caller's player, but `template` only
  reads it; to put a player of your own in the list write `v.push(copy of template)`".
* `[OWN-12]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Giving an object to C.** A C function whose declaration says it keeps
  the object it is given (`[FFI-11]`) takes it by an ordinary hand-over, `widget_take(first)`: the name
  ends and Ember frees nothing. For a C function whose declaration cannot say so (a plain pointer
  parameter, a function with `...`), `second.into_raw()` gives the object's address and stops Ember
  from freeing it; the compiler makes that step itself, so nothing else can skip a value's clean-up.
  `into_raw()` outside `unsafe:` is `E3100` ("`into_raw()` stops Ember from freeing the widget, so a
  mistake leaks it or frees it twice; write it inside `unsafe:`", `[UNS-1]`).
* `[OWN-13]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Words before a value.** Before a value, a word acts on the object the
  value names (for a link or an owner, on its target): `copy of x` (`[OWN-8]`); `owns x`
  (`[OWN-9]`); `shares x`, one more owner, on this thread, that reads it, and `shares mut x`, one more
  owner that may also change it, each written only before a new value, a local or an owner (`[RC-1]`,
  `E2122`); `thread_shared x`, one more owner on any thread, written only
  before a new value (`names = thread_shared Names()`) or a value already `thread_shared` (`E7017`
  otherwise: "`names` is `share_and_keep`'s own object, which it may change; to share it between
  threads, create it shared: `names = thread_shared Names()`"); `weakref x`, a link that does not keep it
  alive (`[WK-11]`); `sharedref mut x`, a changeable link other holders may share (`[LT-46]`); and
  `ref x` and `ref mut x`, views (`[BRW-12]`). An owner made from another may do no more than it:
  `shares mut x` needs `x` to be a name that may change the value (`E3023`: "`g2 = shares mut game`
  would change the `Game` through `game`, which only reads it (`game = shares Game()`, line 1), and an
  owner made from it only reads too; write `g2 = shares game`, or, for two owners that both change the
  game, write `game = shares mut Game()` instead of line 1"). A plain parameter of a `shares mut` type
  only reads the caller's value (`[FN-1]`), so an owner made from it only reads too; a function that
  hands on an owner that may change takes one: `fn setup(owns game: shares mut Game)`, called
  `setup(shares mut game)`. In a lambda's capture list each word means
  what it means before a value (`[CLO-2]`). In a list of names declared without types of their own (a
  capture list, a loop's names, a pattern's names, a lambda's parameters written without types) each
  word belongs to the one name after it, and a name with no word may not follow a name with a word, so
  that no word can be read as covering the next name (`E0116`: "`ref mut` here belongs to `pos` only;
  say what `vel` is: `for ref mut pos, ref vel in q:`, or `ref mut vel` to change it too").

## VII.3 Copy and `copy of`

* `[OWN-7]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A value of a `Copy` type is duplicated bit for bit by `=` and on use,
  and the source stays valid; the duplicate is independent, and no copy runs any code. A `Copy` type
  holds no owner and no link: class objects, `shares` values, `weakref` and `sharedref mut` links,
  `ref mut` views and `MutSpan`s are not `Copy`, and a type with a `drop` of its own is never `Copy`
  (ODR-051). A `Copy` struct copied with `=` from a name that is still used afterwards is not then
  changed through the new name (`E3023`): the line says `copy of` (a copy of your own) or `ref mut`
  (the original), so that no copy is changed by mistake.
* `[OWN-8]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **`copy of x`** makes a copy of the thing itself, by its type's
  `Clone` (`fn clone() -> Self`, the explicit deep copy): of a class object, a new object
  (`p2 = copy of player`); for a `shares` or `sharedref mut` link, a copy of its target. Every `Copy` type
  has `Clone` (`@derive(Copy)` gives it), so `b = copy of a` works for a `Point` marked only `Copy`. A
  value that holds links is copied field by field, as a C++ struct holding a `shared_ptr` and a
  `weak_ptr` is: what it owns alone is copied itself, and each link is copied as a link to the same
  target. For `struct Team:` with `captain: shares Player` and `scout: weakref Player`, `t2 = copy of t`
  is a new `Team` whose `captain` is one more owner of the same player and whose `scout` is one more
  link to it; a `sharedref mut` field is copied as one more holder of the same link. `copy of` is
  `E2116` before what it cannot copy as itself:
  * a `weakref` link, whose target may be gone: "`copy of this.keep` would copy the link, not the node;
    for another link to the same node write `a = weakref this.keep`; for a copy of the node itself write
    `if this.keep exists as n:` and then `c = copy of n`";
  * a value of a view type (`StrView`, `Span[T]`, a struct holding a `ref mut` field): "`w` is a view of
    `line`'s text; to make your own copy write `String(w)`";
  * a type with no `Clone`: "`Player` has no `Clone`, so `copy of` cannot make one; write
    `@derive(Clone)` above `class Player`, or keep a view of it: `p2 = ref p`";
  * a value whose views point into its own `let` field: "`d.words` points into `d.text`, so a copy's
    words would point into `d`'s text; make the copy from its text: `d2 = Document(String(d.text))`".

## VII.4 Views: names, parameters and calls

A **view** is made where a name is bound to a part or to a call that gives a view, where a place is
given to a plain or `ref mut` parameter, walked by a loop, opened or tested, or converted to a `Span`,
`MutSpan` or `StrView`, and where a line writes `ref`, `ref mut` or `sharedref mut` before a place. A
view hands nothing over and makes no copy.

* `[BRW-12]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **A name for a part is a read-only view.** A name is declared by the line
  that first gives it a value; a line inside a loop's body declares it once per round (`[GRM-4]`). A
  name bound to a part (`n = p.name`, `boss = enemies[0]`), or to a call whose result is a view
  (`ref T`, `StrView`, `Span[T]`, a `ref` or `ref mut` place, `[LT-1]`), such as
  `word = line.to_lower().trim()` or `best = a.as_span()`, is a read-only view of it: never a hand-over,
  and never a silent copy, except that a part with no fields of its own (a number, a `bool`, a variant
  with no payload) is copied, as Python binds a number. A call whose result is a new value the callee
  made (a list it built, a list of views included) hands that value to the name, which owns it
  (`[LT-45]` bounds the life of a value that holds views). A word before the part says otherwise:
  `ref mut` makes a name for that very place that may change it (`boss = ref mut enemies[0]`,
  `r = ref mut first_even(ref mut xs)`), and before a `MutSpan` a call gives it says the name may write
  the span's elements (`d = ref mut tracks[dst_name].as_mut_span()`); `copy of` makes a copy of your own
  (`boss = copy of enemies[0]`); the link words make a link (`[OWN-13]`); and `ref` states the default,
  needed before a part only to view a number (`r = ref counts[0]`).
* `[BRW-13]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **`=` on a name that has a value** puts the new value in the place the
  name stands for. A name declared with `=` stands for its own place: its old value is replaced (and
  ends, if it owned something), and if the value is a view, the name now views something else
  (`rest = tail.trim()`, `cur = p`), checked by `[BRW-1]` against its new target. A `ref mut` name stands
  for the place it was made from until it is given another ref: `r = ref mut a` then `r = 20` writes
  `a`, and `r = ref mut b` points `r` at `b`, after which `r = 30` writes `b`. The line that gives it
  another ref says `ref mut` again, for every type, and a read-only `ref b` given to it is `E3023`
  ("`r` may change what it refers to, and `ref b` only reads `b`; to point `r` at `b` write
  `r = ref mut b`, or for a read-only name `rb = ref b`"). A name that holds a `MutSpan` likewise:
  `d[i] = v` writes an element through it, and `d = ref mut other.as_mut_span()` points it at another
  span. A name written **`const ref mut`** is never given another ref, as `const` on a value means it
  never changes: `r = const ref mut a` then `r = ref mut b` is `E3023` ("`r` is `const ref mut a`, so it
  always refers to `a`; to refer to `b` use a new name, `rb = ref mut b`, or make `r` with plain
  `ref mut`: `r = ref mut a`").
* `[BRW-14]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Names that keep their place.** A parameter, a loop name, a pattern name
  and a name opened with `exists as` (`[GRM-44]`) or named by a kind test (`[DSP-4]`) stand for what the
  caller, the loop, the opening or the test gave, and keep it for their whole scope: `=` on one is
  `E3023` ("`line` is the text the caller passed and stays that text for the whole call; for a view of
  your own write `rest = line.trim()`"; "`n` is the number the caller passed; for a number of your own
  write `count = n` and change `count`"), and so is any other change through one that is plain
  (`[BRW-15]`). The one exception is a name opened `exists as copy of v`, a copy of your own, which may be
  changed (`if scores.get(name) exists as copy of v:` then `v += 1`; the map is untouched). A `ref mut`
  one writes the caller's place, and may be given another ref, as any `ref mut` name may: a
  `ref mut dst: MutSpan[float]` parameter given another span points the caller's `d` at it, and
  `ref mut c: Counter` given another ref points `c`, for the rest of the call, at that place.
  `const ref mut dst: MutSpan[float]` writes the caller's elements and is never given another ref, so
  the caller's `d` is the same span after the call.
* `[BRW-15]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **A plain name never changes anything.** A plain parameter, a plain loop,
  pattern or opened name, and a plain local that holds a view never change what they name or what it
  leads to (a `Cell` field, an object behind a `shares` link, the elements of a `MutSpan`). A change
  through one is `E3023`, with the line to write: "`path.pop()` changes the list in `n.state`, but
  `path` only reads it; to change that list through `path`, write `State.Walking(ref mut path):`";
  "`tick` sets `s.frame`, but `s` only reads the caller's clock; write `fn tick(ref mut s: Clock):` and
  call `tick(ref mut clock)`"; "`dst[i] += src[i]` writes an element of the caller's span, but `dst`
  only reads it; write `fn blend(ref mut dst: MutSpan[float], src: Span[float]):` and call it
  `blend(ref mut d, s)`"; "`d[i] = 0.0` writes an element of `tracks[dst_name]`, but `d` only reads it;
  write `d = ref mut tracks[dst_name].as_mut_span()`". A method that may change its object, called
  through a name that only reads it, is `E3023` too (`[EXC-15]`). The types made to be shared between
  threads are used through any name, a plain one included, by their own operations: a `Mutex`,
  `RwLock`, `Atomic` or channel end, and the `guarded by` fields of an object under their lock
  (`with g = m.lock():`; `with log.lock: log.lines.push(...)`; `total.fetch_add(n)`; `tx.send(v)`;
  `rx.recv()`). Each orders its own change (the lock's block, an atomic instruction), and handed to a
  call it takes no word (`[FN-2a]`, Part XI).
* `[BRW-1]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **One name changes, or any number read.** At every point of the
  program a place is reached through any number of read-only views, or through exactly one name that
  may change it, as `[BRW-17]` to `[BRW-20]` and the two rules below say; every one of them is checked
  when compiling, and nothing is checked while the program runs.
  * **A `ref mut` name is alone.** While a `ref mut` name (a parameter, a local, a loop, pattern or
    opened name, a kept `ref mut` field; one that holds a `MutSpan` included) is still used, its place is
    read or changed only through it: another name that may name the same place, a link of the same type
    included, is refused, `E3022` to change it and `E3021` to read it ("`boss` is the only name for
    `enemies[0]` until line 9, and line 7 reads `enemies[0].hp`; read it through `boss`: `boss.hp`"),
    unless the compiler proves the two differ (`if t is not a:`), or proves them the same whole variable
    given to one call (`[BRW-11]`). For a `ref mut` parameter and a place its function reaches by its
    own name (a module variable), the check is made at each call, by what the body does (`[BRW-21]`),
    so the function itself compiles. Two names of elements of one list, at least one `ref mut`, whose
    indexes are not proved different are refused as two such arguments are (`[BRW-5]`). A reshape
    through another name while a `ref mut` name that is not a position is still used is `E3022`, at the
    reshape; a position is ruled by `[BRW-16]`. A call through a `ref mut` name of a stored function
    value uses the name only to copy the function's two words out, before the arguments are given
    (`[CLO-10]`), so the call's arguments may reach the place it names; a later use of the name is
    checked against what the call may have done. `this` is not such a name (`[EXC-15]`).
  * **A read-only name promises that what it reads does not change while it is used.** While a
    read-only view (a plain name for a part, a `ref` name, a plain parameter, a `Span` parameter, a
    plain name holding a `MutSpan`, a plain loop, pattern or opened name, a view a call gave) is still
    used, what it points into is not changed through any other name (`E3021`, at the change) unless the
    compiler proves the two differ; a change that may reshape it ends it instead (`E3060`, at its later
    use). The refusal gives the ways out that compile in that program: "`enemies[0].hp = 1` (line 7)
    changes the enemy `boss` reads (`boss = enemies[0]`, line 5), and `boss` is used on line 9; change
    it after `boss`'s last use, or write `boss = ref mut enemies[0]` and change it through `boss`:
    `boss.hp = 1`". A copy of your own (`boss = copy of enemies[0]`) is restricted by nothing. A `shares`
    owner is an owner, not a view: it sees the changes the value's other owners make (`[RC-1]`).
* `[BRW-2]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Liveness.** A view is in use from where it is made to the last use
  of anything made from it: the view itself, a view made from it, a value returned from a call it was
  given to. Scope does not matter: `n = v.len(); v.push(n)` is legal.
* `[BRW-3]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Reading before the call.** For a method call
  whose object is a place, or an argument given to a `ref mut` parameter, the place may be read while
  the call's arguments are evaluated, and values computed from it may be passed (`v.push(v.len())`); a
  view of the place still in use at the call, because it is itself an argument or is held by one,
  overlaps the changeable argument and is `E3021` (`[BRW-11]`). For
  `fn f(ref mut v: Array[String], s: StrView)` the call `f(ref mut v, v[0])` is therefore refused; for
  `fn f(ref mut v: Array[int], x: int)` the call `f(ref mut v, v[0])` is accepted, because `v[0]` is
  copied in before the call.
* `[BRW-11]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Arguments do not overlap a changeable one.** Two
  arguments of one call (the object a method is called on counts as one), of which at least one may be
  changed (a `ref mut` argument, a `MutSpan` one included; the object of a method that may change it;
  or a function value, which counts as changing every place the functions it may run change and every
  real variable they capture, `[CLO-2]`), may not name one place, and neither may reach into what the
  other owns, unless the compiler proves they differ: different constants, `j` from `i + 1..`, inside
  `if i != j:`, or after `assert_disjoint(a, b)` (with `from std.mem import assert_disjoint`,
  `[DSJ-5]`). Any other possible overlap is refused when compiling: `E3022` where both may be changed,
  `E3021` otherwise. This holds for spans of numbers too: two spans of one list given to one call, one
  of them changeable, are proved apart (`assert_disjoint`, two compares) or refused ("`blend` changes
  the elements of `d` (`tracks[dst_name]`, line 10) while `s` shows `tracks[src_name]` (line 11), and
  the two are one list when `dst_name` equals `src_name`; prove them apart first,
  `assert_disjoint(d, s)` before line 12, with `from std.mem import assert_disjoint` at the top, or
  blend from a copy: instead of lines 10 to 12 write `old = copy of tracks[src_name]` and
  `blend(ref mut tracks[dst_name].as_mut_span(), old.as_span())`"). A function value given to a call
  that changes the call's object is refused likewise ("`LOG.retain(keep)` changes `LOG` while it walks
  it, and `keep` adds to `LOG` too (its line 3); drop the lines first and push the notes after:
  `before = LOG.len()`, `LOG.retain(fn(s) => s != "")`, `dropped = before - LOG.len()`, then
  `for k in 0..dropped: LOG.push(String("dropped an empty line"))`"). Two exceptions:
  1. **The same whole variable under two names.** Where the compiler proves when compiling that two
     `ref mut` arguments, or a `ref mut` argument and a variable the callee uses by its own name (a
     module variable), are one whole variable, the call is allowed and compiled against a copy of the
     function in which the two names are one. `fn add_both(ref mut a: int, ref mut b: int):` whose
     body is `a += 1`, `b += 1`, `println(a)`, called `add_both(ref mut x, ref mut x)`, prints 2;
     `fn rename(ref mut s: Array[String]):` whose body is `LOG.clear()` then
     `s = [String("renamed")]`, called `rename(ref mut LOG)`, leaves `LOG` holding one string (it frees
     nothing: `clear()` empties the list, `s = ...` fills it again). Other calls use the normal copy,
     where a `ref mut` parameter is the only way in. Parts whose positions are not known when compiling
     (`ref mut log[i]` beside `ref mut log[j]`, or beside `log`) stay refused (`E3022`).
  2. **A thing whose changes go only through its lock.** A `thread_shared` object whose every field
     that may change is `guarded by` its lock (or is an `Atomic`, `Mutex` or `RwLock`) may reach one
     call through any number of names, a plain argument and a function value that holds it included:
     `dump(log, fn() thread_shared log: log.push("seen"))`, whose `dump` reads the lines inside
     `with log.lock:` and calls `note()` after the block, is allowed; the lock keeps the two ways in
     apart. A call inside the lock that may take it again is `E7018` (§XI.2).
  For two spans whose lists may be one: E3021 ("`refill` may replace the lists of `w1.lists` through `dst` while `src` shows numbers inside one of them, and `w1` and `w2` may be the same `Wrapper`; give `src` a list of its own: `first = copy of w2.lists[0]`, then `refill(ref mut w1.lists.as_mut_span(), first.as_span())`").
* `[BRW-21]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **The call check: a view argument and what the callee does.** A view
  whose last use is an argument of a call (of a plain, `Span` or `ref mut` parameter) does not live
  across the call: inside it, the parameter makes the promise of `[BRW-1]`, and the compiler holds the
  callee to it. It works out from each function's body which of its view parameters, `this` included,
  it uses after a line that may end or move what they view (a reshape; the end of an object,
  `[RC-5]`), through its own lines and the same fact of the functions it calls (a call through a
  function value, or through an interface, `dyn` or virtual method, by every function the program can
  put there, `[EFF-1]`), with the body's precise facts (a change inside `if a is not b:` is not one for
  `a`). It keeps that fact with the function (in the package's interface file across a package's edge,
  `[EFF-4]`) and checks it at each call: an argument that points into what the callee may end or move
  before its last use of that parameter is `E3031`. Writing a number or a `bool` ends and moves nothing,
  so a method that writes `this.health` through a link that may lead to its own object (a turret aimed
  at itself) is allowed; leaving a lock's `with` block ends nothing either. With `fn note(s: StrView):`
  whose body is `LOG.clear()` then `println(s)`, `note(LOG[0])` is refused ("`note` clears `LOG` (its
  line 3) and then uses `s` (its line 4), and `LOG[0]` is part of `LOG`; give it a copy:
  `note(copy of LOG[0])`, or in `note` use `s` before `LOG.clear()`"); `note("bye")` is allowed, and so
  is `note(LOG[0])` for a `note` that prints before it clears. The object a method is called on counts
  the same way: with `fn hit():` whose body is `ENEMIES.clear()` then `this.hp -= 1`, `ENEMIES[0].hit()`
  is refused ("`hit` clears `ENEMIES` (its line 3) and then changes `this.hp` (its line 4), and
  `ENEMIES[0]` is part of `ENEMIES`; in `hit`, change `this.hp` before `ENEMIES.clear()`"), and a `hit`
  that uses `this` only before the clear is allowed. A `ref mut` parameter counts the same way: with
  `fn rename(ref mut s: String):` whose body is `LOG.clear()` then `s = String("renamed")`,
  `rename(ref mut LOG[0])` is refused ("`rename` clears `LOG` (its line 2) and then writes `s` (its line
  3), and `LOG[0]` is part of `LOG`, so `s` would point at freed memory; rename a copy of your own:
  write `mine = copy of LOG[0]` and `rename(ref mut mine)` in place of this line, or in `rename` write
  `s` before `LOG.clear()`"). Since a `ref mut` parameter is compiled with noalias (`[BRW-22]`), the check
  is wider for it: while it is used, the callee reaches its place through no other name, so an argument
  for it that points into a place the callee reads or changes by another name while the parameter is
  used is refused too (with `fn heal(ref mut p: Player):` whose body is `println(PARTY[0].hp)` then
  `p.hp += 10`, `heal(ref mut PARTY[0])`: "`heal` reads `PARTY[0]` by its own name (its line 2) while
  `p` is still used (its line 3), and `p` is `PARTY[0]`; in `heal`, read it through `p`:
  `println(p.hp)`"), unless it is that same whole variable, proved when compiling (`[BRW-11]`,
  exception 1). Where the fault is in one function stored in a function value (it ends what its
  parameter views and then uses the parameter), the refusal stands on the line that stores it, not on
