  the call through the value, which is right for every other function ("`on_visit` is called with a
  node of the tree (line 21), and this function removes its node from the parent's list (line 41) and
  then reads it (line 42); read it before removing it: move line 42 above line 41"). Only a C function's
  code is unseen; `[FFI-52]` covers it. Nothing is checked while the program runs.
* `[BRW-22]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Noalias.** Every `ref mut` parameter, a `MutSpan` one included, is
  compiled with noalias (C's `restrict`): while it is used, nothing else the function uses reaches its
  place (`[BRW-1]`, `[BRW-21]`); a call compiled against a copy with one name (`[BRW-11]`, exception 1)
  has one name for that place. `this` is never compiled with noalias (`[EXC-15]`), and neither is a
  `sharedref mut` link (`[LT-46]`).
* `[BRW-4]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Disjoint fields.** `ref mut a.x` and
  `ref mut a.y` may be in use together when `x` and `y` are different fields, through any depth of field
  path, for a struct value's fields and a class object's alike (`[EXC-19]`). What two different paths
  may both reach through links is `[BRW-17]`'s.
* `[BRW-10]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **What a method does to its object is worked out
  from its body,** for every method, private or `pub` (`[EXC-15]`): a call `w.bump()` changes only the
  fields `bump`'s body changes, and those its callees' bodies change, so it may be called while a loop
  walks `w.names` if `bump` touches only `w.count`. `fn note(msg: String):` whose body is
  `this.log.push(msg)` changes `this.log`, so `this.note(...)` inside a loop over `this.log` is refused
  (`E3020`) and inside a loop over `this.players` is allowed. Across a package's edge the fact is
  recorded in the package's interface file (`[EFF-4]`), so a change to a `pub` method's body that
  changes what it touches is reported as a change of its interface.
* `[BRW-5]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Indices are not disjoint unless proved.**
  `ref mut a[i]` and `ref mut a[j]`, as two names or as two arguments of one call, are `E3022` unless
  the compiler proves `i` and `j` differ: both constants and different, `j` from `i + 1..`, or the line
  inside `if i != j:`. Nothing is compared while the program runs. With
  `fn collide(ref mut a: Body, ref mut b: Body):`, `collide(ref mut bodies[i], ref mut bodies[j])` in a
  function given `i` and `j` is refused ("`collide` changes `a` and `b` as two different bodies, and
  `bodies[i]` and `bodies[j]` are the same body when `i == j`; write `if i != j:` above this line and
  indent it under it"), and compiles under `if i != j:` or in `for j in i + 1..n:`. The same position
  twice is refused with "both are `bodies[i]`". `get_pair_mut(i, j)`, `split_at`, `chunks_mut`,
  `for ref mut x in xs:`, `swap(i, j)` and `SoA` columns are the library's ways to hold two changeable
  views of one container. `get_pair_mut(i, j) -> Option[(ref mut T, ref mut T)]`, on an `Array` or a
  `MutSpan`, views the container once, checks that both indices are in range and differ, and only then
  makes the two views; otherwise it is `None` and the container is unchanged. The pair points into the
  list it was called on (`[LT-1]` rule 1). Distinct elements of a zero-sized type need not have
  distinct addresses, and nothing about addresses follows from the indices (ODR-068).
* `[BRW-6]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Lending a `ref mut` name.** From a `ref mut` name `r`, a read-only
  view of `r.f` keeps `r` from changing `r.f` while it is used, and `ref mut r.f` lends that part, so `r`
  does not reach it meanwhile. Passing a `ref mut` name to a `ref mut` parameter (`bump(ref mut r)`)
  lends it for the call; it does not hand it over.
* `[BRW-7]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Using a place that is uninitialised on some path, one never given a value there, is `E3050`;
  using one a hand-over may have reached is `[OWN-3]`'s `E3040` (ODR-114).
* `[BRW-8]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A plain or `ref mut` parameter is passed by
  address: the callee reads, or changes, the caller's place (`[FN-1]`, ODR-024). Two kinds are passed as
  a copy instead:
  * a view (a `ref`, `Span`, `MutSpan`, `StrView` or `@view` struct), which is passed as itself and keeps
    the regions it carries;
  * a plain parameter of a `Copy` type that holds no `Cell` or `UnsafeCell`, which goes in registers when
    it is no larger than two pointers, except the object of a method whose result is a view (`[LT-1]`
    rule 1).
  An `owns` parameter receives the value. A view into the own storage of a parameter passed as a copy
  ends with the call: returning it is `E3063`. The choice depends only on the declared first line, never
  on the body; it is an ABI decision and cannot be observed. An instance of a generic function, method
  or type has the generic's declared first line: a parameter its result may point into (the object, or
  a source parameter of `[LT-1]`'s second kind) is passed as the declaration passes it, whatever the
  type arguments, so `Holder[StrView]`'s object is passed by address as `Holder[T]`'s is (ODR-048).
* `[BRW-9]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A view in Safe code is never null, dangling or unaligned.

## VII.5 Views and changes

* `[BRW-16]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Positions.** A name for a list element made by indexing
  (`boss = enemies[0]`, `boss = ref mut enemies[0]`, `p = ps.get(0).unwrap()`), of a list reached
  through locals that own it, parameters, `this` and one-owner fields, is a position: the element is
  found again at each use. The list may grow while the name is used (its buffer is read again after the
  add); anything that may remove, insert, reorder, clear or replace the list ends the name, and a later
  use is `E3060` ("`enemies.remove(0)` (line 8) may put another enemy in the place `boss` names (line
  6), and `boss` is used on line 9; use `boss` before line 8, or name the enemy again after it:
  `boss = ref mut enemies[0]`"), a call that reads elements and removes included. Growing the list is
  not a use of the element. A list reached through a link (a local or field holding a `shares`,
  `shares mut` or `sharedref mut` link) gives addresses, `[BRW-17]`.
* `[BRW-17]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Addresses.** Every other view (a kept view; a view reached through a
  link; a view into a value's own contents: a `String`'s text, an `Array` field's elements, an enum's
  payload; every view a call gives, `[LT-1]`) ends at any change that may reshape what it points into,
  made through any name that may reach it, and a later use is `E3060`. Two paths may reach the same
  object when they lead to values of one type and at least one goes through a link or a kept view,
  unless the compiler knows they differ (different types, a fresh object, inside `if a is not b:`).
  What may reshape is worked out from the code (`[EFF-1]`): the function itself, the functions it
  calls, every function the program can put in a function value or behind a `dyn` method it calls, and,
  at a foreign call, the callbacks C keeps (`[FFI-21]`). So a call through a function value whose stored
  function replaces the text of an object it owns (`rename = fn() owns n: n.name = String("b")`) ends a
  view of that text reached through a link (`s = p.name.trim()` under `if w exists as p:`): `s` is not
  used after `rename()` ("`rename()` (line 9) replaces the node's name (`n.name = String("b")`, line
  6), and `s` views that name's text (line 8) and is used on line 10; use `s` before line 9, or keep your
  own text: `s = String(p.name.trim())`"). A view parameter (a plain, `Span` or `ref mut` one), or
  `this`, and what its function may end or move may be one place too; that is checked at each call
  (`[BRW-21]`). Adding to a list moves only what it stores inline: a view of a class object (a link, a
  kept view, or an address reached through a link), which lives in its own block, is not ended by a
  `push` or an `extend` of the list that owns it (with `players: Array[Player]` and
  `w = Watcher(target=sharedref mut players[0])`, `w.target.hp -= 1` after `players.push(Player())` is
  allowed); one to a value stored inline in the list (a struct element) is. Removing, clearing or
  replacing still ends every view of what it may end.
  For keys viewed across a change of their map: E3060 ("`m.insert(String("z"), 1)` (line 8) changes `m`, whose keys `ks` (line 7) still views on line 9; use `ks` before line 8, or keep your own strings: write `ks = sorted(m.keys().copy_each())` in place of line 7").
* `[BRW-18]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Loops, generators included.** While a `for` loop walks a collection (a
  list, a map, a set or a string), or a generator that walks it (a `gen fn` paused in the middle of it,
  `[LT-1]`) will still be used, nothing changes the collection, whatever the change: nothing is added or
  removed, no element is written or replaced and no field of one changed (`xs[0] = 5`,
  `enemies[0].hp -= 1`), no value under a key replaced (`counts[k] *= 2`, `names[k] = String("bob")`),
  through the collection's own name or through any call that may change it (`[EFF-1]`: a call through
  a function value, a library call given a function that changes it, a `spawn` whose thread changes it
  other than under a lock the loop holds, a foreign call while a callback C keeps changes it, and the
  end of an object whose `drop` changes it, `[DRP-8]`). It is `E3020`, at the change:
  "`enemies.push(...)` adds to `enemies`, which this loop walks (line 3); collect the new enemies in a
  list of your own: write `spawned: Array[Enemy] = []` before the loop,
  `spawned.push(Enemy(hp=5, splits=false))` in place of this line, and `enemies.extend(spawned)` after
  the loop"; "`counts.insert(...)` (line 4) adds to `counts`, whose keys this loop walks (line 3);
  collect the new keys in a list of your own: write `upper: Array[String] = []` before the loop,
  `upper.push(k.to_upper())` in place of this line, and `for u in owns upper: counts.insert(u, 0)` after
  the loop"; "`b.click()` (line 17) adds to `LOG` (through `click`, which runs the handler stored on
  line 9, `log_click`, which pushes to `LOG`) while this loop walks `LOG` (line 16); click after the
  loop: move line 17, `b.click()`, below the loop"; "`d.log.push("open")` (line 3) changes `d.log`,
  which `g` walks (`g = d.replay()`, line 1), and `g` is used again on line 4; push after `g`'s last use:
  move `d.log.push("open")` below line 4". **The loop's own handle may change the item it is on**:
  `for ref mut x in xs: x = 5` gives `[5, 5, 5]`; `for k, ref mut v in counts: v *= 2`;
  `for k, ref mut v in names: v = String("bob")`; and the message gives that line: "`xs[0] = 5` (line
  3) writes an element of `xs`, which this loop walks (line 2); to change the element the loop is on,
  write `for ref mut x in xs:` in place of line 2 and `x = 5` in place of line 3"; "`counts[k] *= 2`
  (line 4) changes `counts`, whose keys this loop walks (line 3); change each value through the loop's
  own handle: write `for k, ref mut v in counts:` in place of line 3 and `v *= 2` in place of line 4".
  Anything else goes after the loop or after the generator's last use (`retain`, `extend`, `Commands`).
  A counting loop `for i in 0..xs.len():`, whose range is fixed when it starts, does not walk `xs`: it
  may write its elements and add to it, but not remove from it (`E3020`: "`enemies.remove(i)` (line 4)
  shortens `enemies`, which `for i in 0..enemies.len():` (line 2) counts over with an end fixed when it
  started; remove after the loop: instead of `if enemies[i].hp <= 0:` (line 3) and line 4, write
  `enemies.retain(fn(e) => e.hp > 0)` after the loop (and remove the `for` line if nothing is left in
  it)"). A `while` loop that tests its position against the list's current length at every step may
  add and remove: it is not a walk, and each index is checked. A call through a function value that may
  take a lock this thread holds, inside a walk under that lock, is `E7018`, not `E3020` (§XI.2):
  the message whose fix compiles is the one shown (`[DIA-28]`).
  For a call through a stored function that may change the walked list: E3020 ("`h(this)` (line 8) may clear `this.handlers` (through `close_all`, stored on line 20) while this loop walks `this.handlers` (line 7); give each handler the Ui to change, `handlers: Array[fn(ref mut Ui)]`, and walk by position instead of the `for` line: `this.current = 0`, `while this.current < len(this.handlers):`, `this.handlers[this.current](ref mut this)`, `this.current += 1`").
* `[BRW-19]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Temporaries.** A temporary lives until the last use of every view made
  from it, lists of views included (`word = line.to_lower().trim()` keeps the lowered string until
  `word`'s last use, `[EXP-4]`). Returning such a view, or storing it where it would outlive the
  temporary, is `E3063`: "`word` is a view of the lowered copy that `line.to_lower()` made on line 2,
  which ends when `clean` returns; return `String(...)` to hand back your own copy:
  `return String(word)`, with the result type `String`". A method that may change its object, called on
  a temporary that ends with the line, is refused when the call's only effect is that change (its body
  changes nothing else, through its arguments or by any other name, and nothing it gives back is used),
  since the change would be lost: `E2140`, "`heal` changes the enemy that `enemy_at(es, 0)` returns, a
  copy that ends on this line, so the change would be lost; to heal the enemy in `es` write
  `es[0].heal()`, or let `enemy_at` give back the enemy itself:
  `fn enemy_at(ref mut xs: Array[Enemy], i: int) -> ref mut Enemy:` with `return ref mut xs[i]`,
  called `enemy_at(ref mut es, 0).heal()`". A call whose result is used stays allowed
  (`line.split(" ").next()`).
* `[BRW-20]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Guards.** A view made through a lock's guard (`g[0]`, `ref g[0]`, a
  slice of `g`) points into the guard and does not leave its `with` block (`E3063`: "this points into
  the locked list, which can change once the lock ends; return a copy, or do the work inside the `with`
  block"); the same for `RwLock`'s `read()` and `write()` and for a `guarded by` field inside
  `with x.lock:` ("this points into the read-locked list, which can change once the lock ends; return a
  copy: `return copy of g[0]`, with the result type `String`").

## VII.6 Regions and their inference

Ember has **no lifetime syntax**. Every view carries a **region**, the set of program points at which
it must be valid, and the compiler infers every region.

* `[LT-5]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Regions of locals are inferred by non-lexical liveness (§XVIII.4). Diagnostics describe them
  in source terms: "the view of `x` on line 12 is still used on line 19".
* `[LT-1]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Where a call's view points.** A call's result
  that is a view, and a view a call puts in through a `ref mut` parameter (`[LT-47]`), point into the
  arguments they may come from. A **source parameter** (ODR-024) is:
  * a parameter whose type is a view, in any mode; or
  * a plain or `ref mut` parameter whose type is not `Copy` even when each of its type parameters is
    taken to be `Copy`: an `Array[T]`, `String`, `Map`, an `owns T` or an arena, a struct or enum without
    `@derive(Copy)`, or a tuple or fixed array holding one of these.
  A source parameter of the second kind is the caller's place (`[FN-1]`, `[BRW-8]`): a result that points
  into it may point anywhere in it, into its own storage or into storage it owns, and the call's view is
  on the argument (`[BCK-1]`), read-only for a plain parameter and changeable for a `ref mut` one. A
  `Copy` parameter that is not a view is not a source parameter (so neither is a plain `x: T`, nor a
  function-type parameter, `[CLO-3]`), and nor is an `owns` parameter that is not a view. Which
  parameters are sources depends only on the declared first line. In an instance of a generic, a
  parameter whose type there is a view is a source of that instance too, of the first kind:
  `Tree[StrView].leaf(v: T)` may return a view of what `v` views, and its callers, which call that
  instance, know it (ODR-048). Where rule 1 below ties the result to `this`, such a parameter is a
  source alongside it when its declared type names a type parameter the declared result names too: the
  result's type says it can hold one, so `Map[StrView, V].entry(k) -> MapEntry[K, V, H]` returns an
  entry holding `k`, while `get(q) -> Option[ref V]` points only into the map (ODR-069).
  For a function whose result is a view:
  1. if it is a method, the result points into `this`;
  2. else, if exactly one parameter is a source parameter, the result points into it;
  3. else, the result points into **all** source parameters together (the caller keeps all of them
     viewed while the result lives).
  Rule 3 always type-checks; it may view more than the function needs. Pointing into an argument means
  pointing into it and into everything it owns (**into**, §VII.1), so a reshape of anything it owns ends
  the view and any other change of it while the view is used is refused (`[BRW-1]`). A returned view
  that points into any other parameter is refused: `E3063` when that parameter is `owns` or is passed as
  a copy (`[BRW-8]`), whose storage ends with the call, and `E3062` otherwise. A call whose result type
  is `ref mut T` or `ref T` is a place (`first(ref mut xs) += 1`; `counts.entry(k).or_default() += 1`),
  and a name bound to it follows `[BRW-12]` (`r = ref mut first_even(ref mut xs)`). A generator method's
  result is such a view, and it walks what it views: after `g = d.replay()`, the list it walks
  (`d.log`) does not change while `g` will still be used (`[BRW-18]`, `E3020`), however `replay` walks
  it, and any other change of `d` while `g` will still be used (`d.angle = 90.0`) is a change of what a
  view a call gave points into (`[BRW-1]`, `E3021`), unless `-> Generator[int] from log` narrows the
  view to `d.log`.
* `[LT-1a]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **`from`.** `-> T from
  name`, written after the result type on the function's first line, replaces the rule the compiler
  would apply: the result points into exactly the named parameter, or into the named field of `this`
  written bare (`-> StrView from src`). The body may then give only a view of what `from` names, and
  any other is `E3062` ("`next_word` returns a view of `this.buf`, but its first line says `from src`;
  return a view of `src`, or write `-> StrView from buf`"). A named parameter is a source parameter
  (`[LT-1]`) or a `ref mut` parameter; naming a plain `Copy` parameter, or an `owns` parameter that is
  not a view, is `E2031`. A bare field name names any field of `this`, whatever the method does with its
  object (`owns this`, or passed as a copy, `[BRW-8]`): for a field whose type is a view, the result
  points into what the field points into, and the call's view of the object ends with the call; for any
  other field (`from log` with `log: Array[int]`), the result points into that field and what it owns,
  and the object is viewed for as long as the result lives. A result read
  through a `ref mut` field points into `this` as well, so it cannot name the field alone (`E3062`):
  an iterator gives no two changeable items. The field may instead be one whose type is a type
  parameter, with a result whose type names one (`Option[I.Item]`); each instance is checked, as a
  source is (`[LT-1]`, ODR-048): where the instance's field and result are views the result points into
  what the field points into, and where they are not it points into nothing. Naming a field when there
  is no `this`, or a field of neither kind, is `E2031`; a name that is both a parameter and a field of
  `this` is `E2118` ("`src` is both a parameter of `next_word` and a field of `Parser`, so `from src`
  could mean either; rename the parameter: for a view of the field write
  `fn next_word(line: StrView) -> StrView from src:`, for a view of the parameter
  `fn next_word(line: StrView) -> StrView from line:`"). The standard library's iterators that read
  through a read-only field say so on `next`, and its iterator adapters on the iterator they wrap, so
  `for k in m:` and `m.keys()` give views that point into the map (`[CTL-1]`), which a program may keep
  across rounds and after the loop. `from` is needed only where rule 1 or 3 points into more than the
  caller can afford, or to let the result point into a `ref mut` parameter of a `Copy` type:

```ember
fn find_word(haystack: StrView, needle: StrView) -> Option[StrView] from haystack:
    i = haystack.find(needle)?
    return Some(haystack[i..i + needle.len()])
```

* `[LT-3]` String literals, `bytes` literals, `static` items and views of them have the `static`
  region, which outlives everything.
* `[LT-4]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A value made in a memory manager's instance
  (`owns Mesh(points=[0.0, 1.0]) using current`, `[ALC-1]`), and every value that holds one, lives no
  longer than that instance, wherever it is kept: keeping or returning it where it would outlive the
  instance is `E3063` ("`boss` holds a mesh made in `current` (line 12), and `current` ends when
  `load_level` returns, so `boss` cannot be returned; make it in an arena the caller keeps:
  `fn load_level(ref mut arena: LevelArena) -> Enemy:`, with `mesh=owns Mesh(points=[0.0, 1.0]) using
  arena`, and in the caller `current = LevelArena()` and `boss = load_level(ref mut current)`"). A value
  whose manager may have several instances keeps its instance's address, one word, so that its growth
  and its end go back to the instance it came from; that address is a kept `sharedref mut` link to the
  instance (`[LT-46]`): the program may use the instance while values made in it live, and each value's
  growth and end change the instance through it. A manager with one instance (`Global`, `System`) costs
  no word. Arena allocations point into the arena (`[ARN-1]`).
* `[LT-44]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A plain or `ref mut` `Arena`, `FixedArena` or
  `ScopedArena` parameter is a source parameter because it is not `Copy` (`[LT-1]`): a function whose
  only source parameter is one arena returns views that point into it, with no word. `from arena` is
  needed only when the function has other source parameters too.
* `[LT-6]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* Named lifetimes are not part of Ember and will
  not be added. Where a relationship between regions cannot be inferred, the diagnostic names the
  restructuring that expresses it: an owned result, an index instead of a view, a view struct, or
  `from`.
* `[LT-7]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Function types.** Each call through a value or parameter of function
  type `fn(P1, …, Pn) -> R` gets fresh regions for its source parameters (`[LT-1]`). `R` may point into
  them only as `[LT-1]` would allow for a function declared with that first line, and then only for the
  time the caller keeps the arguments. So a callee may lend a function value views of its own locals,
  and a function value may return a view of an argument to its caller:

```ember
fn with_local(f: fn(Span[int]) -> int) -> int:
    tmp = [41]
    return f(tmp)

fn first_of(a: Span[int], b: Span[int], pick: fn(Span[int], Span[int]) -> Span[int]) -> int:
    return pick(a, b)[0]

fn main():
    println(with_local(fn(s) => s[0] + 1))
    xs = [1, 2]
    ys = [3]
    println(first_of(xs, ys, fn(a, b) => a))
```

* `[LT-45]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Kept views.** A struct that holds a view (`ref T`, `ref mut T`,
  `sharedref mut T`, `Span[T]`, `MutSpan[T]`, `StrView`, or a struct that holds one) lives no longer than
  what its view fields point into (`[TYP-34]`); `@view` may say so and is checked (`@view` on a type
  that holds no view is `E2030`: "`@view` on `Point`, which holds no view; remove `@view`"). A value that
  holds views (a local list of views, a struct made by a call) lives no longer than what they point
  into, whoever owns it; keeping or returning it where it would outlive that is `E3063` ("`ws` holds
  views of `players`, so it may not outlive it (returned here); let the watchers keep their players
  alive: write `target: shares mut Player` in `Watcher`,
  `players = [shares mut Player(), shares mut Player()]` in place of line 3 and
  `Watcher(target=shares mut players[r])` in place of `Watcher(target=sharedref mut players[r])` on line
  6; or keep positions: write `target: int` in `Watcher`, `Watcher(target=r)` on line 6, and
  `return (players, ws)` with the result type `(Array[Player], Array[Watcher])`"). A class object is
  never a view: a view field of a class says what it points into, `from <let field>` (a `let` field of
  the same object whose contents live in their own heap block: a `String`, an `Array` or an `owns T`)
  or `from static` (text written in the program; on a struct's field too, which then does not make the
  struct a view). A view field of a class without such a `from`, or with one that names what a view
  cannot point into for the object's life (a field that is not `let`, a fixed array, a struct stored
  inline), is `E2118`: "a `Player` keeps `name` after the text it came from may be gone; to keep its own
  copy write `name: String` and `this.name = String(name)`"; "`words` points into `text`, so `text` must
  never change after `init`; write `let text: String`"; "`pair` is stored inside the object, so moving
  the object moves it; keep it in a block of its own: write the field as `let pair: owns Pair`". A
  `from static` field given a view of anything else is `E3063` ("`kind` holds only text written in the
  program, and `name` comes from the caller; write `this.kind = String(name)` with `kind: String`").
  For a view into a field stored inside the value: E2118 ("`buf` is stored inside the value, so moving the value moves it; keep the text in a `String`, which has a block of its own: write the field as `let buf: String`").
* `[LT-46]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **The three kinds of kept view**, by their word:
  * `ref T` reads; any number of names may view one place.
  * `ref mut T` may change, and it is alone: while its holder is still used, the place is not read or
    changed through any other name (`[BRW-1]`); a second holder is `E3022` ("`p` is lent to
    `cam.target`, a `ref mut` field, until its last use on line 17, and line 16 lends it to `hud.target`
    too; if both may change the player, write `target: sharedref mut Player` in `Camera` and in `Hud`,
    and `sharedref mut p` in place of `ref mut p` on lines 15 and 16").
  * `sharedref mut T` may change, and several holders, and the owner, may name one object. On one thread
    any of them may change it at any time; every view into it ends at a reshape made through any of
    them, and a list in it may not change while a loop walks it, whichever holder reaches it
    (`[BRW-17]`, `[BRW-18]`); on two threads it is changed only under a lock, through `Atomic`, or by a
    reduction from scoped tasks (§XI.3, `[THR-13]`). It is written the same way before a value
    (`Watcher(target=sharedref mut players[r])`), it costs nothing while the program runs, and its
    holders get no noalias (`[BRW-22]`). `sharedref` is always followed by `mut` (`E0114`: "a link that
    only reads may be held by any number of names: write `target: ref Player`; `sharedref` is for a link
    that may change its target: `target: sharedref mut Player`").
* `[LT-47]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **A view put in through `ref mut`.** After a call, a caller's place given
  to a `ref mut` parameter whose value is a view may point into what it pointed into before, or into any
  of the call's other arguments (`[LT-1]`). Inside the callee only such a view may be put there: another
  view argument or a part of one, or text written in the program; a view of the callee's own locals or of
  a temporary is `E3063` ("`best` is the caller's view and lives on after `pick_longer` returns, but
  `mine` ends with `pick_longer`; put a view of what the caller gave there (`best = other`), or return a
  list of your own: `-> Array[int]`"). A use of such a view after one of the call's arguments changed is
  `E3060`.
  Its message: E3060 ("`bag.items.push(k)` (line 15) may move the list that `h.view` points into (`pick` may have put a view of `bag` there on line 13), and `h.view` is used on line 16; use `h.view` before line 15").

### Views with several regions

A struct, enum or tuple holding views (a **view type**, `[TYP-34]`) may hold views of independent
sources. The compiler keeps one region per view field, a **region vector**, and never forces them to be
equal.

```ember
struct Bodies:
    positions: MutSpan[f32]
    velocities: Span[f32]

fn integrate(ref mut b: Bodies, dt: f32):
    for i in 0..b.positions.len():
        b.positions[i] += b.velocities[i] * dt

fn main():
    pos: Array[f32] = [0.0, 1.0]
    vel: Array[f32] = [1.0, 1.0]
    b = Bodies(positions=ref mut pos, velocities=vel)
    integrate(ref mut b, 0.5)
    println(pos)
```

* `[LT-14]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A view type carries a compiler-internal region vector with one slot per view field (fields
  proven to share a source may share a slot). It is never written in source (`[LT-6]`).
* `[LT-16]` Constructing a view value keeps each field's region; it never replaces them with their
  intersection.
* `[LT-17]` **Validity is conjunctive.** A view value is usable only while every region a used field
  needs is valid. A field whose source has ended cannot be used even if other fields are still valid.
* `[LT-18]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Every view field is an ordinary view under `[BRW-1]` to `[BRW-22]`;
  multiple regions add no new aliasing rule and weaken none.
* `[LT-20]` Moving, copying, destructuring, passing and returning a view preserves each field's region.
  Projecting one field carries only that field's region.
* `[LT-21]` Assigning a new view into a field recomputes that field's region; the old source is
  released on that path and the new one constrained. Merges of control flow keep every region that may
  reach a field.
* `[LT-22]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A function returning a view type gets, from its body, a summary of
  which result field points into which parameter (and which parameter fields each call uses,
  `[LT-35]`). Callers use the summary; source never states it. Where the summary would need more than
  the first line allows, the result points into every source parameter (`[LT-1]` rule 3), or into what
  `from` names.
* `[LT-23]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* With `from` on a function returning a multi-region view, every field
  of the result points into what `from` names; a field that points into anything else is `E3062`.
* `[LT-24]` A region slot ends at the last use of its own field, not of the whole value.
* `[LT-25]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A view field may not point into another field of the value that contains it (shape B5).
* `[LT-26]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A view extends no lifetime: constructing, copying or storing it
  counts nothing. A view of an object reached through a link does not keep the object alive either; it
  is checked when compiling not to outlive it (`[RC-5]`).
* `[LT-27]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Different regions never prove that two views do not overlap in
  memory; noalias comes only from a `ref mut` parameter (`[BRW-22]`), `[DSJ-*]` and `[SIMD-3]`.
* `[LT-30]` Regions exist only at compile time: two values of one view type with different regions have
  one layout, one ABI, one symbol and one type identity, so region inference causes no code
  duplication.
* `[LT-34]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A view type whose fields all point into one source behaves exactly as a single-region view.
* `[LT-35]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* For each function that can receive a view value, the compiler knows
  which fields the body may read, write, hand over, return or publish. A call requires only the regions
  of those fields. A call through a function value, or through an interface, `dyn` or virtual method,
  counts every function the program can put there (`[EFF-1]`); where the target is a foreign function,
  every field is assumed used and kept.
* `[LT-36]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Treating the view as a whole (passing it where every field may be used, comparing, hashing
  or formatting it, copying or moving it) requires every region to be valid.
* `[LT-38]` Moving one field out moves only that field's constraint; the remaining fields keep theirs.
* `[LT-39]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* An operation that selects a field by a run-time value (reflection, a
  field descriptor) requires every region it could select; a region it needs that has ended is a
  conflict, `E3021`.
* `[LT-42]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A function value that uses a real variable holding a view, or
  captures a view with `ref`, records the regions of the fields it uses and may not outlive them
  (`E3026`, `[CLO-4]`); one that takes a view into its own state with `owns` requires every region to be
  `static` (`[TYP-15]`).
* `[LT-43]` Region tracking never lets a view survive a `yield` that `[CORO-6]` forbids.

## VII.7 Views over containers: `Span` and `MutSpan`

```ember
fn normalize(ref mut xs: MutSpan[f32]):
    total = xs.iter().sum()
    for ref mut x in xs:
        x /= total

fn main():
    buf: Array[f32] = [1, 2, 3]
    normalize(ref mut buf)
    d = ref mut buf.as_mut_span()
    d[0] = d[2]
    println(buf)
```

* `[SPN-1]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* An `Array[T]`, a `[T; N]` or a `String` converts to `Span[T]` or
  `StrView` where one is expected, and to `MutSpan[T]` where one is expected (a `ref mut` parameter, a
  `ref mut` name, or a `MutSpan`-typed field made with `ref mut`, `[BRW-12]`). **The conversion makes a
  view** of the source place with the ordinary rules: the source is not changed through another name,
  handed over or ended while the view is used (`[BRW-1]`), whether the conversion is written implicitly,
  as `as_span()`/`as_mut_span()`, or produced by a call.
* `[SPN-2]` Indexing a view is bounds-checked; `get(i) -> Option[ref T]` does not panic;
  `unsafe: s.get_unchecked(i)` does not check.
* `[SPN-3]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `Span[T]` is `Copy`; `MutSpan[T]` is not. A name or parameter that
  writes a `MutSpan`'s elements says `ref mut` (`d = ref mut a.as_mut_span()`,
  `fn blend(ref mut dst: MutSpan[float], src: Span[float]):`), and a plain one only reads them
  (`E3023`, `[BRW-15]`). A `MutSpan` is lent to a call with `ref mut` before the argument
  (`blend(ref mut d, s)`), which before a span names its elements, so it may stand before a span made in
  the call (`integrate(ref mut p.as_mut_span(), v.as_span(), 0.5)`); a callee that points such a span
  elsewhere changes only that span, which ends with the line. Where a `Span[T]` is expected, a
  `MutSpan[T]` converts to one: a read-only view, so the `MutSpan` is not written while the `Span` lives
  (`[TYP-5]` rule 6, ODR-116).
* `[SPN-4]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `iter()` on a `Span` or `MutSpan` gives read-only views of its
  elements; `for ref mut x in s:` walks a `MutSpan` a `ref mut` name holds and may change each element
  it is on (`[BRW-18]`). `chunks(n)` and `chunks_mut(n)` give consecutive non-overlapping views of `n`
  elements (the last may be shorter); `n == 0` panics in every profile.
* `[SPN-5]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `split_at(i)` on a `Span` returns two `Span`s; on
  a `MutSpan` it lends the view and returns two disjoint `MutSpan`s. `i > len` panics. (There is no
  separate `split_at_mut`: an `Array` is split for changing as `a.as_mut_span().split_at(i)`.) A
  `MutSpan` also has `get_pair_mut(i, j)` (`[BRW-5]`).
* `[SPN-8]` `as_ptr()` and `as_mut_ptr()` return raw pointers; extracting one is safe, using one needs
  `unsafe`, and extraction extends no region.

## VII.8 Destruction

* `[DRP-1]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `fn drop():` runs exactly once per value, at the end of its life.
  It changes its own object as a given, since it ends it, and its first line says nothing about that.
  Calling it explicitly is `E3070`; `mem.drop(x)` ends a value early.
* `[DRP-2]` Locals drop at the end of their block in reverse declaration order; fields after their
  owner's `drop`, in reverse declaration order; collection elements in index order; the active variant
  of an enum; tuple elements in reverse order.
* `[DRP-3]` Temporaries drop at the end of the statement that created them (`[EXP-4]`).
* `[DRP-4]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* A panic inside `drop` aborts the process (`[PAN-1]`). A `drop` SHOULD
  NOT block; `@noalloc` on a type's `drop` is honoured wherever that type is dropped.
* `[DRP-5]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A `drop` body may not take fields out of `this` (`[EXP-6]`); it uses
  `mem.take(ref mut this.f)` on `Option` or `Default` fields. It makes no owner of its own object
  (`[OBJ-5]`).
* `[DRP-6]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Ending an `owns T` ends the `T` and frees its block; ending a class
  object's owner ends the object (its `drop`, then its fields) and frees its block unless `weakref`
  links still hold it (`[OBJ-3]`); ending a `shares`, `shares mut` or `thread_shared` owner subtracts
  one from the count, and the subtraction that reaches zero ends the value (`[RC-1]`); ending a
  `weakref` link subtracts one from its target's weak count (`[WK-11]`); ending a plain view (`ref`,
  `Span`, `StrView`, a `sharedref mut` link) does nothing; ending a guard (`MutexGuard`, an `RwLock`'s)
  unlocks; and ending a view type ends whatever in it needs ending. Carrying a region and needing drop
  are independent properties (`[TYP-1]`) (ODR-053).
* `[DRP-7]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A value whose `drop` may read through a view it holds must be dropped
  while that view's region is valid. A generic type parameter is assumed to be read by `drop` unless the
  type has no `drop` of its own. Violations are `E3060` (shape B7).
* `[DRP-8]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Ending a value counts as a call of its `drop`.** Anything that may end a
  value whose type has a `drop` (a list cleared, a value replaced, a local ending with its function, a
  function value or an `owns dyn I` value replaced or ended with what its state owns, `[CLO-10]`) makes
  the changes that `drop` makes, wherever a value of its type may end, for every rule that needs them
  (`[EFF-1]`). With `class Enemy:` whose `fn drop():` pushes to `LOG`, `enemies.clear()` inside
  `for line in LOG:` is `E3020` ("`enemies.clear()` (line 5) ends every `Enemy` in `enemies`, and an
  `Enemy`'s `drop` pushes to `LOG` (its line 12), which this loop walks (line 4); clear after the loop:
  move line 5, `enemies.clear()`, below the loop"), and a function that may end an `Enemy` changes `LOG`.
  A `drop` may change things outside its object (a log line, leaving a list).

## VII.9 What a newcomer sees

```ember
class Player:
    name: String
    health: float = 100.0

fn total_health(players: Array[Player]) -> float:      # reads the list
    total = 0.0
    for p in players:
        total += p.health
    return total

fn heal_all(ref mut players: Array[Player]):           # may change the players
    for ref mut p in players:
        p.health = 100.0

fn take(owns players: Array[Player]) -> int:           # takes the list over
    return players.len()

fn main():
    ps: Array[Player] = [Player("a"), Player("b")]
    println(total_health(ps))
    heal_all(ref mut ps)
    n = take(ps)
    println(n)
```

Each name says what it is: `players` in `total_health` reads the caller's list, `ref mut players` in
`heal_all` may change it, and `owns players` in `take` takes it over. The call `heal_all(ref mut ps)`
says that `ps` may be changed; `take(ps)` hands `ps` over, and using `ps` after it is `E3040`,
labelled at the hand-over. Nothing in this program names a lifetime, and nothing in it is checked while
it runs.
---

# Part VIII — Classes, Shared Owners and Links

Classes give Ember the object graphs Python programmers expect (objects with identity, parent links,
observers, objects several places own) with deterministic destruction and no garbage collector. A class
object has one owner unless a line says `shares`, as every value does (`[OWN-1]`); a link that does not
keep its target alive is a `weakref`, which the program sets like any field. Everything here is checked
when compiling, except what §VIII.2 and §VIII.5 name: a count, a count's limit, and the test a `weakref`
link makes when it is opened.

```ember
class Node:
    name: String
    children: Array[Node] = []
    parent: weakref Node = None

    fn add(owns child: Node):
        child.parent = weakref this
        this.children.push(child)

fn main():
    root = Node("root")
    root.add(Node("leaf"))
    for c in root.children:
        if c.parent exists as p:
            println(f"{c.name} -> {p.name}")
        else:
            println("orphan")
```

## VIII.1 Object representation

Every class object, and every value held `shares`, `shares mut` or `thread_shared`, is one heap block
with a header:

```text
offset  size  field
0       4     count   u32   its owners
4       4     type    u32   its type index: its type information, and the interface tables reached
                            through it
8       4     weak    u32   its `weakref` links, plus one for all its owners; present only in a value
                            a `weakref` link may reach
8 or 12 …     base-class fields, then own fields (or the shared value), naturally aligned
```

A `thread_shared` value's header (`[RC-4]`):

```text
offset  size  field
0       4     home    u32   the owners its making thread holds; read and written only by that thread,
                            with plain instructions
4       4     type    u32   its type index
8       4     weak    u32   its `weakref` links, plus one for all its owners; atomic
12      4                   unused
16      8     away    i64   atomic: the owners the other threads hold, times 8, and three marks: handed
                            over (the making thread counts here too), queued (it waits in the making
                            thread's queue), ended
24      8     next    ptr   its place in the making thread's queue
32      …     the shared value, naturally aligned
```

* `[OBJ-1]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* The header is 8 bytes: a 32-bit count and a
  32-bit type index. A value a `weakref` link may reach has a third 32-bit number there, its weak
  count, making 12 bytes: every object of a class family (the classes that share one root base class)
  of which some `weakref` link in the program may name an object, and every shared value of a type some
  `weakref` link may name. A `thread_shared` value's header is 32 bytes (verdict 101): its making
  thread's count of its owners, the type index, the weak count, the other threads' count with its
  marks, and its place in the making thread's queue (`[RC-4]`). Which thread made a value is read from
  the header of the memory chunk its block came from, written once when the chunk is made, never from
  the value. The header is part of the runtime ABI (`[VER-4]`). Foreign code never reads it; it calls
  `ember_rt`. An object carries nothing else for the memory model: no access words, and no flags but a
  `thread_shared` value's three marks.
* `[OBJ-2]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* An owner, a link or a view of a class object
  is one pointer, to offset 0. An object's interface tables are reached through its type index, so a
  `dyn I` value of a class object, and an `Option` of one, is one pointer wide. A bare interface name in
  a type position (`s: Shape`, `Array[Shape]`) does not say who owns the value, and is `E2173`:
  "`Shape` is an interface, so `Array[Shape]` does not say who owns the shapes; say who owns them: write
  `shapes: Array[owns dyn Shape]` in place of line 19 (the list is their only owner), and
  `scene = Scene(shapes=[owns Square(side=2)])` in place of line 22" (with `Array[shares dyn Shape]`,
  other names own them too, and each shape is made `shares`). `dyn I` as a parameter's type is a
  read-only view (`ref mut v: dyn I` may change it).
* `[OBJ-3]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* The weak count starts at 1 on behalf of all owners. When the count
  of owners reaches 0 the object is ended (`[WK-3]`): its `drop` chain and its field drops run, and the
  weak count is decremented; the block is freed when the weak count reaches 0, which for a value no
  `weakref` link may reach is at once.
* `[OBJ-4]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* Objects are allocated through the runtime
  allocator (`[RT-1]`), or from the memory manager the class names with `using` (`[ALC-1]`), except as
  `[OPT-1]` permits.
* `[OBJ-5]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **An ended object is never brought back.** Inside a `drop`, and in
  everything it calls (by their summaries, `[EFF-1]`), no owner is made of the object being ended: an
  owner made from `this` (`shares this`, `shares mut this`, `thread_shared this`) is `E3016`, as storing
  `this` anywhere that outlives the call is (`[CLS-7a]`): "`drop` ends this `Player`; an owner made from
  it would point at a freed object; keep a copy of what you need: `NAMES.push(copy of this.name)`".
  `weakref this` stays allowed: the weak count keeps the block, and opening the link finds the object
  ended (`[WK-3]`). Nothing is checked for it while the program runs.

## VIII.2 Owners and counts

* `[RC-1]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Several owners.** `shares x` makes one more owner of what `x`
  names, on this thread, that reads it; `shares mut x` one more that may also change it; and
  `thread_shared x` one more on any thread (`[OWN-13]`). A value made shared lives in a block of its own
  with the header of `[OBJ-1]` (a class object already does), and its owners are counted: making an
  owner adds one to the count, ending one subtracts one, and the subtraction that reaches zero ends the
  value. A value with one owner is not counted: its owner ends it. **Only a whole value is shared**
  (verdict 103): `shares x`, `shares mut x` and `thread_shared x` are written before a new value, a
  local of this function (which becomes one of the owners) or a name that is already such an owner. A
  place that has one owner and is not a local of this function, a list element (`shares mut players[1]`
  of an `Array[Player]`), a field (`shares this.items`) or a plain parameter (`fn keep(p: Player):
  LIST.push(shares p)`), is `E2122`: "`players[1]` has one owner, the list `players`, and no second
  owner can be made of one element; to let other names own the players, make the list share them from
  the start: write `players = [shares mut Player(), shares mut Player()]` in place of line 15". So a
  value in a one-owner place is ended by that place at once, with no count to test. **A count is checked
  before it rolls over:** before each +1 of an owner count it is compared with its maximum, and at the maximum the
  program stops, in every profile: "too many owners of a `Player` (4,294,967,295)" (`[RT-7]`), as
  Rust's `Rc` and `Arc` stop (a `thread_shared` count stops at the lower limit of `[RC-4]`). That is one
  compare per added owner and no extra memory.
* `[RC-7]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Changing a shared value.** A value made shared is changed by its owners
  that may change it: an owner made with `shares mut`, and the name it was first shared from, which
  keeps what it could do. After `other = shares mut items` (or `other = shares items`), `items` may
  still change the list if it could before, and so may `other`; a `shares` owner only reads it
  (`E3023`, `[OWN-13]`). Any `ref mut` name of it and any holder of a `sharedref mut` link to it may
  change it too. That is safe as it stands, with nothing checked while the program runs: one thread
  runs one line at a time; a list does not change while a loop walks it, through whichever of its names
  (`[BRW-18]`); a view of it is checked against every name that may reach it (`[BRW-17]`); and a
  `shares` value never reaches another thread (`E7015`), which is what `thread_shared`, changed through a
  lock, is for. A `thread_shared` value is never changed directly by any owner, only through `Atomic`,
  `Mutex`, `RwLock`, a channel, or a `guarded by` field under its lock (`E7014`: "`names` is shared
  between threads (line 5), so no owner changes it directly, and line 6 pushes to its list; fill the
  list where the object is made: write `names = thread_shared Names(items=[copy of s])` instead of lines 5
  and 6"). How scoped tasks and threads may reach a shared value or a `sharedref mut` link is §XI.3's.
  An object or a shared value carries no access words and no flags for any of this.
* `[RC-2]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **No count where no owner is made.** No count operation is emitted in
  the cases `[RC-2a]` to `[RC-2e]`; each is tested by counting the count operations in the emitted C.
* `[RC-2a]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Passing a shared value to a parameter that is not `owns`
  (`x: shares T` reads the caller's shared value for the call).
* `[RC-2b]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A view of a shared value or an object: a name for a
  part, a loop name, a name opened from a `shares` link, a parameter. Only `[RC-5]` point 2 counts for a
  view.
* `[RC-2c]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A +1 immediately followed by a -1 of the same count with no call or store
  between.
* `[RC-2d]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* An owner handed over (`b = a`, an `owns` argument, `return a`, a value
  stored into a field from a temporary): it moves, and nothing is counted.
* `[RC-2e]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* The loop names of a `for` over a list of `shares` owners, which are
  views, unless the body makes an owner of one (`shares p`).
* `[RC-3]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* Further removals of count operations are allowed
  only when meaning is preserved (`[PHIL-5]`). A value is ended when its last owner ends as the source
  says (an owner's scope ending, its replacement, `mem.drop`) and never earlier: a removal takes away a
  +1 and a -1 only when it moves no `drop`, no outcome of an `exists as` opening and no foreign release
  across that point. A surviving owner in a field, a collection or a function value's state keeps the
  value alive. The last use of a view ends the view, not the owner (`[BRW-2]`) (ODR-063). `unsafe` code
  that keeps a raw pointer into an object keeps an owner of it alive for as long as it uses the pointer;
  `with h:` and `mem.keep_alive(h)` state that where no Safe use does.
* `[RC-4]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* The counts of a value that is not
  `thread_shared` are changed with plain adds and subtracts, and never cross threads (`E7015`).
  **A `thread_shared` value's owners are counted in two numbers** (verdict 101; biased counting, Choi,
  Shull and Torrellas, 2018):
  1. **Home and away.** The thread that made the value counts the owners it holds in the value's home
     count, with plain adds and subtracts; every other thread counts its owners in the away count, with
     atomic ones (`[RT-8]`). The value lives while the two add up to more than zero. Only the making
     thread reads both.
  2. **The hand-over to the making thread.** When another thread ends an owner the making thread
     counted, the away count goes below zero: that thread puts the value in the making thread's queue,
     marking it queued in the same atomic step as its subtract, and only the making thread then ends
     it. The making thread empties its queue at each of its check points: it adds each value's home
     count into its away count, and ends the value when the sum is zero. A queued value is ended by
     nothing else.
  3. **Check points.** The compiler places them: at every loop's back edge, before every call that may
     block the thread (waiting for a lock, `join`, a channel's receive, a sleep) and when the thread
     ends. A value whose making thread has ended is ended at once by the thread that ends its last
     owner.
  4. **Handed over at once.** A thread that stores an owner of a `thread_shared` value where other
     threads can reach it (into a lock-guarded `thread_shared` container, through a channel, into the
     capture of a thread it spawns or of a callback C keeps; every such place is known when compiling)
     first adds its own count of the value into the away count and marks the value handed over; from
     then on every thread, the making thread included, counts in the away count, and a later end on
     another thread never goes through the queue.
  5. **So a value's end is delayed only** when its last owner ends on a thread that did not make it
     and the value was not handed over at a place of point 4 (it travelled inside another object): it
     is ended at its making thread's next check point. Until then it is intact, and a `weakref` link
     opened on another thread may still find it (`[WK-3]`).

  The weak count of a `thread_shared` value is atomic. The away count, and the weak count, are raised
  with one atomic add and their limit is checked on the value the add returns: when the count before
  the add was 2,147,483,647 or more, the program stops ("too many owners of a `Player`
  (2,147,483,647)"; "too many `weakref` links to a `Player` (2,147,483,647)"). That limit is half the
  count's range, so threads racing past it each stop before the count can roll over, whatever their
  number. The home count, and a count that is not `thread_shared`, keep the exact compare of `[RC-1]`
  and `[WK-11]`.
* `[RC-5]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **A view of an object reached through a link.** A view of an object
  reached through a `shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared` or `weakref` link (a name opened from a link,
  `if cam.target exists as p:`; a view made through a `shares mut` field, `t = ref mut ws[i].target`; a
  parameter `x: shares T`, whose life is the call) must not outlive the object. It is checked when
  compiling, and nothing runs for it while the program runs, except for one kind of object (point 2):
  1. **No line or call in the view's life may end an object of that type**: no write to a place that
     owns one (`T`, `owns T`, `shares T`, `shares mut T`, `thread_shared T`, and a place of a function
     type or of `owns dyn I` whose value's state owns one: `h.keep = fn(): pass` ends the function
     stored there before and the node its `owns n` held), no removal from a list that owns them, no end
     of a local that owns one, and no call that may do so, worked out from its code (`[EFF-1]`):
     `remove_all(ref mut players)`, given the list that owns the players; a call through a function
     value that may run `fn() owns players: players.clear()`; the end of an object whose `drop` may end
     one (`[DRP-8]`). After such a line or call the view is not used (`E3060`: "`remove_all(ref mut
     players)` (line 12) may destroy the player `p` reads (`if cam.target exists as p:`, line 10), and
     `p` is used on line 13; use `p` before line 12, or open the link again after it: write
     `if cam.target exists as q:` above line 13, indent line 13 under it and use `q` there"; "`reset()`
     (line 7) may end `Player` objects (it runs the function stored on line 3, which clears the players
     it owns), and `p` reads one (`if cam.target exists as p:`, line 5) and is used on line 8; use `p`
     before line 7, or open the link again after it: write `if cam.target exists as q:` above line 8,
     indent line 8 under it and use `q` there"; "`h.keep = fn(): pass` (line 11) ends the function
     stored there on line 9 and the node it owns (`owns n`), and `p` reads that node
     (`if w exists as p:`, line 10) and is used on line 12; use `p` before line 11"). A one-owner object
     lent read-only cannot be ended while it is lent.
  2. A view of a `thread_shared` object reached through a `weakref` link holds one count for its life,
     as Rust's `Weak::upgrade` does (`[WK-12]`): another thread may end the last owner at any moment,
     which no line of this thread can be checked against. On the thread that made the object, until it
     is handed over (`[RC-4]` point 4), that count is a plain add to its home count; on another thread,
     one atomic add to its away count.
  Across a call that may change an object of the view's type (worked out from the functions it may run,
  `[EFF-1]`), a read-only view of such an object does not live at all (`[BRW-1]`, `E3021`): a walk
  across such a call keeps a `weakref` link and tests it at every step (`[WK-18]`). Where a call fits
  both this and point 1 (it may change and end the object a name opened from a link reads), the message
  shown is the one whose fix compiles (`[DIA-28]`): point 1's `E3060` where using the name before the
  call, or opening the link again after it, compiles (`println(p.hp)` after `reset()`, which may run
  `fn() owns players: players.clear()`), and `[WK-18]`'s `E3021` for a walk, where every view of the walk
  would need opening again.
* `[RC-6]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `ember inspect` lists every count operation that survives inside a
  loop, with the reason it could not be removed, because a surviving count operation blocks
  vectorisation.

## VIII.3 Changes through several names

An object may be reached through several names: its owner, its `shares` owners, `sharedref mut` and
`weakref` links, views. Every rule of §VII.4 and §VII.5 applies to an object's fields as to a struct
value's; this section says what links add. Nothing is checked while the program runs: an object holds
no access words, and no change of a field begins or ends anything at run time.

* `[EXC-1]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A change of an object's field while a read-only
  view into that field, made through another name that may reach the object, is still used is refused
  when compiling (`E3021`, at the change), and a change that may reshape it ends the view instead
  (`E3060`, at its later use), by `[BRW-1]`'s promise; a change through another name while a `ref mut`
  name of the field is still used is `E3022`. There is no setting that turns these rules off
  (`[PHIL-13]`).
* `[EXC-2]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A read of an object's field through another
  name while a `ref mut` name of that field is still used is `E3021` (`[BRW-1]`).
* `[EXC-3]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Which names may reach one object.** Two paths
  may reach the same object when they lead to objects of one class family (the classes that share one
  root base class) and at least one goes through a link or a kept view, unless the compiler knows they
  differ: different classes, a fresh object, or the line inside `if a is not b:`. A possible overlap the
  compiler cannot rule out is refused (`E3022` for a change, `E3021` for a read), with the test that
  proves them apart as the line to write ("`a` is the only name for its turret while `hit` runs, and
  `t`, opened from `a.target`, may be that turret; write `if t is not a:` above line 20 and indent line
  20 under it").
* `[EXC-19]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Fields are separate places.** A view of one field
  of an object and a change of another field never conflict: `for c in this.children:
  this.log.push(c.name)` is accepted. What a method's call touches is the fields its body touches
  (`[BRW-10]`).
* `[EXC-16]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* Giving a field that owns memory a new value
  (`h.items = []`, `h.name = other`) is a reshape: inside a `for` loop over the same field it is
  `E3020` (`[BRW-18]`), and a view into the old value is not used after it (`E3060`, `[BRW-17]`).
* `[EXC-17]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* Writing a number or a `bool` (a field of a `Copy`
  type) moves and frees nothing, so it is not a reshape and ends no view; a method that writes
  `this.health` through a link that may lead to its own object is allowed (`[EXC-15]`). While a
  read-only view of that field is still used, a write through another name that may reach it is
  `E3021` (`[BRW-1]`). Through a `sharedref mut` link, any holder may write it at any time on one thread
  (`[LT-46]`); such a view gets no alias fact another holder could break (`[SIMD-3]`).
* `[EXC-15]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **A method and its object.** Inside a method its
  object is `this`. What a method does to it is worked out from its body (`[BRW-10]`): a method whose
  body changes `this` may change it, one whose body neither changes nor ends anything of `this` only
  reads it, and `owns this` after the parameters takes the object over. A method that may change its
  object is not called through a name that only reads it (`E3023`: "`heal` changes the player
  (`this.hp += 10`, its line 3), and `p` only reads it; write `for ref mut p in players:` in place of
  line 7"). That a method may change its object promises nothing about other names: the same object may
  be reached and changed through a link while the method runs (a turret aimed at itself:
  `if this.target exists as ref mut t: t.health -= 1`, accepted with no check), so `this` is never the
  only name of its object and is never compiled with noalias (`[BRW-22]`). `[BRW-1]`, `[BRW-17]` and
  `[BRW-18]` keep every view and every walk safe, and a call whose object is part of what the method may
  end before its last use of `this` is `E3031` (`[BRW-21]`). `init` sets the fields of the object it
  builds through `this`, as `[CLS-2]` says.

## VIII.4 Inheritance and dispatch

* `[DSP-1]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A call is dispatched statically when the object's static type is a final class or the
  method is not `virtual`.
* `[DSP-2]` A virtual call loads its slot from the object's type table; slots are assigned in
  declaration order, base first, and an `override` reuses the base's slot.
* `[DSP-3]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A call through a `dyn I` value of a class object finds the
  interface's table through the type index and caches the lookup for repeated calls on one value.
* `[DSP-4]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Kind tests.** A value of an interface type (`dyn I`, `owns dyn I`,
  `shares dyn I`) or of a base class is tested for its kind with `is`: `if s is Circle as c:` runs its
  block when `s` is a `Circle` and names it `c` there; `if s is Circle:` tests without a name; other
  kinds are tested with `elif s is Square as q:` and `else:`, which is how a choice among kinds is
  written (there is no "maybe a `Circle`" value to `match` on). The name is declared with its words, as
  a name opened with `exists as` is (`[BRW-14]`): plain `c` is a read-only view, and since a value
  tested in its place stays a place, `if this.pools[k] is Pool[T] as ref mut pool:` names a view of the
  registry's pool that may change it, where the function may change the place. `is` before a type name
  means "is of this kind"; before a value it means "the same object" (`a is b`, which compares
  addresses) or tests for absence (`x is None`). A test that always passes is `E2036` ("`s` is a
  `Circle` already, so this `if` would always run; to name it write `c = s` in place of the `if` line,
  and use `c` in its block, moved out one level"); a test of a type that does not implement the
  interface or derive from the base class, which can never pass, is `E2037` ("`s` is a `Shape`, which
  can never be a `Path`; remove the test: the `if` line and its block"); a name already in use is
  `E2106` ("`s` already names a value (line 1); `as` declares a new name: write `if s is Circle as c:`,
  and `c.r` for `s.r` in its block"). Each test is one type-id compare.
* `[DSP-6]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Casts.** `cast s as Circle` gives the `Circle` and stops the program if
  `s` is not one, in every profile: "`cast s as Circle` on line 9: `s` is a `Square`, not a `Circle`".
  A cast of a place is a place: the name bound from it is read-only unless written `ref mut`
  (`pool = ref mut cast this.pools[k] as Pool[T]`), and `ref mut` taken through a plain one
  (`return ref mut pool.dense[pool.sparse[e]]`) is `E3027` ("`pool` only reads the pool in `this.pools`,
  so `ref mut pool.dense[...]` cannot be taken through it; name it so it may change:
  `pool = ref mut cast this.pools[k] as Pool[T]`"). Each cast is one type-id compare.
* `[DSP-5]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* With the whole program visible, a virtual call with exactly one
  reachable implementation may become a direct call; `--emit-optimization-report` lists each. What a
  call through a `virtual` or interface method may change, read and end is worked out from every
  override and implementation the program has (`[EFF-1]`).

## VIII.5 `weakref` links, parent links and loops of owners

* `[WK-1]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Ember has no cycle collector: a loop of owners, objects that own each
  other through `shares`, `shares mut` or `thread_shared` fields, through the state of function values
  they hold, or through channel ends, would keep its objects alive for ever. So a loop of owners is
  allowed only where the compiler proves it is opened again before its objects lose their last owner
  from outside, and is otherwise refused (`[WK-6]`); a link back that does not keep its target alive is
  a `weakref` (`[WK-11]`).
* `[WK-11]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **`weakref` links.** `weakref T` is a link that
  does not keep its target alive. Its target lives on its own: a class object, or a value held `shares`
  or `thread_shared`. A link may hold no target (`parent: weakref Node = None`). `weakref x` makes a link
  to what `x` names; before a `weakref` link it makes another link to the same target
  (`a = weakref this.keep`). A `weakref` link is not `Copy`, and `copy of` before one is `E2116`
  (`[OWN-8]`). Every `weakref` link holds one weak count on its target: making one adds one, and its
  end, or giving it another target, subtracts one, as Rust's `Weak` (`[WK-18]` gives the one place a
  proved region keeps the block instead); before each +1 the count is compared with its maximum, and at
  the maximum the program stops, in every profile: "too many `weakref` links to a `Player`
  (4,294,967,295)" (`[RC-4]` for a `thread_shared` target). That count is a number in the target's
  header that no name reads, so making or ending a link is not a change of the target: any name may
  make one (`up = weakref p` from a read-only `p`; `child.parent = weakref this` in a method that
  otherwise changes only `this.children`). Making, ending or opening a link touches the target's
  header, so a scoped task does it only for a `thread_shared` target (§XI.3).
* `[WK-16]` *(new in 0.9.15)* A `weakref` of a part (a field, or an element stored inline), whose target
  does not live on its own, is `E2119`: "a `weakref` link needs an object that lives on its own; link to
  the player: `cam.target = weakref player`". A `weakref` link used as its target without opening it,
  and an object stored into a `weakref` place without `weakref`, are `E2020`: "`cam.target` may be gone;
  open it: `if cam.target exists as p:`"; "`=` alone would hand `player` over; write
  `cam.target = weakref player`".
* `[WK-12]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Opening a link.** A `weakref` link is read by
  opening it with `exists as` (`[GRM-44]`): `if cam.target exists as p:` tests the target's header
  (does the object still live?) and runs its block, with `p` a view of the object, when it does;
  `else:` runs when the link holds nothing or its target is ended. Each opening is one test of the
  header, except a parent-link read proved by `[WK-17]`. For a `thread_shared` target the opening adds
  one owner only to a value that is not ended, so an object another thread is ending is never brought
  back, and the view holds that count for its life (`[RC-5]` point 2): on the making thread, until the
  value is handed over (`[RC-4]` point 4), it tests that the home and away counts add up to more than
  zero and adds one to the home count; on any other thread it is one atomic add to the away count,
  undone when the value is marked ended.
* `[WK-2]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* An object is ended when its count of owners reaches zero, whatever
  `weakref` links remain; those links then find nothing when opened.
* `[WK-3]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **An object is ended the moment its last owner lets it go, before its
  `drop` runs**, as C++'s `weak_ptr` and Rust's `Weak` see it: a `weakref` link opened during its
  `drop`, or during the `drop` of anything it owns (a child's `drop` opening `this.parent` while the
  parent is being ended), finds it ended, so the `if ... exists as p:` block is skipped and the
  half-ended object is never read, nor counted again. Ending the link itself (`this.parent = None`)
  stays allowed: it only subtracts the link's weak count in the target's header, which that count keeps
  in memory. A `thread_shared` value whose last owner ends on a thread that did not make it, and that
  was not handed over, is ended at its making thread's next check point (`[RC-4]` point 5), and its
  `drop` runs there.
* `[WK-13]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A `weakref` link to a value held `shares` names the same block as its
  owners.
* `[WK-14]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Ember's `weakref` and `shares` never convert to or from C++'s
  `std::weak_ptr`/`std::shared_ptr` (`[SEL-2]`).
* `[WK-17]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Parent links.** A parent link is an ordinary `weakref` field that names
  the object owning its holder (`parent: weakref Node`), which the program gives its target like any
  field: `child.parent = weakref this`, then `this.children.push(child)`. A read of one is compiled with
  no header test (a plain load and a test for no link) where the compiler proves its target lives; it
  proves it when both of these hold:
  1. **The link follows ownership.** In the package, every line that gives the field a target,
     `x.parent = weakref o`, is followed in the same function, before `x.parent` is read, by a line that
     puts `x` into a place `o` owns alone (`o.children.push(x)`, `o.left = x`); every line that takes
     such an object out of its place without ending it is followed, before that object's link is read
     (there, or in a function it is given to, by that function's summary), by a line that gives the link
     a target the same way or clears it (`c.parent = None`); no list or field holding such objects is
     handed over, replaced or exchanged whole while it holds them; the objects have one owner (not
     `shares`, not `thread_shared`) and their class has no `drop` method of its own; and no other
     package can change the link or those places (`[EFF-4]`). Then an object's parent owns it, so while
     the object lives its parent lives.
  2. **Nothing ends such an object meanwhile.** No line between the point where the object whose link
     is read is known to live (a view of it) and the read can end an object of the link's target type
     (`[RC-5]` point 1).
  A walk up a tree with views (`cur = ref n`, `while cur.parent exists as p:`, `cur = ref p`) is then
  compiled with no test per step; where condition 1 fails, every read tests.
* `[WK-18]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **A walk across a call that may change nodes holds a link and tests it at
  every step.** When a walk calls a function that may change nodes (`this.on_visit(p)`, where the
  program stores in `on_visit: fn(Node)` a function that removes nodes from their parents' lists, and so
  ends them), no view of a node lives across the call (`[RC-5]`): the walk with views is `E3021`
  ("`this.on_visit(p)` (line 21) may end a `Node` (it may run `prune`, stored on line 40, which removes
  a node from its parent's list), and `p` reads a node and is used again on line 23; walk with a link,
  which may outlive its node: instead of `if leaf exists as n:`, `cur = ref n`, the `while` line and
  `cur = ref p`, write `up = weakref leaf`, then `while up exists as n:`, inside it
  `if n.parent exists as p:` with `up = weakref p` and `this.on_visit(p)`, and `else: break`"), and it
  is written with a `weakref` link, which may outlive its node:

```ember,fragment
up = weakref leaf
while up exists as n:            # the node still lives: call it `n`
    if n.parent exists as p:     # its parent, if it has one
        up = weakref p           # the link now names the parent
        this.on_visit(p)         # may end `p`, or a node above it with everything under it
    else:
        break
```

  The call `this.on_visit(p)` itself compiles when no function the program stores in `on_visit` uses its
  node after a line that may end it; one that does is refused where it is stored (`E3031`, `[BRW-21]`).
  **A walk up a tree stops at the first ended parent**: if the call ends `p`, or a node above it with
  everything under it, the link's target is ended and its block is kept by the link's weak count, so
  the next `while up exists as n:` finds it ended and the walk stops; it never visits an ended node, and
  nothing stops the program. **What it costs**: per step, one test of the node's header
  (`while up exists as n:`) and one move of the link's weak count from the node to its parent
  (`up = weakref p`: a subtract and an add); the read of `n.parent`, between the test and the call, needs
  no header test where `[WK-17]`'s condition 1 holds (its condition 2 holds there). **Where proof removes
  part of it**: when the node's class has no `drop` method of its own and its objects are ones no other
  thread can end (not `thread_shared`, and not reachable from a `thread_shared` value), the walk is
  placed in a **deferred-drop region**: an object whose last owner ends during the walk is ended at
  once, as anywhere: the `drop`s of what it owns run then, in their usual order, so the program prints
  what it would with no region, and it and everything it owns are marked ended; only their blocks'
  memory waits, and is freed when the walk ends
  (one add and one subtract of a per-thread counter per region, nothing per step). A link that lives
  only inside the region and is given only objects that live at that moment (`up = weakref p` from the
  view `p`) then holds no weak count, so each step pays only the header test; the first link of each
  walk, `up = weakref leaf`, keeps its count. A walk over objects another thread may end pays the count
  moves. A walk whose visit function changes no node (every function the program stores in `on_visit`
  only reads its node) keeps its views and pays nothing per step.
* `[WK-5]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **The graph of owners.** The compiler builds a graph of owner edges
  among types, after generic substitution, over the whole program: a field holding a `shares`,
  `shares mut` or `thread_shared` value, or a collection of them; a function value's state, from every
  function the program can put there (`[EFF-1]`); a channel end that its own queue can hold; a
  `Retained[ForeignCallback]` token, to the callback's state, which it keeps for C (`[FFI-23]`). `weakref`
  links, `sharedref mut` links, views and raw pointers are not owner edges. A `let` field, set when its
  object is made, can name only objects that exist already, so it never closes a loop.
* `[WK-6]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **A loop of owners is refused unless it is proved opened.** A line that
  closes a loop of owners (`a.next = Some(shares mut b)` after `b.next` names `a`) is refused, unless the
  compiler proves that the loop is opened again before its objects lose their last owner from outside
  (`E3032`: "this closes a loop of owners (`a` → `b` → `a`) that nothing opens again before `a` and `b`
  end, so neither node is ever freed; open it before the function ends: `b.next = None`, or make the
  link back `weakref`: `next: Option[weakref Node]`") (a deliberate error example, so the block is not compiled):

```ember,ignore
class Node:
    name: String
    next: Option[shares mut Node] = None

fn make_pair():
    a = shares mut Node(name=String("a"))
    b = shares mut Node(name=String("b"))
    a.next = Some(shares mut b)
    b.next = Some(shares mut a)        # refused: nothing opens the loop before `a` and `b` end
```

  The same function with `b.next = None` before `a` and `b` end is accepted. Nothing runs for it while
  the program runs.
* `[WK-7]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **What counts as proof.** Proved: a loop made and opened again in code
  the compiler can follow (the same function, the functions it calls), or opened by its owning object (a
  `clear()` it always calls before its last owner ends). Refused: an opening that depends on what is only
  known while running, and a loop handed out of reach (returned, stored where the compiler cannot follow
  it). The same holds for loops through function values' state, `thread_shared` owners and channel
  ends. A `weakref` link back always works. **When a line may close a loop.** A store of an owner
  (`shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared`, a value that holds one, or a function value whose state owns
  one) into a place of an object may close a loop when the stored value's type can reach the holder's
  type through owner edges (`[WK-5]`); such a line is `E3032` unless the loop it closes is proved opened
  (above) or one of these proves it closes none, and every implementation applies exactly these
  (XVIII.4): (1) the stored value was made in this function, on the line or earlier, and since then no
  owner has been stored into it or into anything it owns but values that themselves meet (1)
  (`root.children.push(shares mut child)` with `child = shares mut Node(...)` made above it: a tree
  built from the top down closes nothing); (2) the holder was made in this function and no owner of it
  has been stored anywhere yet (only this function's locals hold it), so nothing the stored value
  reaches can own it.
* `[WK-15]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `ember run` and `ember test` in the `debug` profile
  report the objects still alive when the program exits, by default; `--no-leak-check` turns the report
  off. In Safe Ember nothing leaks through a loop of owners (`[WK-6]`) and nothing ends without its
  clean-up (`[OWN-2]`), so an object in the report was kept by `unsafe` code (`into_raw()`, `[OWN-12]`)
  or by foreign code.
* `[WK-8]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* The run-time report (`[WK-15]`) lists each group of leaked objects that
  own each other, with its classes and fields, and the link to make `weakref`.
* `[WK-4]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* The report names, for each leaked object on a loop of owners, the
  shortest loop through it as a path of `Type.field` edges and the link to make `weakref` (`L3017`).
* `[WK-9]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `ember explain --cycle <path> <Class[.field]>` explains one class or
  field that can close a loop of owners; `ember inspect --cycle <path>` prints the whole graph. A loop
  through a generic container is shown with its instantiated types, and where no static loop can be
  established the command says so.
* `[CLI-18]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* For both commands `<path>` is a package directory (its manifest and
  imports) or a single `.em` file (`[CLI-4]`), and both analyse exactly the same graph of owners
  (`[WK-5]`), classifying each edge as an owner edge or not and showing the shortest loop when there is
  one.

## VIII.6 Stack promotion

* `[OPT-1]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* When escape analysis proves that no owner,
  link or view of an object, a `weakref` link included, outlives the function that made it, the compiler
  MAY place the object in the function's frame with the same header and run its `drop` at scope end.
