  This cannot be observed: how many times an embedding host's allocation functions (`[FFI-27]`) are
  called is not behaviour.
---

# Part IX — Memory Facilities

## IX.0 Choosing a storage mechanism

The declared type decides storage and lifetime; the compiler never picks between them. This table is
the choice, in the order to try (`[SEL-1]`): a design that reaches for a `class` where a `struct` does
pays a heap allocation and a header for nothing, and one that reaches for `shares` where one owner does
pays a count for nothing.

| Mechanism | Ownership | Aliasing | Destroyed | Reach for it when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `struct`, `enum`, tuple | one owner, handed over by `=` | checked when compiling | when its owner ends | **the default**: data with no identity |
| `Array`, `Map`, `Set`, `String` | one owner, handed over by `=` | checked when compiling | when its owner ends | collections |
| `owns T` | one owner, in a heap block of its own | checked when compiling | when its owner ends | one owner, but it must be in a block of its own: recursion, a large value, `owns dyn I` |
| `class` | one owner unless a line says `shares`; a heap block of its own | checked when compiling | when its last owner ends | the thing has identity (`is`), subclasses, or `weakref` links to it |
| `shares T`, `shares mut T` | several owners on one thread, counted | checked when compiling | when its last owner ends | several places own one value; `shares mut` for owners that change it |
| `thread_shared T` | several owners on any threads, counted for several threads (`[RC-4]`) | changed only through `Atomic`, a lock, a channel or a `guarded by` field | when its last owner ends | the same across threads (`[HEAP-10]`) |
| `weakref T` | none | — | never | back links; observing without keeping alive |
| `sharedref mut T` | none: a view several holders share | checked when compiling | never | several holders change one object they do not own, on one thread (`[LT-46]`) |
| `Arena`, `FixedArena` | region | checked when compiling | all at once | many values with one lifetime: a frame, a parse |
| `Pool[T]` + `Handle[T]` | the pool | handles are plain `Copy` values | the pool decides | resources the program recycles: entities, GPU objects |
| `Cell[T]` | the owner's | replaced whole, never viewed | with the owner | a value set whole, by any name that may change its holder |
| `Mutex[T]`, `RwLock[T]`, `Atomic[T]` | the owner's | synchronised | with the owner | changes shared across threads |

* `[SEL-1]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* The order above is the order to try. `ember inspect --alloc`
  reports the mechanism each declaration uses: every local, parameter and field the program writes,
  by the row its declared type picks, and every struct, enum and class it declares, by its kind. A
  type the table has no row for is reported as what it is: a number, `bool`, `char`, `void` or a
  range type as a `value`; a view (`ref T`, `ref mut T`, a span, `StrView`) or a guard as a `view` of
  another's storage; a function value as a `callable`; a raw pointer as a `raw pointer`. Tuples and
  fixed arrays are the first row's (ODR-108).
* `[SEL-2]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `shares` and `weakref` and C++'s `std::shared_ptr`/`std::weak_ptr`
  (`CppShared`, `CppWeak`) never convert into each other: they use different counts, and conflating
  them frees twice (`E5065`, `[WK-14]`).

## IX.1 The heap types

* `[HEAP-1]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Every heap type allocates through `ember_alloc`/`ember_realloc`/`ember_free`, or
  through the memory manager its type names with `using` (`[ALC-1]`), and carries the `Alloc` effect
  where it allocates.
* `[HEAP-2]` Growable buffers double, from a minimum of four elements; `shrink_to_fit` is explicit.
* `[HEAP-8]` *(new in 0.9.9)* Capacity arithmetic is checked: a requested capacity whose byte size
  overflows `usize`, or exceeds the allocator's limit, panics with `capacity overflow` before any
  allocation. No length or capacity computation in the runtime wraps.
* `[HEAP-9]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* Heap storage for elements of type `T` is aligned to at least
  `align_of[T]()`, whatever that alignment is.
* `owns T`: one owner, in a heap block of its own; it reads, and is changed, as its `T`, with nothing
  written in between. `owns dyn I` holds any implementer of `I` (`[IFC-5]`). The line that makes a value
  for an `owns` place says `owns` before it (`mesh=owns Mesh(points=[0.0])`,
  `left=Some(owns Tree(value=2))`; `E2123` otherwise, `[OWN-10]`), and `owns` on a class type is
  `E2114`, since a class object always has a block of its own. It is not `Copy`, and it is `Clone` when
  `T` is: `copy of` it makes a new block holding a copy of the value, so a struct or enum with an `owns`
  field derives `Clone` (`[STR-5]`). `owns dyn I` is `Clone` when `I` requires it
  (`interface I: Clone:`), copying through the entry `I`'s method table holds for it (`[TYP-22]`). A
  foreign type held `owns` is ended through its contract's destructor (Part XVI).
* `[HEAP-3]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A value with several owners (`shares`, `shares mut`,
  `thread_shared`) lives in one heap block that holds its owner count, and, where `weakref` links may
  reach it, its weak count (`[OBJ-1]`). A class object already has its block, so another owner only
  adds one to its count; any other value is put in a block where it is made shared
  (`count = shares mut Counter()`, `other = shares items`), one allocation. Each added owner is first
  compared with the count's maximum (`[RC-1]`).
* `[HEAP-6]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `shares T`, `shares mut T`, `thread_shared T` and `weakref T` are not
  `Copy`: another owner is made only by a line that says so (`shares x`, `shares mut x`,
  `thread_shared x`), and another link only by `weakref x`, each adding one to a count; `=` from a whole
  name hands the owner or the link over, and its end subtracts one.
* `[HEAP-7]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `weakref T` links to a value that lives on its
  own: a class object, or a value held `shares` or `thread_shared`. A `weakref` of a part (a field, an
  element stored inline) is `E2119` (`[WK-16]`).
* `[HEAP-10]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A `shares` owner, and a `weakref` link to a value
  held `shares`, never reach another thread: their counts are plain memory (`E7015`). Shared ownership
  across threads is `thread_shared T`, whose counts are kept for several threads (its making thread's
  owners with plain instructions, the other threads' owners and the weak count with atomic ones,
  `[RC-4]`); no owner changes a `thread_shared` value directly, only through an `Atomic`, a `Mutex`,
  an `RwLock`, a channel or a `guarded by` field under its lock (`E7014`, Part XI).

## IX.2 Arenas

```ember
@derive(Zeroable)
struct Cmd:
    id: int
    cost: f32

fn build(ref mut frame: Arena, n: int) -> MutSpan[Cmd]:
    cmds = ref mut frame.alloc_zeroed[Cmd](n)   # new memory in `frame`, which `cmds` may write
    for i in 0..n:
        cmds[i].id = i
    return cmds

fn main():
    frame = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)
    cmds = build(ref mut frame, 8)
    println(cmds.len())
    frame.reset()                               # allowed: `cmds` is no longer used
```

* `[ARN-1]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `Arena` is a struct, and not `Copy`. Its `alloc*` methods move the
  arena's cursor, so they are called through a name that may change the arena (its owner, or a
  `ref mut` name or parameter: `fn build(ref mut frame: Arena, n: int)`). Each gives a view of memory
  that no earlier view of the arena reaches, and the views point into the arena's memory, not into its
  cursor: an `alloc*` call ends no earlier view and overlaps none, so many allocations are outstanding at
  once, each a place of its own that a `ref mut` name may write. The views live no longer than the arena
  (`[LT-1]`, `[LT-44]`). `reset()`, `scope()` (`[ARN-6]`) and the arena's end may reuse or free that
  memory: each ends every view into the arena, and a later use of one is `E3060`.
* `[ARN-2]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Values placed with `alloc*` are never dropped one by one, so an
  `alloc*` of a type that needs drop is `E3090`, whose help gives the line with `using`. `Arena` and
  `FixedArena` implement `Allocator` (`[ALC-2]`): a value that needs drop is made in an arena as an
  `owns T using frame`, an `Array[T] using frame` or a class object `using frame` (`[ALC-1]`), whose end
  runs its `drop` and gives its block back to the arena, which frees nothing one by one. There is no
  `alloc_nodrop`.
* `[ARN-3]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `alloc(owns v: T) -> ref mut T` hands `v` over into the arena. `alloc_array[T](n) -> MutSpan[T]` requires `T` not to
  need drop and `T: Default`, and initialises each element with `T.default()` in index order (`E2040`
  without `Default`). `alloc_zeroed[T](n) -> MutSpan[T]` requires `T` not to need drop and
  `T: Zeroable`, and fills with zero bytes. Neither stands in for the other: a `Zeroable` type's
  `alloc_array` still calls its `default`, and an implementation fills with zeros instead only where
  that is the same (a scalar's standard `Default`) (ODR-064). `alloc_uninit[T](n) ->
  MutSpan[MaybeUninit[T]]` initialises nothing.
* `[ARN-4]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A growing `Arena` carries `Alloc` on its growth path. `FixedArena`
  (made by `Arena.fixed(ref mut buffer)` from a `MutSpan[u8]`, which it then holds as a kept `ref mut`
  view, `[LT-45]`, or by `FixedArena.with_capacity(n)` at start-up) never grows, carries no `Alloc` on
  allocation, and panics on exhaustion (`try_alloc` returns `Option`). `FixedArena` is the arena for
  `@noalloc` code.
* `[ARN-5]` `ArenaArray[T]` and `ArenaMap[K, V]` are fixed-capacity containers whose storage is taken
  from an arena once, at construction; they never grow or move, so views of their elements stay valid
  while the element and the arena do. Adding past capacity returns `Err(CapacityError.Full)` and changes
  nothing. Their elements, keys and values must not need drop. They live in `std.collections` and are
  not in the prelude.
* `[ARN-5c]` `ArenaArray[T]` provides `len`, `capacity`, `is_empty`, `get(i) -> Option[ref T]`,
  `get_mut`, `push(v) -> Result[void, CapacityError]`, `insert(i, v) -> Result[void, CapacityError]`,
  `remove(i) -> Option[T]`, `clear`, `iter` and `iter_mut` (in index order); indices follow the `Array`
  rules.
* `[ARN-5d]` `ArenaMap[K, V]` (with `K: Eq + Hash`) provides `len`, `capacity`, `is_empty`, `get`,
  `get_mut`, `insert(k, v) -> Result[Option[V], CapacityError]` (replacing returns the old value),
  `remove`, `contains_key`, `clear` and `iter`, which follows insertion order like `Map` (`[STD-11]`).
* `[ARN-5g]` No operation of either container touches the arena after construction: nothing grows,
  moves the arena's cursor or allocates elsewhere.
* `[ARN-6]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `arena.scope() -> ScopedArena` is called through a name that may change the arena, and the
  `ScopedArena` holds a `ref mut` view of it for the scope's life (`[LT-46]`); `with s = frame.scope():`
  allocates from `s` and releases everything at the block's end, last in first out. Using the parent
  while a scope is live is `E3096`, whose help is to allocate from the scope. Scopes nest: `s.scope()`
  opens one inside another.
* `[ARN-7]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* No operation lowers an arena's allocation pointer or reuses its bytes
  while a view into it is used: every such operation ends every view into the arena (`[ARN-1]`), and
  while a value made `using` the arena lives, the arena is changed only through its `Allocator` methods
  (`[ALC-5]`).
* `[ARN-8]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `MaybeUninit[T]` has the size and alignment of `T` and does not claim
  to hold a valid `T`; ending it never ends a `T`. `MaybeUninit[T].uninit()` makes one;
  `write(owns v: T) -> ref mut T` stores without ending the bytes there before;
  `unsafe fn assume_init() owns this -> T` asserts initialisation. `MutSpan[MaybeUninit[T]]` has
  `write_at(i, owns v: T)` and `unsafe fn assume_init() owns this -> MutSpan[T]`. There is no other
  conversion. A `MaybeUninit` never runs its value's clean-up, so for a `T` that needs drop, `uninit()`,
  `write` and `write_at` are `unsafe` operations (`[UNS-1]`), and outside `unsafe:` each is `E3100`
  ("`MaybeUninit` never runs a `Player`'s clean-up, so a value written into it may never be freed;
  write it inside `unsafe:`, or keep the value in an `Option[shares Player]`"); for a `T` with nothing
  to drop they stay safe.
* `[ARN-10]` A panic inside `T.default()` during `alloc_array` aborts (`[PAN-1]`); no partially
  initialised span becomes reachable.
* `[ARN-11]` `Zeroable` is an `unsafe` marker: all-zero bytes are a valid `T`. The scalars, raw
  pointers, a range including zero, and tuples and fixed arrays of `Zeroable` elements are; a struct
  is when it declares `@derive(Zeroable)`, which the compiler proves field by field (`E2080`), since
  only its author can vouch for its invariants (a `NonZero`'s field is an integer). A `ref`, a range
  excluding zero, or an enum whose zero discriminant is invalid is never `Zeroable`. `T: Zeroable` is
  a bound a generic function may state (`alloc_zeroed`, `mem.zeroed`). Being `Zeroable` never changes
  what `alloc_array` does (`[ARN-3]`).

## IX.3 Memory managers: `using` and `Allocator`

```ember
struct Mesh:
    points: Array[float]

struct Enemy:
    hp: int
    mesh: owns Mesh using Arena

fn main():
    level = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)
    boss = Enemy(hp=500, mesh=owns Mesh(points=[0.0, 1.0]) using level)
    println(boss.mesh.points.len())
```

* `[ALC-1]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **The place names the kind, the making line names the instance.**
  `using A` after a type whose value has heap memory of its own (an `owns`, `shares`, `shares mut` or
  `thread_shared` value, a class object, an `Array`, `Map` or `Set`) names the kind of memory manager
  that memory comes from, a type implementing `Allocator`: `mesh: owns Mesh using LevelArena`,
  `names: Array[String] using LevelArena`, `Map[K, V, H] using A`, `Set[T, H] using A`. Without `using`,
  it comes from the built-in manager, `Global`. The line that makes such a value names the instance
  after the value: `boss = Enemy(hp=500, mesh=owns Mesh(points=[0.0, 1.0]) using current)` takes the
  mesh's block from the arena `current` by calling `current.allocate(…)`; a class object is made
  `Enemy(hp=5) using current`, a list `[0.0, 1.0] using current`, and `Array.new_in(current)` makes an
  empty one. A manager type with no fields has one instance (`Global`, `System`, and any such type a
  program declares): it needs none on the making line, and its values keep no instance word; every
  other manager type may have several instances. Checked
  when compiling: the instance is of the kind the place names, and a value given to a `using A` place
  was made in an instance of `A` (`E2020`: "`mesh` takes its memory from a `LevelArena`
  (`mesh: owns Mesh using LevelArena`), and this `Mesh` comes from the built-in manager; say which
  arena: `mesh=owns Mesh(points=[0.0, 1.0]) using current`"); a value made in an instance, and every
  value that holds one, lives no longer than that instance (`E3063`, `[LT-4]`); `using` after any other
  type is `E2114` ("an `int` has no memory of its own to take from `LevelArena`; remove `using`").
  `using` names where that value's own memory comes from; what the value holds comes from where its own
  fields' types say (the `points` list of that `Mesh` from the built-in manager). A value whose manager
  may have several instances keeps its instance's address, one word, so that its growth and its end go
  back to the instance it came from (`[LT-4]`). An allocator type parameter is not Ember: `Box[T, A]` and
  `Array[T, A]` are `E1010`, whose help gives `owns T using A` and `Array[T] using A`.
* `[ALC-2]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `std.mem` declares `pub unsafe interface Allocator` with
  `fn allocate(layout: Layout) -> *mut u8` (null on failure),
  `unsafe fn deallocate(p: *mut u8, layout: Layout)` and
  `unsafe fn reallocate(p: *mut u8, old: Layout, new_size: usize) -> *mut u8`.
  Giving memory back, or moving it, is unsafe, since Ember may still use it and a wrong `Layout` is
  undefined in C: a program's own call is made inside `unsafe:` (`E3100`: "`deallocate` gives memory
  back that Ember may still use, and a wrong `Layout` is undefined in C; write it inside `unsafe:` with a
  `# SAFETY:` note"), and the calls the compiler makes for `using` values are its own. `Layout` holds
  `size: usize` and `align: usize`, both `pub(read)`; its constructor `Layout(size, align)` checks that
  `align` is a power of two and that `size` rounded up to a multiple of `align` fits in an `isize`, and
  panics (`invalid Layout`) otherwise, so no other `Layout` exists. `Global` is the package's configured
  allocator (the one `[ALC-3]` names, else the platform's), so an `Array[T]` never bypasses it; `System`
  is the platform's, which a global allocator may wrap (a counting or tracing allocator delegates to
  `System()`). An allocator that delegates to `Global` from inside the global allocator recurses.
  Implementing `Allocator` is `unsafe` (`unsafe extend A implements Allocator:`, `[TYP-43]`): the
  implementer promises valid, aligned, unaliased memory, which stays valid until it is given back or the
  instance ends.
* `[ALC-3]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* A binary package may replace the global allocator with
  `[build] global_allocator = "module.NAME"` naming a `static` whose type implements `Allocator`; an
  embedding host may pass allocation functions to `ember_rt_init` (`[FFI-27]`).
* `[ALC-4]` Allocation failure in a standard container panics (`out of memory`). `try_reserve` and
  `try_push` report it as a value.
* `[ALC-5]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **An instance stays as its values need it.** While a value made in a memory
  manager's instance lives, the instance is changed only by what allocates from it and gives blocks back
  to it: the `Allocator` methods that value's growth and end call, the making of other values in it, and
  an `Arena`'s `alloc*` (`[ARN-1]`), none of which touches a block already given out. Reading it stays
  allowed (`current.made`); any other change, through any name, is
  `E3021` ("`frame.reset()` (line 26) changes the arena `names` was made in (line 25), and `names` still
  lives; end it first: write `mem.drop(names)` above line 26"). So no safe method of a memory manager
  rewinds it, frees it or gives its bytes out again under a value made in it.

## IX.4 Raw pointers and `unsafe`

```ember
@safety("`p` points to four readable bytes")
unsafe fn read_u32_le(p: *u8) -> u32:
    # SAFETY: the caller makes `p` point to four readable bytes, as this function's @safety says
    unsafe:
        return (p.read() as u32) | ((p.add(1).read() as u32) << 8) | ((p.add(2).read() as u32) << 16) | ((p.add(3).read() as u32) << 24)

fn parse(data: Span[u8]) -> Option[u32]:
    if data.len() < 4:
        return None
    # SAFETY: the length check above guarantees four readable bytes
    unsafe:
        return Some(read_u32_le(data.as_ptr()))
```

* `[UNS-1]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* An `unsafe` context is required to: dereference, read or write
  through `*T`/`*mut T`; offset a pointer; cast between pointers or pointers and integers; call an
  `unsafe fn` (`Allocator.deallocate` and `reallocate` among them, `[ALC-2]`), or through a value of an
  `unsafe` callable type (`[FN-6]`); call an `extern` function without a verified contract (Part XVI);
  access a foreign `static mut` (`[STA-1]`); `transmute`; call `get_unchecked`, `assume_init` or
  `assume_disjoint`; give an object to C with `into_raw()` (`[OWN-12]`); make or write a `MaybeUninit`
  of a type that needs drop (`[ARN-8]`); implement an `unsafe` interface, or declare `Send` by hand
  (`unsafe extend T implements Send:`, `[TYP-43]`). Each of these outside an `unsafe` block is `E3100`,
  whose message says what the code must vouch for and gives the block to write ("`read_u32_le(buf.as_ptr())`
  (line 9) calls an `unsafe fn`, whose callers must make true what its `@safety` says; put line 9 in an
  `unsafe:` block with a `# SAFETY:` note saying why that holds here: above line 9 write `# SAFETY:` and
  the reason, then `unsafe:`, and indent line 9 under it").
* `[UNS-2]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `unsafe` permits exactly those operations. It does not turn off the checks of Parts VII
  and VIII, bounds checks on safe types, overflow checks or type checking.
* `[UNS-3]` `L3010` reports an `unsafe` block containing statements that need no `unsafe`.
* `[UNS-4]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Unsafe code MUST uphold what safe code assumes: every view is
  non-null, aligned, points to a live initialised value of its type, and is used as its word allows (a
  `ref mut` name is the only name of its place while it is used, a `ref mut` parameter's place is
  reached by no other name, and what a read-only view reads does not change while it is used,
  `[BRW-1]`, `[BRW-22]`); every view's length is within its allocation; every class object has a
  correct header, and every owner and every `weakref` link of it is counted there, so unsafe code never
  makes or ends an owner or a link without its count (`[OBJ-1]`); every `StrView` is UTF-8; every value
  is valid for its type (`bool`, `char`, range types, enums); `Send` and `ThreadShared` are respected. A
  raw pointer made from a view is not used after the view's last use, nor after what it points into is
  reshaped or ended.
* `[UNS-5]` `std.mem` provides `Volatile[*T]` (volatile reads and writes), `transmute[A, B]`,
  `copy_nonoverlapping`, `zeroed[T]()` (requires
  `T: Zeroable`) and `MaybeUninit`.
* `[UNS-6]` Inline assembly is `unsafe asm("…", …)` on toolchains that support it and `E5090`
  otherwise.
* `[UNS-7]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Every `unsafe fn` carries `@safety("…")` stating what its callers must
  make true; without it, `L3015` ("`read_u32_le` is an `unsafe fn` that reads through the raw pointer
  `p`, and nothing says what its callers must make true for that; say it above the function:
  `@safety("...")`, with what `p` must point to"). It is the declaration's only note: a `# SAFETY:` note
  on an `unsafe fn` line is `W3013` ("`read_u32_le` says what its callers must make true with
  `@safety`; a `# SAFETY:` note says why one block is sound and goes above each `unsafe:` block inside
  it: remove this line"). The standard library carries `@safety` on every unsafe function it exports.
* `[UNS-8]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* Every `unsafe:` block, and every `unsafe`
  implementation (`unsafe extend`, `unsafe extern`, `unsafe overlay`), carries a safety note
  (`[LEX-23]`) saying why the code is sound: `# SAFETY: …` or `# SAFETY(category): …` on the line
  before it or at the end of its first line. Without one, `W3012`. `ember tcb` lists every block with
  its note, its category and the obligations of the unsafe functions it calls.
* `[UNS-10]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `UnsafeCell[T]` (in `std.mem`) is the primitive beneath `Cell`,
  `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Atomic` and `Once`: `UnsafeCell(v)`, `unsafe fn get() -> *mut T`,
  `fn into_inner() owns this -> T`. It hands out no safe view, checks nothing, is never `Copy` and never
  `ThreadShared` (it is `Send` when `T` is), and is refused in `@no_alias_checks` code (`E3105`).
  Diagnostics never suggest it.
* `[UNS-10a]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `UnsafeCell` suspends no rule globally: the checks of Parts VII and VIII, region, type
  and bounds checking all still apply around it. Unsafe code may break the aliasing rules inside an
  abstraction built on it, and must never let a conflicting view escape into Safe Ember.
* `[UNS-11]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Only inside `unsafe`.** Anything that can break a safety promise
  (misuse memory, race, leak, skip a promised check, or reach memory the rules cannot see) is possible
  only inside an `unsafe` block, and no switch turns a safety check off, in any build or profile:
  `@no_runtime_checks` is not Ember (`E0104`: "there is no switch that turns safety checks off, in any
  build; to forbid run-time alias checks here write `@no_alias_checks`; to skip one bounds check you
  have proved, write `xs.get_unchecked(i)` inside `unsafe:` with a `# SAFETY:` note"). `unsafe` is one
  word with one meaning by position: before a declaration (`unsafe fn`, `unsafe interface`, an
  `unsafe fn(…)` type) it says that whoever uses it must vouch, with `@safety` saying what they must make
  true (`[UNS-7]`); before a block or an implementation (`unsafe:`, `unsafe extend`, `unsafe extern`,
  `unsafe overlay`) it says that this code vouches, with `# SAFETY:` saying why (`[UNS-8]`).
* `[UNS-12]` *(new in 0.9.15)* An `unsafe fn` body is not itself an `unsafe` context: each unsafe
  operation in it sits in an `unsafe:` block of its own, with its note, and one outside such a block is
  `E3100` ("`read_u32_le` is an `unsafe fn`, which says its callers must vouch; the reads through `p` on
  line 4 are this function's own unsafe steps, and nothing says why they are sound; put line 4 in an
  `unsafe:` block with a `# SAFETY:` note saying why the read is safe: above line 4 write `# SAFETY:` and
  the reason, then `unsafe:`, and indent line 4 under it").

## IX.5 Layout

* `[LAY-2]` *(new in 0.9.9)* Layout attributes change layout exactly as stated, in every profile and on
  every backend, and are never ignored (`[ATT-6]`):
  * `@layout(c)` — the target C ABI layout (the default for every struct, `[TYP-11]`);
  * `@packed` — no padding; unaligned fields are read and written by byte copies; taking a reference
    to one is `E2170`;
  * `@align(N)` — raises the type's alignment to `N` (a power of two up to 4096); `size_of` becomes a
    multiple of `N`, and every place and heap buffer holding the type honours it (`[HEAP-9]`);
  * `@repr(u8|u16|u32|u64|i8|i16|i32|i64)` — an enum's discriminant type; it is not written on a
    struct (`E0104`, ODR-139).

  `@packed` and `@align(N)` are not written on one type, and a `@packed` type holds no field whose
  type states an alignment with `@align`: no padding and a size that is a multiple of `N` cannot
  both hold, so either is `E0104` (ODR-138). A SIMD vector states its alignment too (it is aligned
  to its size, `[SIMD-1]`), so a `@packed` type holding one is `E0104` as well (ODR-157). `@align(N)`
  on an enum without payloads raises its alignment and rounds its size up like any other type's.
* `size_of[T]()`, `align_of[T]()` and `offset_of[T](field)` are compile-time functions.

## IX.6 Handles and pools

```ember
from std.collections import Pool, Handle

struct Texture:
    width: int
    height: int

fn main():
    pool = Pool[Texture]()
    h = pool.insert(Texture(width=64, height=64))
    println(pool.get(h).is_some())
    pool.remove(h)
    println(pool.get(h).is_some())        # stale handle: None
```

* `[HND-1]` A `Handle[T]` is a plain `Copy` value (index and generation). Every lookup compares the
  generation, in every profile, and a stale handle yields `None` (or panics in `pool[h]`).
  `unsafe: pool.get_unchecked(h)` skips the comparison.
* `[HND-2]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* `Handle[T]` is a `u64`: 32 bits of index and 32 of generation.
  `Pool[T, Bits]` may narrow it (`Pool[T, Split20]` gives a 20-bit index and a 12-bit generation in a
  `u32`).
* `[HND-3]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A slot whose generation is exhausted is retired and never reused, so an old handle can never
  become valid again. A retired slot's memory stays with the pool until the pool ends: a pool keeps one
  retired slot for each slot reused as many times as its generation can count (with `Split20`, one for
  every 4,096 reuses of a slot), a bounded cost that keeps that promise. When every slot is retired or
  live, `insert` panics and `try_insert` returns `Err(CapacityError.Full)`.

## IX.7 `Cell`, and changes checked when compiling

```ember
struct Sprite:
    frame: Cell[int]

fn advance(ref mut s: Sprite):          # setting a `Cell` needs a name that may change its holder
    s.frame.set(s.frame.get() + 1)

struct Scene:
    entities: Array[int] = []

    fn add(e: int):
        this.entities.push(e)

fn main():
    s = Sprite(frame=Cell(0))
    advance(ref mut s)
    scene = Scene()
    scene.add(7)
    println(s.frame.get(), scene.entities.len())
```

* `[CELL-1]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `Cell[T]` holds a `T` that is replaced whole: `Cell(v)`, `set(v)`,
  `replace(v) -> T`, `take() -> T` (for `T: Default`), `into_inner()`, `get() -> T` for `T: Copy`, and
  `update(f)` for `T: Copy` or `T: Default`. Setting it is a change of the place that holds it, made
  through a name that may change that place: a `ref mut` name, `this` in a method called through such a
  name, or an owner of a `shares mut` value (through a plain name, `E3023`, `[BRW-15]`). `set` and
  `replace` store the new value before dropping the old one, since the old value's `drop` may read the
  cell.
* `[CELL-2]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `Cell` never hands out a view of its contents, so it needs no run-time check; `get` is
  a load and `set` a store, with the count changes of any owner or link in the value (`[HEAP-6]`).
* `[CELL-3]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `Cell[T]` is not `ThreadShared`; it is `Send` if `T` is.
* `[CELL-4]` `Cell[T]` is `Copy` when `T` is.
* `[CELL-13]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **No change is checked while the program runs.** Every change is made
  through a name that may make it, and the checks of Parts VII and VIII are made when compiling: no value
  carries a borrow flag or an access word. A value several owners change on one thread is held
  `shares mut` (`[RC-7]`); a value threads share and change is `thread_shared`, with an `Atomic`, a
  `Mutex`, an `RwLock` or `guarded by` fields (Part XI); a field a method changes is changed through
  `this` (`[EXC-15]`). `RefCell`, `Ref`, `RefMut`, `borrow` and `borrow_mut` are not Ember (`E1010`:
  "`RefCell` is not part of Ember; write the field plainly, `entities: Array[int]`, and change it in a
  method: `fn add(e: int):` with the body `this.entities.push(e)`; for a scene several objects own and
  change, make it once, `s = Scene(entities=[])`, write the field that keeps it in each owner as
  `scene: shares mut Scene`, and give each owner its share where it is made, for example
  `Panel(scene=shares mut s)`").

## IX.8 Establishing disjointness

When two views come from sources the compiler cannot tell apart (two values of one map, two lists
reached through links), and the structural ways (`split_at`, `chunks_mut`, `get_pair_mut`,
`if i != j:`, SoA columns) do not apply:

```ember
from std.mem import assert_disjoint, check_disjoint

fn blend(ref mut dst: MutSpan[float], src: Span[float]):
    for i in 0..dst.len():
        dst[i] = dst[i] * 0.5 + src[i] * 0.5

fn mix(ref mut tracks: Map[String, Array[float]], dst_name: StrView, src_name: StrView):
    d = ref mut tracks[dst_name].as_mut_span()
    s = tracks[src_name].as_span()
    assert_disjoint(d, s)          # stops the program if the two names are one track
    blend(ref mut d, s)

fn mix_any(ref mut tracks: Map[String, Array[float]], dst_name: StrView, src_name: StrView):
    d = ref mut tracks[dst_name].as_mut_span()
    s = tracks[src_name].as_span()
    match check_disjoint(d, s):
        Ok(_):
            blend(ref mut d, s)
        Err(_):
            pass                   # one track: blending it with itself leaves it as it is
```

* `[DSJ-1]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `check_disjoint(a, b) -> Result[void, void]`
  compares the two views' address ranges, and gives `Ok(())` when they do not overlap and `Err(())`
  when they do: two comparisons. It reads both views and takes neither (`[FN-1]`), so they stay usable
  after it. Its result is `@must_use`: an unused one is `W2190` ("to stop when they overlap, write
  `assert_disjoint(d, s)`, with `from std.mem import assert_disjoint` at the top; to handle both cases,
  write `match check_disjoint(d, s):`"). In its `Ok` branch the two names are known not to overlap, as
  inside `if i != j:`.
* `[DSJ-2]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* The fact belongs to the two names, not to a program point: from
  `assert_disjoint`, after the call; from `check_disjoint`, inside its `Ok` branch. Giving either name
  another value (`d = ref mut other.as_mut_span()`) drops it.
* `[DSJ-3]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Where the fact holds, the two names are treated as not overlapping,
  so they may be given to one call where one of them is changeable (`[BRW-11]`), and the backend marks
  them `restrict`/`noalias` (`[SIMD-3]`).
* `[DSJ-4]` It applies to `Span`, `MutSpan`, `SoA` columns and arena views; two single-object
  references are `E3095`.
* `[DSJ-5]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `assert_disjoint(a, b)` makes the same comparison and stops the
  program if the views overlap, saying where and which names: "`assert_disjoint(d, s)` on line 11: the
  two spans overlap (`dst_name` and `src_name` name one track)". Both forms record a
  `RuntimeCheck(Aliasing)` site whose reason is `establishes_static_fact` (`[EFF-11]`), unless the
  compiler already knows the ranges are disjoint, in which case no comparison is emitted.
* `[DSJ-6]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `check_disjoint` and `assert_disjoint` are usable in `@noalloc` and
  `@nosync` code. They are the one run-time alias check there is, so inside `@no_alias_checks` each is
  `E4030` ("`mix` is `@no_alias_checks`, and `assert_disjoint(d, s)` (line 18) compares the two spans
  while running; blend from a copy, which needs no check: instead of lines 16 to 19 write
  `old = copy of tracks[src_name]` and `blend(ref mut tracks[dst_name].as_mut_span(), old.as_span())`,
  or remove `@no_alias_checks`", `[EFF-12]`).
* `[DSJ-7]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `assume_disjoint(a, b)`, an `unsafe fn`, gives the two names the fact
  without checking; violating it is undefined behaviour.
* `[DSJ-8]` There is no form that checks in one profile and assumes in another (`[PHIL-13]`).
* `[DSJ-9]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `check_disjoint_all(v1, …, vn)` and `assert_disjoint_all(v1, …, vn)`
  handle 2 to 8 views pairwise, as `check_disjoint` and `assert_disjoint` do.
* `[DSJ-10]` *(new in 0.9.15)* Making a view and comparing two address ranges read no element: in `mix`
  above, `s = tracks[src_name].as_span()` and `assert_disjoint(d, s)` are allowed while `d`, a `ref mut`
  name of a list's elements, is in use, and the first element read through `s`, in `blend`, comes after
  the two are proved apart. A read of an element through `s` before the proof is `E3021` (`[BRW-1]`).
---

# Part X — Effects, Contracts, Determinism and Cost

## X.1 Effects

The compiler infers, for every function, an **effect set** drawn from:

| Effect | Introduced by |
|---|---|
| `Alloc` | a heap allocation: constructing an allocating type (a class object, a value put in its own block by `owns`, `shares` or `thread_shared`), container growth, an allocating literal or f-string, a function value's state placed on the heap (`[CLO-10]`), arena growth |
| `Sync` | an atomic read-modify-write stronger than relaxed, a lock, a channel operation, thread spawn or join, making or ending a `thread_shared` owner or a `weakref` link to a `thread_shared` value, and opening such a link (the view it gives holds an atomic count) |
| `Lock` | acquiring a `Mutex`/`RwLock` (including `try_lock`), or holding a `Lock` with `with x.lock:` |
| `Block` | an operation that may wait: a blocking lock (`with x.lock:` included), `join` and the end of a `with scope` block, `sleep`, a blocking receive or read |
| `Io` | file, socket and console operations |
| `Panic(Explicit)` | `panic`, `assert*` (`assert_disjoint` included), `unwrap`, `expect`, `todo`, `unreachable`, `cast x as T`, allocation failure |
| `RuntimeCheck(k)` | a safety check the compiler emitted rather than proved away, for `k ∈ {Aliasing, Bounds, Stale, Arithmetic}` |
| `Unsafe` | the body contains `unsafe` or the function is `unsafe fn` |
| `FFI` | a call to an `extern` function |
| `Nondet` | a result that may differ between runs or machines (`[DET-2]`) |

* `[EFF-1]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Effects, and the function's **summary** (what it may change, read and
  end, `[EFF-24]`), are computed from each function's body and its callees', over the call graph, with
  recursive groups taking the union of their members. An operation's effects are its own and those of
  everything it runs where it runs: the methods and function values it calls (a `Display` a formatter
  invokes, a function an adapter applies), the copies, count changes and drops it performs (ending an
  object counts as a call of its `drop`, `[DRP-8]`), and the argument and default expressions it
  evaluates. Calling a generator runs none of its body; each `next` carries the effects of the body up
  to the next `yield`, and dropping a suspended one those of the drops it performs (ODR-057).
* `[EFF-2]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A call through a function value contributes the
  effects of every function the program can put there. For a type parameter bounded by a function type
  (`[F: fn(Item)]` above `fn for_each(owns f: F) owns this:`) that is the function given, per instance.
  For a parameter, field, list element or local of a function type, it is every lambda and named
  function stored into that type anywhere in the program, a library's included. For an interface, `dyn`
  or `virtual` method, it is every implementation and override the program has. A foreign function
  pointer (`extern "C" fn`) contributes the effects its type declares, and all effects if none are
  declared. A contract is written on a function type above a `type` line that names one (verdict 106):
  `@noalloc` above `type Handler = fn()`; every function stored into a place of that type is checked
  against it, with the contract's code, and a call through such a place has no effect the contract
  excludes. An interface method may declare contracts; its implementations MUST satisfy
  them (`E4010`).
* `[EFF-3]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* An `extern` function carries the effects its contract declares
  (`@ffi(effects=[…])`), `FFI` at least. What a call of one may change through the callbacks C keeps is
  `[EFF-26]`'s.
* `[EFF-4]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Effects and summaries are part of a function's interface.** Inside a
  package they are used freely. Across a package's edge, a fact for which a word exists counts only as
  written (a `pub` function's bounds, `E2040`), and every other worked-out fact is recorded in the
  package's interface file: each function's effect set and summary (`[EFF-24]`), with the chains of
  calls that messages name; the effects of the scoped tasks it starts; and the function values the
  package stores into a function type and the callbacks it hands to C, which a program that uses the
  package counts wherever such a value is called and at every foreign call (`[EFF-26]`). A change to any
  of them is reported as an interface change and re-checks every caller: an edit inside one function,
  or a library update (two lines of a function swapped, so that a use of a parameter falls below a line
  that clears what it views), can make a line elsewhere stop compiling, and the message names the chain
  of calls. A parent link proves itself (Part VIII) only when no other package can change it or the
  places that own its holders. What a generic function changes through its type parameters' methods is
  worked out for each instance, by the package that compiles that instance.
* `[EFF-9]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `RuntimeCheck(k)` enters a function's effect set
  when a check of kind `k` survives the compiler's profile-independent proofs in its body. `Arithmetic`
  covers integer overflow, division by zero, shift amounts and negative integer exponents, and the
  compare of an owner count or a weak count with its limit before it grows; `Bounds` covers indices,
  slices and chunk sizes; `Aliasing` covers the compare of `assert_disjoint` and `check_disjoint`
  (`[DSJ-1]`), the one run-time alias check there is; `Stale` covers handle generations and the test of
  a target's header that opens a `weakref` link (`exists as`).
* `[EFF-10]` The effect set records only which kinds occur. Per-site detail — every emitted check with
  its kind, location, mechanism and reason, and every removed check with the proof that removed it — is
  written to the safety side table that `ember inspect --safety` reads.
* `[EFF-11]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Every emitted check carries one reason, and diagnostics use it:

  | Reason | Meaning | What the programmer can do |
  |---|---|---|
  | `not_provable_in_principle` | the property depends on run-time data | nothing; the check is permanent |
  | `not_proven_by_analysis` | the property may hold but was not proved | restructure per the hint, or report the gap |
  | `requested_by_type` | the programmer chose a type whose use is checked (a `weakref` link, each opening of which tests its target's header) | change the type to change the cost (a view, where the target outlives it) |
  | `inherent_to_mechanism` | the check is what the mechanism is (a handle's generation compare) | use another mechanism |
  | `establishes_static_fact` | the check proves a property once, and the names it checked are treated as having it afterwards (`assert_disjoint`, `[DSJ-1]`) | nothing |

* `[EFF-18]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Effects are independent: a blocking `Mutex.lock`, and `with x.lock:` on
  a `Lock`, have `Sync + Lock + Block`; `try_lock` has `Sync + Lock`; a blocking read has `Io + Block`.

### What a function does

* `[EFF-24]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **What a function does is worked out from its code.** Beside its effect
  set the compiler works out, for every function, its summary: what it may change, read and end, and
  through which chain of calls. It is computed over the same call graph as `[EFF-1]`, from the
  function's own lines; from the functions it calls; for a call through a function value, an interface,
  a `dyn` or a `virtual` method, from every function the program can put there (`[EFF-2]`); from what
  the threads, tasks and jobs it starts and the callbacks it hands to C change, now or later
  (`[EFF-26]`); and from the `drop` of every object it may end (`[DRP-8]`), a function value or an
  `owns dyn I` value replaced or ended counting the `drop`s of what its state owns. A `drop` changes its
  own object as a given. The summary also records which elements of a list the function touches;
  whether it only adds at the end of a `ref mut` list parameter (`push`, `extend`) and reads or writes no
  element already in it; whether it gives the link of an object it is given a target before reading it
  (Part VIII); which of its view parameters, `this` included, it uses after a line that may end or move
  what they view; what it reaches by other names while a `ref mut` parameter is used; and which locks it
  may take, or needs held (`[THR-18]`). No word on a function's first line says any of it: `changes`,
  `reads` or another clause after a function's brackets is `E0100` ("`changes FRAME` is not Ember: the
  compiler works out what `tick` changes from its body; write `fn tick():`").
* `[EFF-25]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **The summary decides every rule that needs it, and nothing is checked
  while the program runs.** It decides: a walk of a collection and a call that may change it (`E3020`,
  `[BRW-18]`); a read-only name and a call that may change what it reads (`E3021`); a call that hands a
  function a part of what it may end or move before its last use of that parameter (`E3031`,
  `[BRW-21]`); a view of an object reached through a link and a call that may end the object (`E3060`);
  a function value stored where it would change its holder (`E3022`); a call that may take a lock this
  thread holds (`E7018`, `[THR-19]`); what tasks and threads change (`[THR-11]`, `[THR-20]`); `init`
  calling a method before every field its body reads is set (`E2100`); and what a `@cached` method's
  result depends on (`[EFF-27]`). A fact worked out from a body never changes what a line does: it
  decides only whether a line compiles, or removes a test that would always pass. A message about a
  change a call makes names the chain of calls that makes it, and no message asks for a word on a first
  line:

  ```ember
  static mut LOG: Array[String] = []

  fn note(owns msg: String):
      LOG.push(msg)

  fn tick():
      note(String("tick"))

  fn main():
      LOG.push(String("start"))
      for line in LOG:
          println(line)
          tick()
  ```

  ```text
  error[E3020]: `tick()` (line 13) adds to `LOG` (through `note`, line 4) while this loop walks `LOG` (line 11); call `tick()` after the loop: move line 13 below the loop
  ```

* `[EFF-26]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **A call that runs a function makes its changes; storing one does not.** A
  call through a function value makes the changes of every function it may run, and a function value
  given to a call counts as an argument that changes every place its functions change and every real
  variable they capture (`[BRW-11]`). A call that runs a function by itself counts as making everything
  that function changes, now or later: `thread.spawn`, `scope.spawn`, `jobs.submit` and a job scope's
  `submit` (Part XI); a library function that calls the function it is given
  (`scores.for_each(fn(s): LOG.push(copy of s.name))` changes `LOG`); whatever drives an iterator
  adapter that keeps one (`for x in it:`, `it.sum()`); and a foreign function's parameter whose contract
  says `callback(retained)` or `callback(once)`, through which C keeps the function and runs it during
  later foreign calls (a `callback(borrowed)` parameter runs it during the call, as `for_each` does).
  Putting a function value in a field, a list, a local or an iterator adapter changes nothing the
  function changes; the call that later runs it does. **A foreign call may run the callbacks C keeps**:
  C code cannot be read, so a call of a foreign function counts as possibly running every callback C
  keeps, on the threads their contracts allow, and makes the changes they make, for its caller and every
  function that calls it, unless the foreign function's declaration says `@ffi(no_callbacks)`, a fact
  the programmer vouches for (`[TCB-1]`; Part XVI says which Ember code C may run). A generic body's
  calls of its type parameters' methods make the changes those methods make for the types it is given,
  worked out for each instance.
  Its message: E3020 ("`scores.for_each(...)` (line 4) pushes to `LOG` (through the function it is given) while this loop walks `LOG` (line 3); call it after the loop: move line 4 below the loop").
* `[EFF-27]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **What a `@cached` result depends on.** A `@cached` method's result
  depends on the fields its body reads, worked out from its body (`[EFF-24]`), and the kept result is
  cleared by every change, through any name, to one of them: the compiler places the clear at each line
  that may make such a change. A change that does not pass through the method's object cannot be cleared
  that way, so a `sharedref mut` link, or a `shares mut` owner, made into anything a `@cached` method of
  its holder reads is `E2117` at the line that makes it ("`s.items[0]` is read by `Shelf.first_name`,
  which is `@cached` and would not see a change made through this link; link the shelf instead,
  `sharedref mut s`, or remove `@cached`"); a link to the whole holder is allowed, since every change
  through it passes through the holder. A reload that changes a `@cached` method's body clears every
  kept result of its type (Annex B).

## X.2 Contracts

A contract attribute states an effect the function must not have.

| Contract | Forbids | Code |
|---|---|---|
| `@noalloc` | `Alloc` | `E4001` |
| `@nosync` | `Sync` | `E4002` |
| `@noblock` | `Block` | `E4003` |
| `@noio` | `Io` | `E4041` |
| `@nolock` | `Lock` | `E4042` |
| `@nopanic(explicit)` | `Panic(Explicit)` | `E4040` |
| `@no_alias_checks` | `RuntimeCheck(Aliasing)` | `E4030` |
| `@deterministic` | `Nondet` (Part X.3) | `E4070` |
| `@realtime` | the manifest's set, by default `@noalloc @nolock @noblock @nopanic(explicit)` | per contract |

* `[EFF-5]` Each contract in the table forbids its effect in the function's effect set; a violation is
  the listed error.
* `[EFF-6]` A contract is checked over the whole reachable call graph — callees, drop glue, default
  arguments, operator and interface implementations reached statically — and a violation names the full
  chain to the offending operation:

  ```text
  error[E4001]: @noalloc function `cull` reaches an allocation
    cull -> collect_visible -> Array.push -> ember_alloc
  ```

* `[EFF-12]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `@no_alias_checks` permits `RuntimeCheck(Bounds)`, `(Arithmetic)` and
  `(Stale)`; it forbids only `RuntimeCheck(Aliasing)`, the run-time compare of `assert_disjoint` or
  `check_disjoint`, because a data-oriented inner loop can always do without it: spans the compiler
  proves apart need no compare, and a copy needs none (`E4030`: "`mix` is `@no_alias_checks`, and
  `assert_disjoint(d, s)` (line 18) compares the two spans while running; blend from a copy, which needs
  no check: instead of lines 16 to 19 write `old = copy of tracks[src_name]` and
  `blend(ref mut tracks[dst_name].as_mut_span(), old.as_span())`, or remove `@no_alias_checks`").
  `@static_safe` is `E0104` ("`@static_safe` is now `@no_alias_checks`: it forbids run-time alias checks
  only; bounds and overflow checks still run; write `@no_alias_checks`").
* `[EFF-17]` `@nopanic(explicit)` is spelled with its argument; bare `@nopanic` is `E0104` with a fix-it,
  so that no reader takes it to mean "cannot abort" (`[EFF-16]`).
* `[EFF-20]` `@noio` forbids `Io`, including console output; `println` in a `@noio` function is `E4041`.
* `[EFF-21]` `@nolock` forbids `Lock`, including `try_lock`, which never blocks but still takes a lock.
* `[EFF-7]` `@assume_noalloc(call)`, an expression admitted only inside `unsafe` (`E0104` elsewhere),
  has the call's type and value and overrides the analysis for that one call, which the compiler
  cannot see into: the call is taken to carry no `Alloc`, and the programmer is answerable for it, as
  for any `unsafe` obligation (`[UNS-7]`) (ODR-060).
* `[EFF-8]` An `override` inherits its base method's contracts.
* `[EFF-14]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Contracts compose; the usual inner-loop set is `@no_alias_checks
  @noalloc @nosync @nopanic(explicit)`, one per line.
* `[EFF-15]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* Effects and contract verdicts are computed once,
  after the profile-independent proofs, and are identical in every profile (`[PHIL-13]`). The proofs
  that count are exactly those this document specifies — `[OPT-2]`, `[RNG-4]`, `[SIMD-7]` and the
  parent-link proof of Part VIII, which removes the header test of a parent-link read — and a verdict is
  computed **as if every one of them were applied wherever its conditions hold**, whether or not the
  emitted code keeps the check a proof would remove. So every implementation reaches the same verdict;
  an implementation may remove further checks from the code it emits, but that never changes a verdict.
  Adding a proof to the list is a language revision (`[VER-9]`) and makes more programs satisfy a
  contract, never fewer.
* `[EFF-16]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `@nopanic(explicit)` forbids only the panics the
  programmer writes and allocation failure. Arithmetic, bounds, aliasing and stale checks, and a count's
  compare with its limit, are `RuntimeCheck` kinds and are allowed under it; the diagnostics and error
  page for `@nopanic(explicit)` MUST say so. A function that is `@nopanic(explicit)` **and** free of
  `RuntimeCheck` — two facts `ember inspect --safety` reports together — has no panic the effect model
  knows of; it can still stop on what the model does not cover (`[PHIL-11]`: exhaustion outside
  `Alloc`, a hardware fault, foreign code breaking its contract) (ODR-057). (`NonZero[T]` divisors and
  range facts remove division checks entirely, `[STD-4]`.)
* `[EFF-19]` `@realtime` names the contract set declared by the manifest of the package that declares
  the function (`[realtime] contracts = […]`), by default `@noalloc @nolock @noblock
  @nopanic(explicit)`. It is a marker for that set and not a timing guarantee. A diagnostic arising from
  it names both the failed contract and `@realtime`.
* `[EFF-23]` *(new in 0.9.9)* A contract attribute whose checking an implementation has not built is rejected with
  `E0900` (`[PHIL-12]`); it is never accepted unchecked.

## X.3 Determinism

Lock-step networking, replays and golden-image tests need two runs of a program on the same input to
compute the same bits, on one machine and across machines running the same binary.

* `[DET-1]` `@deterministic` on a function or module is a contract: `Nondet` MUST NOT appear in its
  effect set (`E4070`, naming the operation and the chain).
* `[DET-8]` `@deterministic` on a module applies to every function in it, with no opt-out. A foreign
  function is deterministic only if its declaration says `@ffi(deterministic)`, which is an asserted
  fact reported by `ember tcb`; `@deterministic` on an `extern` block is `E0104`.
* `[DET-9]` `ember inspect --deterministic <item>` prints whether the item satisfies `[DET-1]` and, if
  not, the shortest chain to each `Nondet` source; a function that relies on asserted foreign facts is
  reported as such, not as verified.
* `[DET-2]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `Nondet` is introduced by exactly: floating-point
  contraction, reassociation or any `@fastmath` relaxation; a transcendental function from the platform
  library instead of `std.math.det`; observing a pointer or an object's address as an integer, or
  hashing one; making a `RandomState`, directly or as a `Map`'s or `Set`'s hasher; the wall clock, the
  monotonic clock, the system random source, thread and job completion order; reading padding bytes,
  recorded where a pointer to a type with padding is reinterpreted as a pointer to another type; any
  `extern` function not declared `@ffi(deterministic)`. Iterating a `Map` or `Set` is **not** `Nondet`:
  their order is insertion order (`[STD-11]`). A reduction of scoped tasks, combined in spawn order, is
  not `Nondet` either (`[THR-21]`). Reading uninitialised memory is not `Nondet` but undefined, outside
  Safe Ember (`[PHIL-10]`): an `unsafe` obligation (ODR-136).
* `[DET-3]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A `@deterministic` function may call only `Nondet`-free functions; a
  call through a function value counts every function the program can put there, and a function given
  through a type parameter is checked per instance (`[EFF-2]`).
* `[DET-4]` `std.math.det` provides `sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `exp`, `log`, `pow`, `atan2` and `sqrt` for
  `f32` and `f64` returning the same bits on every supported target. Each takes either type and
  answers in it (`det.sin(x)` of an `f32` is an `f32`); an `f32`'s result is its `f64` result
  rounded once. Each is within one unit in the last place of the exact result, `atan2` within 1.3;
  `sqrt` is IEEE 754's, correctly rounded. An integer is converted by the program (ODR-046).
* `[DET-5]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Inside a `@deterministic` function the backend never contracts,
  reassociates or fuses; a `@fastmath` or `@fp(allow_fma)` function there is `E4072` ("`dot` is
  `@deterministic`, and a fused multiply-add rounds once where two operations round twice; remove
  `@fp(allow_fma)`"). `@fp(contract)` is `E0104` ("`@fp(contract)` is now `@fp(allow_fma)`: it lets the
  compiler fuse `a * b + c` into one fused multiply-add; write `@fp(allow_fma)`").
* `[DET-6]` `@deterministic` constrains results, not timing.
* `[DET-7]` The cross-machine claim holds for one binary. `ember build --build-id` prints a hash over the
  inputs of a reproducible build (`[BLD-13]`) so peers can confirm they run the same one.
* `[DET-10]` *(new in 0.9.9)* A deterministic program runs with a defined floating-point environment: round to nearest,
  ties to even; no flush-to-zero or denormals-are-zero; no trapping exceptions. The runtime establishes
  it at start-up and on every thread it creates, and foreign code that changes it is outside the
  guarantee.

## X.4 The cost model

* `[COST-1]` **Zero cost, defined.** An abstraction is zero-cost *for a use* whose dynamic checks are
  all proved away when the emitted code contains no instruction that equivalent hand-written C —
  C upholding the same invariant — would not contain.
* `[COST-2]` Every implicit cost is one of: **guaranteed elided** (emitting it is a defect);
  **guaranteed present**; **conditionally elided** (the compiler MAY remove it with a proof and reports
  whether it did); **implementation-defined** (not constrained, such as code size; two conforming
  implementations may differ); **not observable** (erased).
* `[COST-3]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **The costs.** Everything
  the memory model checks is checked when compiling; what runs is only what this table lists.

| Cost | Class | Condition, and what the programmer can do |
|---|---|---|
| Bounds check on `a[i]` | conditionally elided | removed by loop versioning (`[OPT-2]`) and range facts; `get_unchecked` in `unsafe` |
| Overflow check on integer arithmetic | conditionally elided, **every profile** | removed by range facts; checked once per group in vectorised loops (`[SIMD-7]`); `@overflow(wrap)` or `wrapping_*` for code that wants wrapping |
| A second pass of a loop, then `retain` | conditionally fused | a loop that queues removals and the `retain` that follows it are fused into one pass where nothing between them reads the list; otherwise two passes (1.71x of one-pass C as written, 1.00x fused) |
| Floor `//` and `%` on signed integers | guaranteed present, small | one compare-and-adjust over C's truncation; free for a positive constant divisor; `div_trunc`/`rem_trunc` give C's |
| Division-by-zero and shift-range checks | conditionally elided | removed for constants, `NonZero` divisors and range facts |
| Owner count +1 / -1 | guaranteed present | only where a line makes or ends a `shares`, `shares mut` or `thread_shared` owner (`[THR-1]`), and nowhere else; a plain add for `shares`, and for `thread_shared` on the thread that made the value until it is handed over (`[RC-4]`); an atomic one on other threads; each +1 is checked against the count's limit, one compare and a branch never taken (`[COST-6]`) |
| A `thread_shared` value's two counts | guaranteed present | a 32-byte header, 16 bytes more than one atomic count's (`[OBJ-1]`); a test of the thread's queue at each check point (`[RC-4]`), and the queue's work for a value whose last owner ends on another thread without a hand-over. Measured against one atomic count (`tasks/96/redesign/measure-0.9.15/brc/REPORT.md`, 15 runs per cell): a thread's own values 25% faster on 1 to 8 threads, the camera program 89 ms against 544 ms; reading another thread's values 3% slower on 1 thread and 17% to 28% faster on 2 to 8; one thread handing copies to all 0.93x to 1.05x; a random mix 9% to 13% slower; a pipeline (made on one thread, ended on the next) 27% slower on 1 thread and the same on 2 to 8 |
| `weakref` link made, given another target, or ended | guaranteed present | one add or one subtract of the target's weak count, the add checked against its limit; atomic for a `thread_shared` target; a parent link pays it too, one add when `child.parent = weakref this` runs and one subtract when the link changes or the child ends |
| Opening a `weakref` link (`if w exists as p:`) | conditionally elided | one test of the target's header (during the target's `drop` the object is already ended, and the same test finds it gone); a parent-link read the compiler proves (Part VIII) is a load and a test for no link |
| A view of a `thread_shared` object opened from a `weakref` link | guaranteed present | one count held for the view's life, since another thread may end the last owner at any moment: a plain add on the thread that made the object until it is handed over, an atomic one elsewhere (`[RC-5]` point 2) |
| A walk up a tree across a call that may change nodes | guaranteed present | per step, one test of the node's header and one move of the link's weak count (a subtract and an add); where the node's class has no `drop` of its own and no other thread can end its nodes, the walk runs in a deferred-drop region and the count moves go, leaving the header test; a walk whose visit function changes no node keeps its views and pays nothing per step |
| A view of an object reached through a link; a `sharedref mut` link | not observable | checked when compiling: no count and no deferred-drop region around the view |
| Stale-handle check | guaranteed present, **every profile** | the guarantee is the check; `get_unchecked` in `unsafe` |
| Kind test or cast | guaranteed present | one type-id compare per `if s is Circle as c:` and per `cast s as Circle` (Part VIII) |
| `assert_disjoint` | guaranteed present | two compares where the program writes it (two spans of one list given to one call, one of them changeable); the call is then compiled with noalias; none when the compiler knows the spans apart |
| `Cell` access | not observable | a load or a store |
| Interface call through `dyn` | guaranteed present | one indirect call |
| Virtual method call | conditionally elided | a load of the slot and one indirect call (`[DSP-2]`); direct when one implementation is reachable (`[DSP-5]`) |
| Generic call, monomorphised | not observable | a direct, inlinable call |
| Generic call, shared (`[MONO-6]`) | guaranteed present | one indirect call per bound method; only above a declared instantiation budget |
| A function given through a type parameter (`[F: fn(Item)]`) | not observable | a direct, inlinable call; one instance per function given |
| A call through a function value (a parameter, field, list element or local of a function type) | guaranteed present | one indirect call; a call through a list element or a field first copies the value's two words, its code and its state, out of it |
| A function value's state | guaranteed present | a variable kept with a capture word (`owns`, `copy of`, `shares`, `thread_shared`, `weakref`) lives in the function value's own state (`[CLO-10]`), and costs nothing beyond it; a captured real variable stays at its own address and costs nothing; a function that ends its own state while it runs and then uses it holds one count on that state across the call |
| `some I` return | not observable | the concrete type is known |
| Generator resume | guaranteed present | one jump on the state; the frame never allocates; a `for` over a list inside the generator reads its position again after each resume |
| Collection literal producing a heap collection | guaranteed present | one allocation (`Alloc`); a fixed-array context allocates nothing |
| String literal producing a `String` | guaranteed present | one allocation and copy; a `StrView` context allocates nothing |
| f-string | guaranteed present | allocates; `format_to` into a buffer does not |
| `?` converting an error into `AnyError` | guaranteed present, failure path only | one allocation (`[ERR-11]`); a concrete error type moves without allocating |
| `copy of`; `owns`, `shares` or `thread_shared` before a new value | guaranteed present | `copy of` makes a copy by the type's `Clone`; `owns`, `shares` and `thread_shared` put a new value in its own block, one allocation; nothing is copied or allocated where no line says so |
| Contract and range-type annotations | not observable | compile time only |
| Floating-point contraction off | guaranteed present | `a * b + c` is two roundings and two instructions, where C compilers often fuse them; `fma(a, b, c)`, `x.mul_add(b, c)` or `@fp(allow_fma)` give one (`[TYP-9]`) |
| 64-bit `int` | guaranteed present | `int` is `i64`, so an `Array[int]` moves twice the bytes of C's 32-bit `int`; dense numeric data uses `i32`/`f32` elements (`L4003`) |
| Sorting floats | not observable | `sort` on floats compares by IEEE totalOrder (`[TYP-37]`), a few integer instructions per compare |
| Arena allocation | guaranteed present | a pointer bump |
| A value made `using` a memory manager | guaranteed present | each allocation and free of the value is the manager's own work (an arena: a pointer bump, nothing freed one by one); a value whose manager may have several instances keeps one word, its instance's address, so that its growth and its end go back to that instance; none for `Global` or `System` |
| Allocation | guaranteed present | a call that allocates (a collection growing, a `String` built), reported per site; `@noalloc` refuses it (`[EFF-1]`) |
| `contains` | guaranteed present | the `contains` an `x in c` selects: linear for an array or view, constant for a set or map (`[STD-8a]`) |
| A lock | guaranteed present | where the program takes one (`with x.lock:`, `m.lock()`): the lock C takes; nothing per use of a `guarded by` field (`[THR-18]`) |
| Scoped tasks and their reductions | guaranteed present | one private accumulator per task and one combine per task at the join, as C's per-thread counter; no atomic per change (`[THR-21]`) |
| `@cached` method | guaranteed present | one flag test per call, and one store, clearing the flag, at each line that may change a field its body reads (`[EFF-27]`); on an object several threads reach, the result is filled once under a once-flag |
| Stack probe | guaranteed present | one touch per page of a frame larger than a page (`[RT-12]`); none for smaller frames |
| FFI call | guaranteed present | one direct call for an ABI-direct C function |
| A C callback | guaranteed present | the checked trampoline (Part XVI): C holds a tagged number, never an address; each call compares the callback's generation, and, in every profile, the thread of a `threads(creator)` callback and the used-up mark of a `callback(once)` one |
| What a function changes, reads and ends; the thread rules; the arena checks | not observable | all checked when compiling (`[EFF-24]`); a library function given a function is one instance per function, as Rust's generic `F: FnMut`; a call that names one whole variable twice is compiled against its own copy of the function (`[BRW-11]`), one more copy of its code and nothing while running |

* `[OPT-2]` For a counted loop over `a..b` that indexes views at `i + c` for constants `c`, with the
  views' bases and lengths invariant in the loop, the compiler MUST emit one entry test that all indices
  the loop can produce are in bounds, an unchecked body taken when it passes, and the checked body
  otherwise. Behaviour is unchanged in every case.
* `[OPT-3]` The loop bound in `[OPT-2]` may be written `s.len()`, a separate local the loop does not
  assign, or a constant; the three are treated alike.
* `[COST-4]` `ember inspect --cost <item>` prints every row that applies to an item, and for each
  conditionally elided cost whether it was removed and by which proof.
* `[COST-5]` A rule that introduces an implicit cost MUST add a row to this table; `rule_index.py` fails
  CI on a new implicit cost with no row.
* `[COST-6]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **What stops the program, and what it says.** Of the costs above, these
  may stop the program, in every profile (`[PRF-4]`); each says so in the names of the program that
  stopped (the example's names in quotes):

  | Check | The stop's text |
  |---|---|
  | `assert_disjoint` (`[DSJ-1]`) | "`assert_disjoint(d, s)` on line 11: the two spans overlap (`dst_name` and `src_name` name one track)" |
  | a one-thread owner count at its maximum | "too many owners of a `Player` (4,294,967,295)" |
  | a one-thread weak count at its maximum | "too many `weakref` links to a `Player` (4,294,967,295)" |
  | a `thread_shared` owner count at its limit (`[RC-4]`) | "too many owners of a `Log` (2,147,483,647)" |
  | a `thread_shared` weak count at its limit (`[RC-4]`) | "too many `weakref` links to a `Log` (2,147,483,647)" |
  | the type-id compare of `cast s as Circle` | "`cast s as Circle` on line 9: `s` is a `Square`, not a `Circle`" |
  | the checked trampoline: a call after the token ended | "C called the callback registered on line 16 after its token ended; it was unregistered" |
  | the checked trampoline: a `callback(once)` function called a second time | "C called the callback registered on line 29 a second time; it was registered `callback(once)`, so it may run only once" |
  | the checked trampoline: a `threads(creator)` callback on another thread, checked in every profile | "C called the callback registered on line 16 on another thread, but its contract says `threads(creator)`" |
  | a bounds check | "index 3 is out of bounds for a length of 3; use `.get(i)` for an `Option`" |
  | adopting one live object twice (`[FFI-36b]`) | a panic naming both places that adopted it |
  | a GPU draw reading past what is bound (`[GPU-12]`) | the text `[GPU-12]` gives |

  The number a count's text names is the limit that count reached: for a one-thread count, its
  maximum; for a `thread_shared` count, the limit Part VIII keeps below its maximum. The two count
  limits are tested with a count that is easy to fill (`[TST-31]`); the language has no test-only
  shortcut.
---

# Part XI — Concurrency and Parallelism

Ember has OS threads, scoped tasks that may use the caller's own variables, a job system, and parallel
loops. Safe Ember has no data races (`[PHIL-10]`): two threads touch one memory location at the same
time only when both accesses read it, or when the location is an `Atomic`, or is protected by a lock
(a `Mutex`, an `RwLock`, or a `Lock` that fields are `guarded by`) or a channel. The rules below are how
that holds without a garbage collector: every one is checked when compiling, and nothing runs for them
but the locks, atomics and counts the program's own words ask for.

```ember
import std.thread
from std.sync import Atomic, Lock

class Stats:
    words: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    tags: Array[String] guarded by lock = []

fn scan(stats: Stats, text: StrView):
    for w in text.split_whitespace():
        stats.words.fetch_add(1)
        if w.starts_with("#"):
            with stats.lock:
                stats.tags.push(String(w))

fn main():
    stats = Stats()
    texts = [String("#ember is fast"), String("no tags here"), String("#python #c")]
    with scope = thread.scope():
        for t in texts:
            scope.spawn(fn() ref t: scan(stats, t))
    println(stats.words.load(), "words")
```

Each task uses `main`'s real `stats` and looks at its round's text with `ref t`; `scan` changes
`stats.words` through its `Atomic` and `stats.tags` under the lock that guards it, so the tasks never
change one place unordered.

## XI.1 What may reach another thread

* `[THR-8]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A type is **`Send`** when a value
  of it may be handed over to another thread: nothing reachable from it (its fields, its elements, what
  its `owns` parts hold, a function value's state) is a one-thread owner (`shares T`, `shares mut T`), a
  `weakref` link to a value that is not `thread_shared`, or bound to the thread that made it (a lock's
  guard, a `Scope` or `JobScope`, a raw pointer, a `threads(creator)` handle). Structs, enums, tuples,
  fixed arrays, collections and class objects are `Send` when every component is; an `owns T` when `T`
  is; `ref T` and `Span[T]` when `T` is `ThreadShared`, `ref mut T` and `MutSpan[T]` when `T` is
  `Send`; a `thread_shared T`, and a `weakref` link to one, when `T` is `Send` and `ThreadShared`;
  `dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: Send:`). Of the function types, `thread_shared fn()` is
  `Send` (`[THR-1]`). A `Send` view still goes only where it cannot outlive what it views: to a scoped
  task or a job of a scope, never to an unscoped thread (`[THR-2]`). `Send` is inferred from the
  words and written only in bounds; the author of a type that holds a raw
  pointer declares it with `unsafe extend T implements Send:` and a `# SAFETY:` note (`E3100` without
  `unsafe`: "`Counter` holds a raw pointer, so the compiler cannot tell that another thread may have
  it; say that you vouch for it: write `unsafe extend Counter implements Send:` with a `# SAFETY:` note
  above it"). A thread-bound value sent to another thread is `E7008`.
* `[THR-9]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A type is **`ThreadShared`** when several threads may
  hold and read one value of it at once. It is inferred like `Send` and written only in bounds
  (`[T: ThreadShared]` above `fn keep(xs: Array[T]) -> int:`) and in messages; `Sync` in a bound is
  `E1010` ("`Sync` is the effect `@nosync` forbids, not a property of a type; for 'threads may share
  it' write `[T: ThreadShared]` above `fn keep(x: T)`"). Structural types are `ThreadShared` when every
  component is. `ref mut T`, `Cell`, `UnsafeCell`, raw pointers, `shares T`, `shares mut T`, and a
  `weakref` link to a value that is not `thread_shared` are not. `Atomic[T]`, `Once`, `Lock`,
  `Mutex[T]` for a `Send` `T` (one thread at a time holds its `ref mut T`), `RwLock[T]` and
  `thread_shared T` for a `T` that is `Send` and `ThreadShared` (several threads hold a `ref T` at
  once: `RwLock[Cell[int]]` is not `ThreadShared`), and a channel's `Sender` are.
* `[THR-1]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **A value several threads own is made
  `thread_shared`.** `thread_shared x` makes one more owner of `x`, which may be on any thread; it is
  written before a new value (`st = thread_shared Stats()`) or on a value already `thread_shared`
  (`fn() thread_shared st:`), and on a value made otherwise it is `E7017` ("`names` is
  `share_and_keep`'s own object, which it may change; to share it between threads, create it shared:
  `names = thread_shared Names()`"). A `thread_shared` value lives until its last owner ends. Its
  owners are counted in two numbers, its making thread's and the other threads' (atomic), and its weak
  count is atomic (`[RC-4]`); each is compared with its limit before it grows (Part VIII). Three rules keep it safe:
  * **no owner changes a `thread_shared` value directly** (`E7014`: "`names` is shared between threads
    (line 5), so no owner changes it directly, and line 6 pushes to its list; fill the list where the
    object is made: write `names = thread_shared Names(items=[copy of s])` instead of lines 5 and 6");
    its state changes only through an `Atomic`, a `Mutex`, an `RwLock`, a channel end, or a field
    `guarded by` a lock, under that lock (`[THR-18]`);
  * everything reachable from it is `Send` (`[THR-8]`): a one-thread owner, a `weakref` link to a value
    that is not `thread_shared`, or a plain `fn()` value reachable from it is `E7015` at the line that
    makes it `thread_shared` ("`Bus.handlers` holds plain `fn()` values, and a `thread_shared Bus` may
    run them on any thread; write `handlers: Array[thread_shared fn()] = []` in `Bus`");
  * **`thread_shared fn()`** is a function any thread may run. It holds only `thread_shared` owners,
    values handed over to it and copies, never a one-thread owner or a `weakref` link to one (`E7015`:
    "`on_event` keeps functions any thread may run (`thread_shared fn()`), and this one holds `count`, a
    `shares mut` owner, which stays on one thread; share the counter between threads: write
    `count = thread_shared Counter()` in place of line 12, give `Counter` the field
    `n: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)` (with `from std.sync import Atomic` at the top), and pass
    `fn() thread_shared count: count.n.fetch_add(1)`"). A list, field or parameter whose functions may
    run on any thread says so in its type: `handlers: Array[thread_shared fn()] guarded by lock = []`.

  As a parameter's type, `log: thread_shared Log` reads the caller's value with no count, and
  `owns log: thread_shared Log` takes one owner. A class needs no mark to be shared between threads:
  `@sync` is not Ember (`E0104`: "`@sync` is gone: a class needs no mark to be shared between threads,
  and `Stats`'s fields are `Atomic`, which threads may change as they are; remove `@sync` (line 1)").
* `[THR-2]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **A one-thread value never reaches another
  thread.** A `shares` or `shares mut` owner counts its owners with plain adds, and every object that is
  not `thread_shared` counts its `weakref` links with plain adds. So no such owner, and no `weakref`
  link to such a value, reaches another thread by any route: captured or held by a function any thread
  may run (`thread_shared fn()`, the function of `thread.spawn` or `jobs.submit`, a callback C may run on
  another thread), handed to an unscoped thread or a job, or reachable from a `thread_shared` value
  (`[THR-1]`); and neither does a view of a place this thread owns, which an unscoped thread may outlive
  (`E7015`, whose message gives the words to write: the value made `thread_shared` from the start, or a
  copy). **Making, ending or opening a `weakref` link touches its target's header** (its weak count, and
  the test that it still lives): in a scoped task, a job, or any function that may run on another thread
  than its target's owner, it is allowed only for a `thread_shared` target, whose counts are kept for
  several threads and whose opened view holds a count (`[RC-4]`, `[RC-5]` point 2; `E7015`: "`players[0]` counts its links without atomics, and
  the task on line 9 makes one too; make the links after the scope, or make the player
  `thread_shared`"). An object handed whole to another thread while a `weakref` link on this thread
  points at it is `E7015`, since this thread could open the link while the other thread ends the object
  ("`names` goes to another thread, and `w` (line 15), a `weakref` link on this thread, still points at
  it, so this thread could read it while the other thread ends it; give the thread a copy of its own:
  write `h = thread.spawn(fn() copy of names: names.items.len())` in place of line 16"). So an object
  that stays on one thread needs no atomic count.
* `[THR-7]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `thread_shared` means exactly: the value may have owners on several
  threads, its counts are kept for several threads (`[RC-4]`), and no owner changes it directly (`[THR-1]`). It does not make a method
  atomic: two operations on `Atomic` fields, or a read and a store of one
  (`if n > this.longest.load(): this.longest.store(n)`), are two steps another thread may come between;
  a read and a change that must stay together are made under one lock (`[THR-18]`). A diagnostic MUST
  NOT describe `thread_shared` or `ThreadShared` as "thread-safe".
* `[THR-13]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **The data-race guarantee.** In Safe Ember every
  place two threads can reach is one of these, and each is ordered or only read:
  * a place a scoped task reads: neither the parent nor another task changes it until the join
    (`[THR-11]`); the loop's own variable reaches a task only as the task's own copy, or as a view of the
    element it is on, which the walked collection keeps unchanged until the join (`[THR-17]`);
  * a place tasks change by a reduction: each task has its own accumulator, and the join orders them
    (`[THR-21]`);
  * an `Atomic`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, channel end or `guarded by` field: ordered by the atomic or by the
