    lock, which the thread that touches it holds (`[THR-3]`, `[THR-18]`);
  * a value handed over to the other thread, which the giver no longer has, and from which no one-thread
    value is reachable (`[THR-2]`, `[THR-8]`);
  * a `thread_shared` value: no owner changes it directly, and its counts are kept for several threads (`[THR-1]`, `[RC-4]`);
  * a module variable: a `static` never changes (`[STA-1]`), and a `static mut` is reached only by the
    main thread and its scoped tasks, or is `guarded by` a lock (`[THR-20]`);
  * a `sharedref mut` target: a scoped task changes it directly only where neither another task nor the
    parent may touch it before the join, or by a reduction (`E7007`); an unscoped thread never holds one
    (`E7015`).

## XI.2 Threads and synchronisation (`std.thread`, `std.sync`)

```ember
import std.thread
from std.sync import Sender, channel

fn produce(tx: Sender[int]):
    for i in 0..10:
        tx.send(i * i).expect("receiver is gone")

fn main():
    tx, rx = channel[int](capacity=64)
    producer = thread.spawn(fn() owns tx: produce(tx))
    total = 0
    for v in rx:
        total += v
    producer.join()
    println(total)
```

* `[THR-10]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `thread.spawn` runs a function on
  a new thread, which may outlive the function that started it. It takes a function any thread may run,
  `[R]` above `pub fn spawn(owns f: thread_shared fn() -> R) -> JoinHandle[R]:`, so a function that holds
  a one-thread value is `E7015` (`[THR-1]`, `[THR-2]`), and `R` MUST be `Send` (`E7015`, `E7008`). What
  the function holds from its maker is written in its capture list (`[THR-17]`). `h.join() -> R` waits
  and returns the result. Dropping a `JoinHandle` detaches the thread. **Starting a thread counts as
  making everything its function changes, now or later** (`[EFF-26]`): a `thread.spawn` inside a walk of
  what the thread changes is `E3020` ("start it after the loop"), except where the thread makes that
  change under a lock the walk holds, when the new thread waits for the lock until the loop ends; joining
  such a thread inside that lock is `E7018` (`[THR-19]`).
* `[THR-17]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **What an unscoped thread holds, and the loop's own variable.** An unscoped
  thread (`thread.spawn`), a job submitted outside a scope (`[JOB-2]`) and a callback C keeps (Part XVI)
  say in their capture list everything of their maker's that they use: `owns x` (handed over; the
  maker's `x` ends), `thread_shared x` (one more owner), or `copy of x` (a copy of their own); a name
  used with no word is `E7004` ("this thread may outlive `share_plain`, so it cannot use
  `share_plain`'s `names`; say what the thread holds: `fn() owns names:` (handed over), or create it
  shared, `names = thread_shared Names()`, and write `fn() thread_shared names:` (one more owner)").
  `shares` and `shares mut` captures, and a `weakref` capture of a value that is not `thread_shared`,
  are allowed only where the function stays on this thread, which a callback whose contract says
  `threads(creator)` or `threads(main)` does, checked by the trampoline in every profile (Part XVI). A
  module variable (`RESULTS`) needs no word. **The loop's own variable**, which the loop gives another
  element every round, and a local of one round, which ends with it, are given to a task or a thread
  with a word. `copy of t` gives it its own copy (for a `String`, one allocation and copy per task):
  `thread.spawn(fn() copy of r: worker(r))`. For a scoped task, `ref t` lets it look at the element `t`
  is on in that round, with no copy, since the walked collection cannot change until every task has
  ended at the end of the `with scope` block (`scope.spawn(fn() ref t: total +=
  t.split_whitespace().count())`). `ref t` where the function may still run after the element changes
  or ends is `E3026`: a `thread.spawn` thread may outlive the loop ("the thread may still run after the
  loop has moved on and `texts` is gone; give it its own copy: `thread.spawn(fn() copy of t: ...)`").
  The loop's name used with no word is `E3026` for a scoped task, whose message gives both words ("the
  task may still run in a later round, when `t` names another text; give it its own copy,
  `scope.spawn(fn() copy of t: ...)`, or let it look at this round's text, `scope.spawn(fn() ref t:
  ...)`"), and `E7004` for a `thread.spawn` thread, whose message gives `copy of t`.
* `[THR-16]` *(new in 0.9.9)* When `main` returns, or `process.exit` is called, the process ends: other
  threads stop without running destructors, no static is freed and no drop runs. The `debug` leak
  report (`[WK-15]`) runs only if no other thread is still running, and otherwise says how many were.
* `[THR-3]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `Mutex[T]` is a value type. `m.lock()` blocks and
  returns a `MutexGuard[T]`, a view of `m` that reads through to `ref mut T` (`[TYP-14]`); the mutex is
  released when the guard ends, which `with g = m.lock():` places at the end of the block.
  `m.try_lock() -> Option[MutexGuard[T]]` never blocks. A guard belongs to the thread that took the
  lock: sending it to another thread is `E7008` ("`g` is the guard of `m`'s lock, which belongs to the
  thread that took it; take the lock inside the task: write `fn add_one(m: Mutex[Array[int]]):` with the
  body `with g = m.lock():` and, inside it, `g.push(1)`, above line 11, and `scope.spawn(fn():
  add_one(m))` in place of line 16"). A view made through a guard (`g[0]`, `ref g[0]`, a slice of `g`)
  does not leave the `with` block (`E3063`: "this points into the locked list, which can change once the
  lock ends; return a copy, or do the work inside the `with` block"), and the same holds for `RwLock`'s
  guards and for a `guarded by` field inside its lock (`[BRW-20]`). There is no poisoning: a panic aborts
  the process (`[PAN-1]`). `RwLock[T]` has `read()` (a shared guard, `ref T`) and `write()` (an exclusive
  guard). `Once` runs an initialiser exactly once (`[STA-3]` is built on it). A `Mutex`, `RwLock`,
  `Atomic` or channel end is changed through any name, a plain one included, by its own operations, and
  an argument given to one takes no word at the call (`ref mut` before it is `E3028`: "`top` takes the
  lock of `scores` itself; a `Mutex` takes no word at the call: `top(scores)`").
* `[THR-18]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **`Lock` and `guarded by`.** A `Lock` is a lock with no value inside;
  `with x.lock:` holds it for the block. `guarded by lock` after a field's type (or a `static mut`'s,
  `[THR-20]`) names the `Lock` that must be held for every read and change of that field outside `init`:
  the field is used only inside `with x.lock:` on the same object `x` (the same name, not given another
  object in the block; `this.lock` in a method), on the thread that holds it (`E7013`: "`words` is
  guarded by `lock`; change it inside `with stats.lock:`"; "`b.words` is guarded by `b.lock`, and this
  block holds `a.lock`; write `with b.lock:`"). Several fields may name one lock, and a class may have
  several locks; `init` sets guarded fields without the lock.
  * A `guarded by` field is a `Mutex` written as ordinary fields, and follows a `Mutex`'s rules: it is
    changed under its lock through any name that reaches its object, a plain one included, with no word
    at the call (`fn add_line(log: Log):` whose body is `with log.lock:` and, inside it,
    `log.lines.push(String("hi"))`). An object whose every field that may change is `guarded by` its
    lock, or is an `Atomic`, `Mutex` or `RwLock`, may reach one call through any number of names, a plain
    argument and a function value that holds it included (`dump(log, fn() thread_shared log:
    log.push("seen"))`): the lock keeps the ways in apart (`[BRW-11]`).
  * A function whose body uses a guarded field without taking its lock is worked out to need that lock
    held (its summary, `[EFF-24]`), and is called only where the lock is held (`E7013`).
  * **A direct call that takes a lock this thread already holds enters the callee past it**, without
    taking it again, only where the compiler proves it is the very lock held: the same name, or `this`
    of the object whose lock is held (`with log.lock: log.push("a")`, where `push` takes `this.lock`).
    Where the callee's lock may be the held one and may not be, the call is `E7018` ("`other.push` takes
    `other`'s lock, and `other` may be `held`, whose lock this thread holds; write `if other is not
    held:` above line 13 and indent line 13 under it").

  ```ember
  from std.sync import Lock

  class Log:
      lock: Lock = Lock()
      lines: Array[String] guarded by lock = []

      fn push(s: StrView):
          with this.lock:
              this.lines.push(String(s))

  fn main():
      log = Log()
      with log.lock:
          log.push("a")
          println(log.lines.len())
  ```

* `[THR-19]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **A wait for a lock this thread holds is refused when compiling.** Inside a
  lock's `with` block, these are `E7018`, with no loop needed and nothing checked while the program runs:
  a call through a function value, or through a `dyn` or `virtual` method, that may run a function taking
  a lock of the kind this thread holds (a `Log`'s lock, while it holds `log`'s: the compiler cannot tell
  which object's lock a stored function takes, so one that takes another `Log`'s lock is refused too, and
  the way out moves one line); a join of a
  thread, or the end of a `with scope` block, whose task changes what the held lock guards; and a direct
  call that may take the held lock and is not proved to enter past it (`[THR-18]`). The messages: "`note()`
  may run the function stored on line 12, which takes a `Log`'s lock (`log.push`, under `lock`), and this
  thread holds `log`'s lock, so taking it again would wait for ever; call `note()` after the
  `with log.lock:` block: move line 16 below the block"; "`t.join()` (line 16) waits for the thread
  started on line 15, whose function changes `RESULTS` under `RESULTS_LOCK`, and this thread holds that
  lock, so each would wait for the other for ever; join after the `with RESULTS_LOCK:` block: move line
  16 below the block". Inside a walk under that lock, such a call is `E7018`, not `E3020`, whose fix
  (after the loop, still inside the lock) would still wait for ever ("this loop walks `log.lines` (line
  9) under `log`'s lock, and `note()` (line 11) may run the function stored on line 4, which takes a
  `Log`'s lock, so it would wait for the lock this thread holds; call `note()` after the `with log.lock:`
  block: move line 11 below the block").
* `[THR-20]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Module variables and threads.** A `static mut` (`[STA-1]`) is reached only
  by the main thread and the tasks of scopes it opens, unless it is `guarded by` a `static` `Lock` and
  used inside `with` that lock: a function that may run on another thread (reachable from
  `thread.spawn`, from a job submitted outside a scope, from a callback C may run on a thread other than
  the main one, or from an `@unsafe(export("name", threads=any))` or `@unsafe(export("name", threads=creator))`
  function) and reads or
  changes it is `E7012` ("`tick` changes `FRAME` and `LOG`, module variables of the main thread, and this
  thread runs beside it; guard both with one lock: write `from std.sync import Lock` at the top,
  `static TICK_LOCK: Lock = Lock()`, then `static mut FRAME: int guarded by TICK_LOCK = 0` instead of
  line 1 and `static mut LOG: Array[String] guarded by TICK_LOCK = []` instead of line 2, and put
  `tick`'s body inside `with TICK_LOCK:`"). A `static` of a type that changes only through itself
  (`Lock`, `Atomic`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, a channel end) is usable from any thread. **A `drop` runs where
  the last owner ends.** The last owner of a `thread_shared` value may end on any thread that holds a
  count of it: an owner, or a view opened from a `weakref` link, which holds one for its life. So a
  function that may run on another thread and holds such a count counts as possibly running that
  value's `drop`, and the `drop` of everything it owns: what they change is changed on that thread, and
  a module variable of the main thread they reach is `E7012`.

  ```ember
  import std.thread
  from std.sync import Lock

  static RESULTS_LOCK: Lock = Lock()
  static mut RESULTS: Array[int] guarded by RESULTS_LOCK = []

  fn worker(x: int):
      r = x * x
      with RESULTS_LOCK:
          RESULTS.push(r)

  fn main():
      worker(1)
      handles: Array[thread.JoinHandle[void]] = []
      with RESULTS_LOCK:
          for r in RESULTS:
              handles.push(thread.spawn(fn() copy of r: worker(r)))
      for h in owns handles:
          h.join()
      with RESULTS_LOCK:
          println(RESULTS.len())
  ```

* `[THR-14]` *(new in 0.9.9)* `Atomic[T]` exists for the integer types, `bool` and raw pointers.
  Every operation takes `order: MemoryOrder = MemoryOrder.SeqCst` (`Relaxed`, `Acquire`, `Release`,
  `AcqRel`, `SeqCst`); an order an operation does not support (`Acquire` on a store) is `E7006`.
  `fetch_add`/`fetch_sub` **panic when the result overflows**, like `+` (`[TYP-8]`); the overflowed
  value has been stored, and another thread may observe it before the process aborts.
  `checked_fetch_add` never stores an overflowed value (it is a compare-exchange loop and returns
  `Option`), and `wrapping_fetch_add` wraps without a check.
* `[THR-15]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `channel[T](capacity=n) -> (Sender[T], Receiver[T])` is
  a bounded many-producer, one-consumer queue; `channel_unbounded[T]()` has no bound and allocates as it
  grows. `Sender` is `Send`, `ThreadShared` and `Clone` (`copy of tx` is another sender of the same
  channel); `Receiver` is `Send`. `tx.send(v) -> Result[void, SendError[T]]` blocks while the queue is
  full and returns the value when the receiver is gone; `rx.recv() -> Option[T]` blocks and returns
  `None` once every sender has ended and the queue is empty; `try_send`/`try_recv` never block. A
  `Receiver` is iterable; the loop ends at `None`. **When the `Receiver` ends, so do the values still
  queued**: it takes them out under the channel's lock and ends them after letting the lock go, so a
  `Sender` queued in its own channel (`tx.send(copy of tx)`) does not keep the channel alive.
* `[THR-4]` In the `debug` profile the runtime records the order in which each thread takes locks and
  prints `warning: lock order inversion` with both acquisition sites when two threads take two locks
  in opposite orders. It never changes a program's behaviour.
* `[THR-6]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A type whose `drop` a safety guarantee depends on is
  `@must_drop`. A `@must_drop` value MUST NOT be stored in a class field, a `shares` or `thread_shared`
  value, an `owns` block, a collection or a function value's state (a capture word), held across a
  `yield` (`[CORO-13]`), or returned from the function that created it (`E3015`); every value's `drop`
  runs at its end. The standard library applies it to `Scope` and `JobScope` only. It is structural: a
  struct, enum, tuple or generic type that owns a `@must_drop` value is `@must_drop` too, whatever its
  own `drop` does, so wrapping one hides nothing; a view of one is not, since it lives no longer than the
  value it views. A `Scope` or `JobScope` cannot be put in a wrapper at all (`[THR-5]`) (ODR-054).

## XI.3 Scoped tasks

A scoped task may use the caller's own variables, because the scope does not end until every task in it
has finished.

```ember
import std.thread

fn sum_halves(xs: Span[int]) -> int:
    left, right = xs.split_at(xs.len() // 2)
    with scope = thread.scope():
        a = scope.spawn(fn() => left.iter().sum())
        b = scope.spawn(fn() => right.iter().sum())
        return a.join() + b.join()

fn count_words(texts: Array[String]) -> int:
    total = 0
    with scope = thread.scope():
        for t in texts:
            scope.spawn(fn() ref t: total += t.split_whitespace().count())
    return total
```

* `[THR-5]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `thread.scope()` returns a `Scope`, which MUST be
  bound by a `with` (`E3014` otherwise). The `with` block is ordinary code of the enclosing function:
  `return`, `break`, `continue` and `?` inside it mean what they mean anywhere else. On **every** exit
  from the block — falling off its end, a jump, or `?` — the scope first joins every task spawned in it
  that has not been joined, and then the exit completes; the value of a `return` is computed before the
  join. The `Scope` binding is a view whose life is the block and is `@must_drop` (`[THR-6]`): it cannot
  be handed over, stored, returned or held in a function value's state. A `with scope` block that ends
  inside a lock's `with` block, when a task's function changes what that lock guards, is `E7018`
  (`[THR-19]`).
* `[THR-11]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `scope.spawn` takes a plain function, `[R]` above
  `fn spawn(owns f: fn() -> R) -> ScopedJoinHandle[R]:`. A task needs no capture words but for the
  loop's own variable and a local of one round (`[THR-17]`): it uses the caller's real variables, which
  outlive it. What each task changes and reads is worked out from its body and every function it may run
  (`[EFF-24]`), and is checked against the other tasks and the parent until the task's join: `h.join()`
  on its handle, or the end of the `with scope:` block for a task not joined before it (verdict 104).
  After `h.join()` the parent may change or read what that task used, in the same block
  (`counts[0] += 1` after `h.join()`), checked only against the tasks not yet joined: two of them
  changing one place, or one reading a place another changes, is `E7007`, other than by a reduction
  (`[THR-21]`), under a lock, or through an `Atomic`. A task that reads a place before changing it needs
  the lock, which keeps the read and the change together ("two tasks change `stats.total` (line 19), and
  each reads it first (`if stats.total < 10:`, line 18), so each may see a total the other is changing;
  guard it, which keeps the read and the add together: write `from std.sync import Lock` at the top, in
  `Stats` `lock: Lock = Lock()`, `total: int guarded by lock = 0` and `fn add_below(limit: int, n:
  int):` whose body is `with this.lock:`, inside it `if this.total < limit:` and inside that
  `this.total += n`, and call `stats.add_below(10, x)` in place of lines 18 and 19"). A task started
  inside a walk of what it changes is `E3020` ("`scope.spawn(...)` (line 6) starts a task that pushes to
  `names` (`fn(): names.push(String("x"))`), which this loop walks (line 5); start it after the loop:
  move line 6 below the loop"), not `E7007`, whose fix would leave the walk refused. A task makes, ends
  or opens a `weakref` link only to a `thread_shared` target, and makes no `shares` owner (`[THR-2]`).
  `R` MUST be `Send`. `h.join() -> R` waits early.
* `[THR-21]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Reductions.** A task's `total += e` (and `-=`, `*=`, `|=`, `&=`, `^=`,
  `max`, `min`, `push`, `extend`, `add`, `m[k] op= e`) on a local, or on a field of an object the tasks
  reach (`scope.spawn(fn() copy of x: stats.total += x)`), a field reached through two `sharedref mut`
  links to one object included, is a reduction: each task adds into a private accumulator, and the
  accumulators are combined into the place at the join, in spawn order. Nothing reads the place before
  the join (`E7007`: "tasks add their parts to `total`, which is known only once the `with` block (lines
  11 to 14) ends; read it after the block: remove line 14 and write `println(total)` above line 15").
  Each task's accumulator has the place's type, and its operations are checked as the place's are, and
  so are the combining operations at the join (verdict 105): a whole-number total is the one adding one
  by one gives whenever no task's own total overflows (`a.target.hp -= 1` and `b.target.hp -= 2` from
  two tasks, `a` and `b` linking one player whose `hp` is 10, leave 7 every time), and a task whose own
  total overflows stops the program there (`[TYP-8]`), even where adding one by one would not
  (`[[-100], [100, 100]]` summed into an `i8` by two tasks stops in the second, at 100 + 100, where
  adding one by one gives 100); a decimal total may differ from it in the last digit (`for part in [[0.1], [0.2, 0.3]]:` with
  `scope.spawn(fn() copy of part: for x in part: total += x)` gives `0.6`, where adding one by one gives
  `0.6000000000000001`), and is the same on every run, so it is not `Nondet` (`[DET-2]`). A plain
  assignment from a task (`a.target.hp = 5`) and a task that reads the current value
  (`if stats.total < 10: stats.total += x`) need a lock (`E7007`). A `thread.spawn` thread has no
  reductions: it changes what other threads reach under a lock, or, where it only adds, through an
  `Atomic`.
* `[THR-12]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* Tasks that must run in sequence and share data use two
  scopes in sequence: the join at the end of the first is the ordering, and the views of the first end
  there.

## XI.4 Parallel loops

```ember
class Player:
    hp: int = 10

fn integrate(ref mut pos: MutSpan[float], vel: Span[float], dt: float):
    @parallel(chunk=4096)
    for i in 0..pos.len():
        pos[i] += vel[i] * dt

fn hurt_all(ref mut players: Array[Player]):
    @parallel
    for ref mut p in players:
        p.hp -= 1
```

* `[PAR-1]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A `@parallel` loop splits a range (`for i in 0..n:`) or a list walked by
  element (`for ref mut p in players:`) into chunks, and runs its body over each chunk on the job system
  (§XI.5). Over anything else it is `E7016` ("`@parallel` splits a range or a list into chunks, and
  `while i < idx.len():` (line 4) in `place` is neither; instead of `i = 0`, the `while` line and
  `i += 1`, write `for i in 0..idx.len():`").
* `[PAR-2]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Iterations MUST be independent.** The body MUST NOT contain `break`,
  `return`, `yield`, or a `continue` naming an outer loop, and what it uses from outside follows the
  rules of a scoped task (`[THR-11]`, `[THR-2]`). In a loop over a range, for each place `P` written in
  the body the compiler collects every index expression through which `P` is accessed in the body,
  **reads included**. The loop is accepted only if (a) each has the form `i + k` for a constant `k`;
  (b) all of them share **one** `k`; and (c) `P` is the elements of a `MutSpan` or an `SoA` column the
  loop uses, not a place reached through a link (`shares`, `shares mut`, `sharedref mut`,
  `thread_shared`), a `Cell` or a raw pointer. A loop walked by element hands each chunk its own elements
  through the loop's `ref mut` name, and writes nothing else but declared reductions (`[PAR-3]`); its
  list holds each element once, so a list whose objects may be in it twice (`Array[shares mut Player]`)
  is refused. Otherwise `E7010`, whose message gives the lines that make the loop compile ("the parallel
  loop writes `xs[idx[i]]`, and two rounds may have the same `idx[i]`, so two threads could write one
  element; run the loop on one thread: remove `@parallel` (line 7)"; "`players` holds `shares mut
  Player` objects, and one object may be in the list twice, so two chunks could change it at once; give
  each player one owner: write `players: Array[Player] = []` in place of line 3, and
  `players.push(Player(hp=10))` in place of `players.push(shares mut p)` on line 5"); where an `Atomic`,
  `chunks_mut` or `@parallel(reduce=…)` makes the loop compile, the message gives that line.
* `[PAR-2a]` A violation of clause (b) is `E7011`, `parallel loop has a loop-carried dependency on
  <place>`, naming both offsets and offering: two `@parallel` loops, a reduction, or a serial loop.
* `[PAR-2b]` The analysis reads through the body's calls as if inlined: each call to a function
  `[CG-C-3]` places in the inline header, recursively until a call is recursive — never according to
  what the C compiler chose to inline. A call it cannot see into that receives a captured `MutSpan`
  or column defeats the proof for everything reachable through that argument (`E7010`) (ODR-062).
* `[PAR-3]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* `@parallel(reduce=[total: +, best: max])` declares variables combined
  after the loop; inside the body each chunk has its own copy. Each chunk reduces its iterations left
  to right, and the chunk results are then combined in chunk order, so the result is the same on
  every machine (`[PAR-5]`); for floats it can differ from the serial left-to-right sum, which is
  why a float reduction must be declared. A whole-number reduction's chunk results have the variable's
  type and stop the program on overflow, as `[THR-21]`'s task totals do (verdict 105): the result is the
  serial one whenever no chunk's own total overflows, and since chunk boundaries depend only on the trip
  count and `chunk`, whether it stops does not depend on the machine.
* `[PAR-4]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* A `@parallel` loop has the effects `Sync` and `Block` (it waits for
  its chunks) and not `Alloc`: its chunk descriptors live in the calling frame and the job queues have
  a fixed capacity; when they are full the calling thread runs the chunk itself.
* `[PAR-5]` *(new in 0.9.9)* **Parallel results do not depend on the machine.** Chunk boundaries are a
  function of the trip count and `chunk` only (a default `chunk` is a function of the trip count
  only), and reductions combine per-chunk results in chunk order. A `@parallel` loop therefore
  computes the same bits whatever the worker count and scheduling, and is not `Nondet` (`[DET-2]`).

## XI.5 The job system (`std.jobs`)

The job system is a pool of worker threads with work-stealing queues. The runtime starts it before
`main` in any program that uses `@parallel` or `std.jobs`, with the worker count from the manifest
(`[jobs] workers = "auto"`, meaning logical cores minus one).

```ember
import std.jobs
from std.math import Vec3

fn integrate(ref mut pos: MutSpan[Vec3], vel: Span[Vec3], dt: f32):
    for i in 0..pos.len():
        pos[i] += vel[i] * dt

fn age(ref mut life: MutSpan[f32], dt: f32):
    for i in 0..life.len():
        life[i] -= dt

fn step(ref mut pos: MutSpan[Vec3], vel: Span[Vec3], ref mut life: MutSpan[f32], dt: f32):
    with s = jobs.scope():
        s.submit(fn(): integrate(ref mut pos, vel, dt))
        s.submit(fn(): age(ref mut life, dt))
```

* `[JOB-1]` A job's captured state is stored inline in its queue slot when it fits in 64 bytes and in
  one heap allocation otherwise (`Alloc`, reported by `ember inspect --alloc`).
* `[JOB-2]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `jobs.scope()` follows `[THR-5]` and `[THR-11]`:
  `s.submit` on a `JobScope` takes a plain function (`owns f: fn()`), whose jobs may use the caller's own
  variables, and the block's exit joins them. `jobs.submit` outside a scope takes a function any thread
  may run, `pub fn submit(owns f: thread_shared fn()) -> JobHandle:`, as `thread.spawn` does
  (`[THR-10]`, `[THR-17]`): a function that holds a one-thread value is `E7015`, and a name used with no
  capture word `E7004`. `jobs.wait(h)` waits for it.
* `[JOB-3]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `s.submit_after(deps, f)` starts `f` only after
  the jobs in `deps` have finished. It orders execution; it does not relax `[THR-11]`, which treats
  every job of a scope as running at once. (The 0.9.8 declared read/write access sets, verified only in
  debug builds, are removed: a safety property checked in one profile is not a guarantee, `[PHIL-13]`.)
* `[JOB-5]` `jobs.local_arena()` returns an arena view for the current job, reset when the job ends;
  allocations from it cannot escape the job.

## XI.6 Async

`async` and `await` are reserved words (§II.4). Ember's workloads are covered by threads, scoped tasks,
jobs and generators (§VI.5a); a later version may add structured async over the job system, in which
a view may not cross an `await` unless the future is scoped. Generators are designed so that this
remains possible: a generator frame is a sized value, and the same frame lowering serves an
`async fn`.
---

# Part XII — Data-Oriented Programming

Data-oriented code keeps each field of many objects in its own contiguous array, walks those arrays
in tight loops, and lets the machine's vector units do several elements per instruction. Ember makes
that layout a one-word change and makes the loops provably free of aliasing, so they run at C speed
with the safety checks either proved away or hoisted out.

## XII.1 `SoA[T]`

```ember
from std.math import Vec3

struct Particle:
    pos: Vec3
    vel: Vec3
    life: f32

fn integrate(ref mut pos: MutSpan[Vec3], vel: Span[Vec3], dt: f32):
    for i in 0..pos.len():
        pos[i] += vel[i] * dt

fn main():
    ps = SoA[Particle].with_capacity(100_000)
    ps.push(Particle(pos=Vec3.ZERO, vel=Vec3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0), life=2.0))
    integrate(ref mut ps.pos, ps.vel, 0.016)  # two columns at once: never one place
    ps[0].life -= 0.016                     # writes one element of the `life` column
    p = ps.get(0)                           # Option[SoARef[Particle]]: names particle 0, no copy
    snapshot = copy of ps[0]                # a Particle of your own, gathered from the columns
```

* `[SOA-1]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* `SoA[T]` is a **compiler-known type constructor**, like `Cell`: for
  any struct `T` it is a growable container holding one column per field of `T`. No derive is needed.
  `T` MUST be a struct (`E2071` otherwise). A field marked `@soa(flatten)` whose type is a struct is
  split into one column per field of its own (`ps.pos.x`); otherwise a struct field is one column.
* `[SOA-2]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `ps.f` names the column of field `f`: a view of that column's elements, a `MutSpan[F]`,
  which supports everything a `MutSpan` supports and converts to `Span[F]` where one is expected
  (`[SPN-3]`). Like every `MutSpan`, it writes the elements only through a name or argument that says
  `ref mut` (`d = ref mut ps.pos`; `integrate(ref mut ps.pos, ps.vel, dt)`), and only where `ps` itself
  is reached through a name that may change it (`E3027` otherwise); a plain name holding a column only
  reads it (`E3023`). Different columns
  are different places, as different fields are (`[BRW-4]`), so any number of them may be named or
  given to one call at once, changeable or not. A length-changing operation (`push`, `pop`,
  `swap_remove`, `retain`, `clear`) is a reshape of all of `ps`: it may move the block every column
  lives in, so it ends every view of a column (`E3060` at a later use), and it may not run while a loop
  walks `ps` or one of its columns (`E3020`).
* `[SOA-6]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `ps[i]` is an **element proxy**: `SoARef[T]`, a read-only name of element
  `i`, and `ref mut ps[i]` an `SoAMut[T]`, a name of it that may change it. A proxy is a position: it
  finds element `i` again at each use, so adding to `ps` keeps it, and a removal, reorder or clear ends
  it (`E3060` at a later use). A proxy's field `ps[i].f` is a place in column `f` at index `i`; reading
  or writing it touches that column only, and no `T` is assembled. `ps.get(i) -> Option[SoARef[T]]`
  names element `i` as `ps[i]` does, with no copy, as `Array.get` does. `copy of ps[i]` gathers a `T`
  of your own (for `T: Clone`) by the proxy's `load()`, the method `copy of` runs here as it runs
  `clone` elsewhere; `load()` written at a use is `E1010` ("write `copy of ps[0]`"). `ps[i] = v`
  scatters a value. `for p in ps:` yields `SoARef[T]`, `for ref mut p in ps:` yields `SoAMut[T]`. While
  an `SoAMut[T]` is still used it is the only name of its element: a column named separately that
  reaches the element is refused (`E3021` to read it, `E3022` to change it); while an `SoARef[T]` is
  still used, a change of its element through another name is `E3021`.
* `[SOA-3]` `SoA[T]` provides `len`, `is_empty`, `push`, `pop`, `swap_remove`, `retain`, `clear`,
  `reserve`, `with_capacity`, and `sort_by_key` over any column; every operation keeps the columns
  aligned element for element.
* `[SOA-7]` *(new in 0.9.9)* All columns of one `SoA[T]` live in **one heap block**, each column
  starting at an address aligned to the larger of 64 bytes and its element type's alignment. Growth
  reallocates the block once. A column's base pointer is therefore suitable for aligned vector loads.
* `[SOA-4]` `ArenaSoA[T]` is the fixed-capacity, arena-backed form, under the rules of `[ARN-5]`.

## XII.2 SIMD

```ember
from std.simd import f32x8

fn scale(xs: Span[f32], ref mut out: MutSpan[f32], k: f32):
    assert(xs.len() == out.len() and xs.len() % 8 == 0)
    kv = f32x8.splat(k)
    for i in (0..xs.len()).step_by(8):
        v = f32x8.load(xs[i..i + 8])
        (v * kv).store(ref mut out[i..i + 8])
```

* `[SIMD-1]` `std.simd` provides vector types `f32x4`, `f32x8`, `f32x16`, `f64x2`, `f64x4`, `f64x8`,
  the signed and unsigned integer vectors of 8 to 64-bit lanes, and mask types. They are `Copy` value
  types aligned to their size. On the C backend they lower to the target's intrinsics through
  `ember_simd.h`, with a scalar fallback on targets without them; on the LLVM backend, to LLVM's
  vector types (`[CG-LL-2]`). `f32x8.LANES` is the lane count;
  `simd.native_lanes[T]()` is the target's preferred count, a compile-time constant.
* `[SIMD-8]` *(new in 0.9.9)* Vector operators are lane-wise and follow the scalar rules: integer
  lanes panic on overflow (`[TYP-8]`) unless the function is `@overflow(wrap)` or the code calls
  `wrapping_add` and friends; float lanes are IEEE with no contraction (`[TYP-9]`).
* `[SIMD-4]` Horizontal operations (`reduce_add`, `reduce_min`, `reduce_max`), shuffles with a
  constant lane list, gathers, scatters, `fma`, and approximations named `_approx` (`rsqrt_approx`,
  `rcp_approx`) are provided.
* `[SIMD-9]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* SIMD memory operations are bounds-checked like indexing. `V.load(s)` and
  `v.store(s)` require `s.len() >= V.LANES`; `V.gather(s, idx)` and `v.scatter(s, idx)` check every
  lane's index against `s.len()`; each failure is a `Bounds` panic naming the lane. A store and a
  scatter write the caller's elements, so their span is a `ref mut` parameter, and the call says so:
  `v.store(ref mut s)`, `v.scatter(ref mut s, idx)` (`E3028` without it). The unchecked forms
  (`load_unchecked`, `store_unchecked`, `gather_unchecked`, `scatter_unchecked`) are `unsafe fn`. A
  `load` or `store` at a loop's induction variable is covered by the entry test of `[OPT-2]`.
* `[SIMD-2]` `@simd` on a `for` loop is a request and a report: the compiler tries to vectorise the
  loop and `--emit-optimization-report` says whether it did and why not. It never changes meaning.
  `@simd(assert)` makes failure `E4020`.
* `[SIMD-3]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* Alias facts given to the backend (`restrict` on the C backend, `noalias` on the LLVM backend) MUST be derived, never assumed. Two views
  are marked disjoint only when (a) the compiler related them to one owner and proved their ranges
  disjoint; (b) they come from owners proved distinct in the same function; (c) they are results of
  `split_at`, `chunks_mut` or distinct `SoA` columns; (d) they carry a fact established by
  `assert_disjoint` (`[DSJ-1]`), which stops the program when they overlap, or asserted by
  `unsafe assume_disjoint`; or (e) one of them is a `ref mut` parameter, a `MutSpan` one included:
  every call is checked, when compiling, to give it a place the function reaches by no other name while
  the parameter is used, so every `ref mut` parameter is compiled with `noalias` (a call that names one
  whole variable twice is compiled against its own copy of the function, in which the two names are
  one). A view built by `unsafe` code or received through FFI may alias until (d) is applied. A view
  reached through a link (a `shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared` or `sharedref mut` link, or a view
  kept in a struct or a list), and `this`, get an alias fact from (a)–(c) only when the compiler proves
  that no other path the loop uses reaches the same object (the two have different types, one is an
  object made in this function, or the loop is inside `if a is not b:`), because a write through
  another link may change what it views. `this` is never compiled with `noalias`: a method that changes
  its object may also reach it through a link. Two views being live at once is not a proof, and neither
  is a plain parameter's word.
* `[SIMD-5]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* **Vectorisable form**, which `@simd(assert)` checks, is computed by
  Ember and never delegated to the C compiler. A loop is in vectorisable form when: its trip count is
  known before entry; every memory access is to a local or to a view at a unit-stride affine index of
  the induction variable; every written place is accessed at one constant offset (`[PAR-2]`(b)); every
  written view is disjoint from every other accessed view by `[SIMD-3]`; every call in the body is
  to a function `[CG-C-3]` places in the inline header, read through as `[PAR-2b]` says, whatever
  the C compiler then does (ODR-062); the body has none of `Alloc`, `Sync`, `Block`, `Io`, `FFI`,
  `Panic(Explicit)`; no integer division or remainder in the body is by a divisor that is not a
  constant, nor, at 64 bits or more, by a constant that is not a power of two, since no vector
  instruction set does either and such a loop runs one iteration at a time (ODR-088); every
  `RuntimeCheck(Bounds)` has been removed by `[OPT-2]`; every
  `RuntimeCheck(Arithmetic)` is removed, is one `[SIMD-7]` permits grouping (grouping is then
  required), or belongs to a running total `[SIMD-7]` proves safe block by block; the loop has one exit; and every floating-point reduction is declared by `@parallel(reduce=…)` or the function is `@fastmath`.
  `E4020` names the first clause that fails, and for a remaining check its reason (`[EFF-11]`).
* `[SIMD-7]` *(new in 0.9.9)* **Grouped overflow checks.** In a loop whose body has none of `Sync`,
  `Io`, `FFI`, `Unsafe` and `Block`, the compiler MAY check integer overflow once per group of
  iterations (a vector's width times the unroll factor) instead of once per operation, and in a loop in
  vectorisable form (`[SIMD-5]`) it MUST: it computes the group with wrapping arithmetic, accumulates the lanes' overflow bits, and panics at the end of the
  group, reporting the source location of the first overflowing iteration. This is not observable:
  the body's writes go only to memory this thread owns, and the process aborts before anything reads
  them. Bounds checks are never grouped. An integer **running total**, a local the loop changes only
  by `total = total ± x` (`total += xs[i]`), is not grouped: each partial sum waits for the one
  before, so grouping its checks would only add work (ODR-086). It is vectorised under checked
  arithmetic only when no partial sum can overflow in any grouping, which the compiler proves in one
  of two ways. From the element and accumulator widths, versioning the loop on the trip count as
  `[OPT-2]` does: a sum of 32-bit elements into an `int` is safe for fewer than 2³¹ elements. Or, for
  a signed total of *w* ≥ 16 bits, at run time over each block of 64 iterations: the total lies in
  [−2^(w−2), 2^(w−2)) at the block's start and every value the block adds or subtracts lies in
  [−2^(w−9), 2^(w−9)), so no partial sum can leave the type in any order, and the block runs without
  per-operation checks. A block that fails the test runs checked, and so does the rest of the loop. A
  running total proved safe neither way keeps a check on every operation, and its loop is not in
  vectorisable form.
* `[SIMD-6]` The C compiler's own vectorisation report is corroborating evidence only.
  `--emit-optimization-report` prints it labelled as the host compiler's opinion, after Ember's
  vectorisable-form verdict; its absence or disagreement is never an error.

## XII.3 ECS (`std.ecs`)

The entity-component system is an ordinary library, EnTT's design (EnTT 3.x: `entt::registry`, its
views, groups, signals and snapshots) written in Ember: a `Registry` holds entities and one pool per
component type, and a program walks the entities that have a set of components through a view. Any
type is a component, with no registration. There is no scheduler: the library runs nothing on its own,
and the compiler gives it no support of its own.

```ember
from std.ecs import Registry
from std.math import Vec3

@derive(Copy)
struct Position:
    value: Vec3

@derive(Copy)
struct Velocity:
    value: Vec3

@noalloc
fn integrate(ref mut reg: Registry, dt: f32):
    for e, ref mut pos, ref mut vel in reg.view_mut[(Position, Velocity)]():
        pos.value += vel.value * dt

fn main():
    reg = Registry()
    e = reg.create()
    reg.emplace(e, Position(value=Vec3.ZERO))
    reg.emplace(e, Velocity(value=Vec3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)))
    integrate(ref mut reg, 0.016)
```

* `[ECS-1]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `Entity` is a 32-bit generational handle: a 20-bit index and a 12-bit
  generation (`Handle` with `Split20`, `[HND-2]`), EnTT's default `entt::entity`; `Entity.NULL` is all
  ones (`entt::null`). The compact split is kept so entity ids match engines that use it; general `Pool`
  handles are 64-bit (`[HND-1]`).
* `[ECS-2]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Each component type is stored in a pool of its own, a sparse set: a
  dense `Array[T]` of the values, the entities in dense order, and a sparse index by entity
  (`basic_sparse_set` with `basic_storage`); removal is swap-and-pop. A pool is one contiguous array, not
  paged: no Ember name can keep a view into a pool across a change that may move it (§VII), so a stable
  address is never needed, and one array walks at least as fast. A component type's identity is the
  64-bit FNV-1a hash of its fully qualified name, which `std.core.type_name[T]()` gives (a function the
  compiler knows, as Rust's `std::any::type_name`): `ecs.type_hash[T]()`, stable across builds and
  modules. The registry keeps its pools as `pools: Map[u64, owns dyn AnyStorage]`: each pool has one owner,
  with no count, and `reg.storage[T]()` reaches its own pool as a place,
  `pool = ref mut cast this.pools[ecs.type_hash[T]()] as Storage[T]` (`[TYP-44]`, `[DSP-4]`); the pool
  type is `Storage[T]`, EnTT's `storage<T>` (`std.collections.Pool[T]` is the handle pool, `[HND-1]`).
* `[ECS-3]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **The registry.** `Registry` (EnTT's `entt::registry`) is a class:
  `create() -> Entity` and `create_at(hint: Entity) -> Entity`; `destroy(e) -> u32` (the entity's next
  generation); `valid(e)`, `current(e)`; `clear()` and `clear_of[T]()`; `emplace(e, owns value: T) -> ref
  mut T`, `emplace_or_replace(e, owns value: T) -> ref mut T`, `replace(e, owns value: T) -> ref mut T`
  (a stop when `e` has no `T`), `patch[T](e, f: fn(ref mut T)) -> ref mut T`, `insert(entities:
  Span[Entity], value: T)` for a `T: Clone`; `remove[T](e) -> int` (0 when absent) and `erase[T](e)` (a
  stop when absent); `get[T](e) -> ref T` and `get_mut[T](e) -> ref mut T`, `try_get[T](e) -> Option[ref
  T]` and `try_get_mut[T](e) -> Option[ref mut T]`, `get_or_emplace(e, owns value: T) -> ref mut T`;
  `all_of[(A, B)](e)` and `any_of[(A, B)](e)`; `orphan(e)`; `storage[T]() -> ref mut Storage[T]`, which a
  `for e, ref mut value in reg.storage[T]()` walks. Several types are one tuple type (`[(A, B)]`), since
  Ember has neither variadic generics nor overloading (`[TYP-19]`). A view a method gives points into the
  registry (`[LT-1]`), so the registry is not changed through another name while it is used (§VII).
* `[ECS-4]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Views.** `reg.view[(A, B)]()` walks the entities that have every
  listed component and gives each item read-only (`for e, a, b in reg.view[(A, B)]():`);
  `reg.view_mut[(A, B)]()` gives every item `ref mut` (`for e, ref mut a, ref mut b in
  reg.view_mut[(A, B)]():`), which changes the values in place. The items of one entity are values of
  different types, so they never name one place. `.exclude[(C,)]()` leaves out the entities that have a
  `C`. A view has `each(f)`, `get[T](e)`, `contains(e)`, `size_hint()`, `front()` and `back()`. A view
  walks its smallest pool and probes the others. The library implements its view interface for tuples
  of 1 to 8 types with a blanket implementation over the element types (`[GRM-34]`), so any type is a
  component.
* `[ECS-5]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Changing the registry while a view walks it.** A view walks the
  registry's pools, so while a `for` loop walks a view, adding, removing, creating or destroying through
  the registry is refused when compiling, as for any collection a loop walks (`[BRW-18]`, `E3020`: "`reg.destroy(e)`
  (line 6) changes `reg`, whose pools this loop walks (line 4); collect the entities in a list of your
  own: write `dead: Array[Entity] = []` before the loop, `dead.push(e)` in place of this line, and `for d
  in dead: reg.destroy(d)` after the loop"). The values themselves change through the view's `ref mut`
  items. EnTT allows some such changes through paged pools; Ember collects first and changes after.
* `[ECS-6]` Iteration order is insertion order with swap-remove holes: deterministic for a given
  sequence of operations.
* `[ECS-7]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Any type is a component, with no registration and no derive. A tool
  that needs a list of component types reads the program's own types (Part XIV).
* `[ECS-8]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Signals, sorting, context, groups, snapshots.** `on_construct[T]()`,
  `on_update[T]()` and `on_destroy[T]()` give a signal; `.connect(f)` and `.disconnect(f)` take a
  `f: fn(ref mut Registry, Entity)`, which the registry calls after the change is made, when no view of
  a pool is in use, so a listener that changes the registry is safe (the call check, `[BRW-21]`, holds
  for the library's own code). `sort[T](less)` and `sort_as[To, From]()` reorder a pool. `ctx()` keeps
  one value per type (`emplace`, `get`, `get_mut`, `find`, `contains`, `erase`). `group[(A, B)]()` packs
  the owned pools in one order. `Snapshot`, `SnapshotLoader` and `ContinuousLoader` save and load a
  registry through an archive given as a type parameter; `RuntimeView` walks pools chosen while the
  program runs; `Handle` pairs a registry and an entity.
* `[ECS-9]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **No scheduler.** The library runs no systems: a program calls its own
  functions on the registry. Work it runs at once goes through `std.thread` or `std.jobs` with the rules
  of Part XI, and two pieces of work run at once that may touch one pool, one changing it, are refused
  when compiling, worked out from every function the program can put there; nothing compares them while
  the program runs.
---

# Part XIII — Error Handling

A failure the caller can handle is a **value**: a function that can fail returns `Result`, and `?`
passes a failure up. A failure that means the program is wrong — an index out of range, an overflow,
a broken invariant — is a **panic**, which stops the process (`[PAN-1]`). There are no exceptions and
no hidden control flow: every place a function can return early is marked by `?` or `return`.

```ember
import std.fs

@derive(Error)
enum ConfigError:
    @error("line {line}: expected `key = value`")
    Syntax(line: int)
    @error("line {line}: `{key}` is not a number")
    NotNumber(line: int, key: String)

fn parse(text: StrView) -> Result[Map[String, int], ConfigError]:
    out: Map[String, int] = {}
    for n, line in text.lines().enumerate():
        key, sep, value = line.partition("=")
        if sep.is_empty():
            return Err(ConfigError.Syntax(line=n + 1))
        match value.trim().parse[int]():
            Ok(v):
                out[key.trim()] = v
            Err(_):
                return Err(ConfigError.NotNumber(line=n + 1, key=String(key.trim())))
    return Ok(out)

fn main() -> Result[void]:
    text = fs.read_to_string("app.cfg")?            # io.Error -> AnyError
    cfg = parse(text).context("reading app.cfg")?   # ConfigError -> AnyError, with a message
    println(cfg)
    return Ok(())
```

## XIII.1 `Result`, `Option` and `?`

* `[ERR-1]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* `Option[T]` is absence: `Some(v)` or `None`. `Result[T, E = AnyError]`
  is success or failure: `Ok(v)` or `Err(e)`. Both are ordinary enums in the prelude, and neither
  parameter is bounded: `Result[int, int]` is a `Result`. An operation that needs more of `E` says so
  (ODR-050): `?` into another error type needs `From[E]` (`[ERR-2]`), printing one needs `Display`,
  walking its causes needs `Error` (or is `AnyError`'s own, `[ERR-8]`), and converting one into
  `AnyError` needs `E: Error`.
* `[ERR-9]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* The error parameter defaults to `AnyError` (§XIII.2), so
  `fn load(path: StrView) -> Result[Texture]` is a function that can fail with any error. A library that
  wants callers to `match` on its failures names a concrete error type.
* `[ERR-2]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `e?` on a `Result[T, E]` in a function returning `Result[U, F]`
  evaluates to the `Ok` payload, or returns `Err(F.from(err))`. On an `Option[T]` in a function
  returning `Option[U]` it evaluates to the `Some` payload or returns `None`. When `E` and `F` are the
  same type the error is handed over with no call. `?` in a function returning neither is `E2180`.
  `?` on an `Option` in a function returning `Result`, or on a `Result` in a function returning
  `Option`, is `E2181`, whose fix-its are `.ok_or(err)?` and `.ok()?`.
* `[ERR-4]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `Option` and `Result` provide `is_some`/`is_none`,
  `is_ok`/`is_err`, `unwrap`, `expect`, `unwrap_or`, `unwrap_or_else`, `unwrap_or_default`, `map`, `map_err`,
  `and_then`, `or_else`, `ok`, `err`, `ok_or`, `ok_or_else`, `filter`, `take`, `replace`, `as_ref`,
  `as_mut`, `iter`, and `context` (`[ERR-10]`). `unwrap` and `expect` panic with the error's `Display`
  text. `Option[T]`'s `fn as_ref() -> Option[ref T]` and `fn as_mut() -> Option[ref mut T]` give a
  view of the payload where it is, whatever `T` is (ODR-094): a pattern binds a `Copy` payload by
  value (`[GRM-13]`), so these are how a function hands out a view into an `Option` it holds; the
  view points into the `Option`, and `as_mut` is called through a name that may change it.
  The methods that take a function are eager: each takes its object over (`owns this`), takes the
  function as a type parameter (`[CLO-14]`) and calls it at most once, before it returns, handing
  the payload over to it, except `filter`, whose function reads it (ODR-025):
  * `Option[T]`: `[U, F: once fn(owns T) -> U]` above `fn map(owns f: F) owns this -> Option[U]`;
    `[U, F: once fn(owns T) -> Option[U]]` above `fn and_then(owns f: F) owns this -> Option[U]`;
    `[F: once fn(T) -> bool]` above `fn filter(owns f: F) owns this -> Option[T]`;
    `[F: once fn() -> Option[T]]` above `fn or_else(owns f: F) owns this -> Option[T]`;
    `[F: once fn() -> T]` above `fn unwrap_or_else(owns f: F) owns this -> T`; and
    `[E, F: once fn() -> E]` above `fn ok_or_else(owns f: F) owns this -> Result[T, E]`;
  * `Result[T, E]`: `[U, F: once fn(owns T) -> U]` above `fn map(owns f: F) owns this -> Result[U, E]`;
    `[F, G: once fn(owns E) -> F]` above `fn map_err(owns f: G) owns this -> Result[T, F]`;
    `[U, F: once fn(owns T) -> Result[U, E]]` above
    `fn and_then(owns f: F) owns this -> Result[U, E]`;
    `[F, G: once fn(owns E) -> Result[T, F]]` above `fn or_else(owns f: G) owns this -> Result[T, F]`;
    and `[F: once fn(owns E) -> T]` above `fn unwrap_or_else(owns f: F) owns this -> T`.
* `[ERR-5]` `Result` is `@must_use`: discarding one is `W2190` (an error under `-D warnings`). A value
  is used when it is bound, returned, passed, matched, or has `?` or a method applied.
* `[ERR-7]` **Identity conversion.** The prelude provides `From[T]` for every `T` (`from(v) = v`), so
  `?` propagates an unchanged error type. A user `extend T implements From[T]` is `E2041`.

## XIII.2 Error types and `AnyError`

* `[ERR-3]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `Error` is the interface of error types:
  `Display + Debug` with `fn source() -> Option[ref dyn Error]` (default `None`) (§IV.8).
  `@derive(Error)` on an enum or struct implements `Display` from `@error("…")` attributes — one per variant, whose `{name}` and
  `{0}` placeholders name the variant's fields — and implements `Debug` if it is not already derived.
  A variant marked `@from` whose single field is an error type gets `From` for that type and returns it
  from `source`.
* `[ERR-8]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **`AnyError`** is the
  prelude's "any error" type: a `dyn Error` held alone (`owns dyn Error`) plus an optional chain of
  context messages. It implements `From[E]` for every `E: Error`, so `?` converts any error into it,
  and `Display`, `Debug`, `source`, `[E]` above `fn downcast_ref() -> Option[ref E]`, and `[E]` above
  `fn is() -> bool`. **`AnyError` does not implement `Error`** — otherwise `[ERR-7]` and
  `[ERR-8]` would both supply `From[AnyError]` for `AnyError`. An `AnyError` passed through `?` into
  another `AnyError` is handed over (`[ERR-7]`). `AnyError.msg(owns text: String)`, a `static fn`,
  is an error whose text is `text`, so a function whose error type is `AnyError` fails with a message as `return
  Err(AnyError.msg(f"no such file: {p}"))`.
* `[ERR-10]` *(new in 0.9.9)* `r.context(msg)` on a `Result[T, E]` whose `E` converts into `AnyError`
  (`AnyError: From[E]`, `[ERR-8]`) returns a `Result[T, AnyError]`
  whose error, if any, displays as `msg: <original>`; `r.with_context(fn() => …)` builds the message
  only on failure. Context messages stack.
* `[ERR-11]` *(new in 0.9.9)* **The cost of `AnyError`.** Converting an error into `AnyError`
  allocates, once, on the failure path; that path carries `Alloc` (`[EFF-1]`). A concrete error type
  moves through `?` without allocating, which is why `@noalloc` code names its error types.
* `[ERR-12]` *(new in 0.9.9)* An `Err` returned from `main` (`[FN-8]`) prints `error: <Display>` to
  standard error, then one `caused by: <Display>` line for each cause in its chain — an `AnyError`'s
  own chain (`[ERR-8]`), or each `source` of an `E: Error` — and exits with status 1. An `E` that is
  `Display` but not `Error` has no chain and prints its message alone (ODR-050).

## XIII.3 Panics or errors

* `[ERR-13]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* The standard library follows one convention, and user code SHOULD: an
  operation whose failure is a bug in the caller panics (`xs[i]` out of range, `m[k]` for a missing
  key, integer overflow, `unwrap` on `None`); an operation whose failure depends on the world or on
  input returns `Result` or `Option` (`xs.get(i)`, `m.get(k)`, `parse`, every I/O call). Each
  panicking accessor has a non-panicking twin, and the panic message names it
  (`index 7 is out of bounds for a length of 3; use .get(i) for an Option`). The one exception is console input,
  which panics at end of input (`[STD-10]`), as Python's `input` raises.
* `[ERR-6]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* A foreign function's status code becomes a `Result` at the binding
  (Part XVI): an `@ffi(status=VkResult, ok=VK_SUCCESS, error=VkError)` overlay turns a `VkResult`
  return into `Result[void, VkError]`.

Python's `try`, `except`, `raise` and `finally` are not Ember syntax; each is diagnosed with the Ember
form (`[DIA-21]`): `raise e` → `return Err(e)`, a `try` body → `?` on each fallible call, `except E`
→ `match` on the result, `finally` → `defer:`.
---

# Part XIV — Compile-Time Programming

Ember runs ordinary Ember code at compile time. There is no second language for it, no macro system,
and no `comptime fn` marker: a function can run at compile time when what it does can.

```ember,fragment
from std.math import TAU
import math.det

@layout(c)
struct Vertex:
    pos: [f32; 3]
    normal: [f32; 3]
    uv: [f32; 2]

fn sine_table() -> [float; 256]:
    t = [0.0; 256]
    for i in 0..256:
        t[i] = det.sin(TAU * i as float / 256.0)
    return t

const SINE: [float; 256] = comptime(sine_table())

comptime:
    assert(mem.size_of[Vertex]() == 32, "Vertex layout changed; update the shader")
```

## XIV.1 Compile-time evaluation

* `[CT-1]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* These are evaluated during compilation: `comptime(e)`; `comptime:`
  blocks; `const` initialisers; array lengths and `const` generic arguments; and `static`
  initialisers that qualify under `[STA-3]`. Any function may be called there if its effect set
  contains nothing beyond `Alloc`, `Panic(Explicit)` and `RuntimeCheck` — no `Io`, `FFI`, `Sync`,
  `Block`, `Unsafe` or `Nondet`. Allocation is served by the evaluator's own heap.
* `[CT-6]` *(new in 0.9.9)* `comptime(e)` is an expression whose value is `e` evaluated at compile
  time. `e` may refer to constants, generic parameters, and statics initialised at compile time, not
  to run-time locals (`E6005`).
* `[CT-7]` *(new in 0.9.9)* A `comptime:` block at item level, or as a statement, runs once during
  compilation for its checks. A failed `assert` or any other panic there is `E6004`, which shows the
  panic message and the compile-time call chain.
* `[CT-2]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.10)* An operation that cannot run at compile time — an `extern` call, a
  thread, a clock, `unsafe` pointer access outside the evaluator's heap, I/O — is `E6010`, naming the
  call chain. A raw pointer made from an integer (`0 as *mut T`, `-1 as *mut T`) is a compile-time
  value: it is an address, read by nothing, and a `const` of pointer type may hold one; a pointer into
  the evaluator's heap may not leave it (`E6010`) (ODR-145). Two inputs are provided: `comptime.read_file(path)` (relative to the package root, and only inside the
  package directory, `E6010` otherwise, so a dependency's build cannot read the builder's files) and
  `comptime.env(name)`. Both are recorded as build inputs.
* `[CT-3]` Each evaluation is limited to 10⁸ steps and 256 MB of evaluator heap by default
  (`[comptime]` in the manifest); exceeding either is `E6001`.
* `[CT-4]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.10)* Compile-time evaluation is deterministic by construction: the evaluator
  has no source of `Nondet` (`[DET-2]`). A transcendental function runs at compile time when the
  source names `std.math.det`'s, with the same result it gives at run time; the platform library's
  `sin` is `Nondet` and does not run at compile time, and the evaluator never puts `det.sin` in its
  place (ODR-056). The evaluator is the compiler's own (`[CLI-21]`): a `const` value is never computed
  by building and running a C program, and the test suite runs every program both compiled and on the
  evaluator and fails on any difference. The evaluator computes integer and floating-point results exactly as the target does, including overflow panics
  and the target's pointer size, endianness and layout. The lexical overflow policy is the same
  at compile time and run time (`[TYP-8]`, ODR-084), including module constants and arithmetic
  inside a function; calling another function preserves that function's policy. A result is cached with its inputs (source,
  `read_file` contents, `env` values).
* `[CT-5]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Where results live.** A compile-time result is placed in the image as
  constant data. A value that owns heap memory (`Array`, `String`, `Map`, an `owns T`, …) is handled so
  that no run-time code ever grows, changes or frees constant data:
  * in a `static` (not `static mut`) whose type gives no name a way to change the value (no `Mutex`,
    `RwLock`, `Cell`, `Atomic` or `guarded by` field on the path to it), the value is materialised in
    read-only memory; statics are never dropped;
  * in a `static mut`, and in any other `static` whose memory a safe operation may write
    (`static LOG: Mutex[Array[String]] = Mutex([])`), the initialiser runs at run time on first access
    (`[STA-3]`), producing an ordinary heap value, so `static mut LOG: Array[String] = [String("start")]`
    may later grow, or replace its strings, without touching constant data;
  * a `comptime(e)` whose type owns heap memory is materialised once, as constant data, and the
    expression is a read-only view of it, with no copy: `t = comptime(table())` then `t[i]` reads the
    table made when compiling, and a change through `t` is `E3023`. `copy of comptime(e)` makes a value
    of your own, which may grow (`Alloc`).

  A `const` cannot own heap memory (§V.7).

## XIV.2 Reflection

* `[RFL-1]` `reflect[T]()` at compile time returns a `TypeDesc`: name, kind, size, alignment, fields
  (name, type, offset, attributes), variants, and attributes. It is not available at run time.
* `[RFL-2]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `@reflect` on a type emits run-time type information: `type_info[T]()`, and
  `h.type_info()` on a class object, return a `ref TypeInfo` with the same field descriptors. Tables
  no code reaches are removed at link time.
* `[RFL-3]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* **User attributes are declared.** A struct marked `@attribute` may be
  written as an attribute on the fields and declarations of `@reflect` types: `@Range(min=0.0,
  max=1.0)` is checked exactly like the constructor call `Range(min=0.0, max=1.0)`, and its value is
  readable through `TypeDesc` and `TypeInfo`. An attribute that names no built-in attribute and no
  visible `@attribute` struct is `E0104` (`[PHIL-12]`).

`std.ser` declares the descriptions (ODR-158): `TypeDesc` (`name`, `kind: TypeKind`, `size`, `align`,
`fields: Array[FieldDesc]`, `variants: Array[VariantDesc]`, `attributes: Array[AttributeDesc]`), and
`TypeInfo` is the same type. A description owns its text (`String`), so it is no view and lives in a
`static`; it owns arrays, so it is no `const` (`static D: TypeDesc = reflect[Point]()`). A field names
its type by name (`type_name`): a description of each field's type would not end for a recursive
type. A class field's offset is counted from the end of the object header, which the runtime owns
(`[OBJ-1]`). An attribute is its name and its arguments as `(name, AttrValue)` pairs, `AttrValue`
being `Int(i64)`, `Float(f64)`, `Str(String)`, `Bool(bool)` or `Char(char)`: a user attribute's
argument is named by the field it sets, a built-in attribute's positional argument by its position,
and a name written as an argument (`@derive(Eq)`) is its text. An `@attribute` struct's fields are
of those types (`E0104` otherwise). `@reflect` implements `std.ser.Reflect`, which `type_info[T: Reflect]()`
asks for (`E2040` without it), and a class derived from a `@reflect` class is `@reflect` too;
`reflect[T]()` outside what compile time evaluates is `E6010`.

`std.ser` declares the serialisation interfaces (ODR-159): `Writer` (a struct's `begin_struct(name,
version)`, `field(name)` before each field's value and `end_struct()`; an enum value's
`begin_variant(name)` and `end_variant()`; `begin_list(count)`/`end_list()`; `write_none()`,
`write_int`, `write_float`, `write_bool`, `write_str`) and `Reader` (the same, reading: `begin_struct()`
gives the version and `next_field()` each field's name in the data's order, `None` after the last;
`next_element()`, `read_none()`, `skip_value()`). A struct's version is the highest `@ser(since=N)` of its
fields, 0 with none. `std.ser.json` writes a struct as an object of its fields, `"$version"` first when
above 0; an enum value as an object whose `"$variant"` names the variant, followed by its payload's
fields; `None` as `null`. `std.ser.binary` is self-describing, a tag byte before each value, so a reader
skips a field it does not know. A field missing from the data takes its type's `Default` under
`@ser(default)` or `@ser(since=N)`.

## XIV.3 Derives

* `[DRV-1]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `@derive(…)` requests generated implementations. The built-in derives,
  and exactly what each generates, are:

  | Derive | Generates |
  |---|---|
  | `Copy` | the marker, and `Clone` with it, so `copy of` works on the type; every field MUST be `Copy`, the type MUST have no `drop`, and it MUST be a struct or an enum, since a class object is never `Copy` (`E2080`) |
  | `Clone` | field-wise clone (implicit per `[STR-5]`), which `copy of` runs: a field the value owns alone is cloned itself, and a link field is copied as one more link to the same target (a `shares` or `shares mut` field one more owner, a `weakref` field one more `weakref` link, a `sharedref mut` field one more holder) |
  | `Eq` | field-wise equality in declaration order; enums compare variant first (implicit per `[STR-5]`) |
  | `Debug` | `Point(x=1.0, y=2.0)` for a struct, `Shape.Circle(r=1.0)` for a variant, `Mode.Fast` for a unit variant; strings quoted (implicit per `[STR-5]`) |
  | `Display` | on a unit-only enum, the variant name; on a struct or payload enum, the `Debug` text |
  | `Ord` | lexicographic over fields in declaration order, each by `cmp`, the next only when it gives `Equal`; enums by variant order, then fields |
  | `Hash` | feeds each field in declaration order; enums feed the variant index first |
  | `Default` | each field's declared default, else its type's `Default`; for an enum, the variant marked `@default` |
  | `Error` | `[ERR-3]` |
  | `Serialize`, `Deserialize` | §XIV.4 |
  | `Zeroable` | `[ARN-11]` |

  A derive whose requirement a field does not meet is `E2080`, naming the field. The generated code
  is ordinary Ember that `ember inspect --expand <type>` prints.
* `[DRV-2]` User-defined derives are not in this version; `macro` is reserved for them.

## XIV.4 Serialisation (`std.ser`)

* `[SER-1]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `@derive(Serialize, Deserialize)` implements the method
  `[W: ser.Writer]` above `fn serialize(ref mut w: W) -> Result[void, SerError]` and the function
  `[R: ser.Reader]` above `static fn deserialize(ref mut r: R) -> Result[Self, SerError]`, over a
  field-tagged, versioned format; both are monomorphised per format, and each call says `ref mut`
  before the writer or reader (`p.serialize(ref mut w)`, `Point.deserialize(ref mut r)`).
  `std.ser.binary` and `std.ser.json` provide a writer and reader each. Field attributes: `@ser(skip)`, `@ser(rename="…")`,
  `@ser(default)`, `@ser(since=N)`.
* `[SER-2]` *(new in 0.9.9)* Deserialising never produces an invalid value: a range-typed field is
  checked (`[RNG-10a]`), an unknown enum tag is an error, and a missing field without `@ser(default)`
  or `@ser(since=…)` is an error.
---

# Part XV — The Standard Library

The standard library is one package, `std`. This Part fixes what every implementation provides and
what each operation means; `std/**/*.em` holds the exact signatures and becomes normative for
anything this Part leaves open.

## XV.1 Organisation and conventions

* `[STD-6]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `std` is layered, and each layer depends only on the ones before it: **core** (scalars,
  `Option`, `Result`, views, fixed-capacity containers, math, SIMD), **alloc** (`Array`, `String`,
  `Map`, `Set`, and the heap blocks of `owns` and `shares` values), **sync** (atomics, locks, channels, threads, jobs), **io** (console,
  files, time, processes) and **ffi**. A package that declares `[package] layers = ["core"]` may use
  only core; this is how firmware and kernels use Ember.
* `[STD-1]` Every function in `std.core`, `std.mem`, `std.math`, `std.simd` and `std.arena` is
  `@noalloc` unless its documentation says it allocates.
* `[STD-13]` *(new in 0.9.9)* **One naming convention.** Names are `snake_case` words joined by
  underscores (`starts_with`, `to_upper`, `push`, `is_empty`). Where Python's name for a **method**
  differs (`append`, `strip`, `startswith`, `upper`, `splitlines`), there is no second name: the call
  is `E2072`, `no method 'append' on Array[int]`, whose help names the Ember method
  (the full table is Appendix E). A Python name that Ember keeps (`partition`, `items`, `count`, and
  the built-in functions of `[STD-26]`) keeps Python's meaning (`[PHIL-14]`).
* `[STD-26]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Python's built-in functions.** The prelude has these functions, with
  Python's meaning; each reads its argument as a `for` loop does (`[CTL-1]`):
  * `len(x)` is `x.len()`: an `int` for a collection or view, and for a range its count
    (`[STD-19]`), in the smallest type that holds it by the numbers the compiler knows
    (`len(0..n)` with `n: int` is an `int`). `len` of a `StrView` or `String` is
    `E2073`: Python counts characters and Ember's `s.len()` counts bytes, so the help offers both
    `s.char_count()` and `s.len()`.
  * `range(stop)`, `range(start, stop)`, `range(start, stop, step)` count as Python's do, including a
    negative `step`; `step == 0` panics. `range(n)` is `0..n`, and every form compiles to a counted
    loop (`[CTL-3b]`).
  * `enumerate(it, start=0)`, `zip(a, b)` (stops at the shorter) and `reversed(x)` (for what can run
    backwards) return lazy iterators, as Python 3's do.
  * `sum(it, start=0)`, `any(it)` and `all(it)` consume an iterable (of numbers, of `bool`s);
    `any(x > 0 for x in xs)` uses a generator expression (`[GRM-38]`).
  * `sorted(it, key=None, reverse=false) -> Array[T]` returns a new sorted array (stable) of the items
    the iterator gives, and copies none. Over an iterator of views (`sorted(m.keys())`) it is a list of
    views, a value that holds views, which lives no longer than what they point into (`[TYP-15]`): a
    change that may reshape `m` ends it (`E3060` at a later use). A list of items of your own is
    written `sorted(m.keys().copy_each())` (`[STD-19]`).
  `min` and `max` stay two-argument functions; `xs.iter().min()` gives an `Option` for a collection.
* `[STD-14]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* Failure follows `[ERR-13]`: a caller's bug
  panics; a failure of the world returns `Result` or `Option`. The non-panicking twin `[ERR-13]` asks
  for is an accessor's (`Mat4.col`/`col_checked`, `CppShared.get`); a constructor's or a mutation's
  caller's bug (`stepped(0)`, `BitSet.insert` of a negative, `Entity.new` out of range, `Registry.emplace` on
  a dead entity, `normalize` of zero, `split` on an empty separator) panics with none. Every
  allocating function is documented as allocating and carries `Alloc`.

* `[STD-29]` *(new in 0.9.15)* `std.mem.Volatile[*T]`'s `read_volatile` and `write_volatile` are
  `unsafe fn`s (`[UNS-5]`) whose `@safety` asks the caller for a pointer that is valid for a read (a
  write) of a `T` **and aligned to `T`'s alignment**: a volatile access through a misaligned pointer is
  undefined in the C it compiles to, so the caller's promise names it.

## XV.2 Console output, input and formatting

* `[STD-9]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `print(a, b, …, sep=" ", end="")` and `println(a, b, …, sep=" ",
  end="\n")` write their arguments' text to standard output separated by `sep`;
  `eprint`/`eprintln` write to standard error. They are compiler-known and are the only calls with a
  variable number of positional arguments (`[TYP-26]`). An argument's text is its `Display` text when
  its type has `Display`, and its `Debug` text otherwise, which is Python's `str` → `repr` fallback; a
  type with neither is `E2040`, whose help is to implement `Display`. A class object always has
  `Debug`, its class and address
  (`[TYP-36]`), so a class without a written `Display` prints by it (ODR-113). `println()` prints an
  empty line.
* `[STD-2]` Printing allocates only to build an f-string argument; `println("literal")`,
  `println(some_str)` and `println(n)` for a number are `@noalloc`.
* `[STD-10]` *(new in 0.9.9)* `input(prompt="") -> String` prints the prompt, flushes, reads one line
  and returns it without the line ending. The prelude's console functions treat a console failure as
  fatal, as Python does when the exception is not caught: end of input or a closed stream panics, and
  the message names the `Result` forms in `std.io` (`stdin().read_line()`).
* `[STD-18]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `format(value, spec="") -> String` formats one value with a format spec
  (`[LEX-19]`), like Python's `format`; the spec is a string literal, checked against the value's type
  where it is written, as an f-string's is (`E2250`, ODR-168).
  `format_to(ref mut buf: MutSpan[u8], …) -> Result[StrView, FmtError] from buf` formats into a
  caller's buffer, called `format_to(ref mut buf, …)`, and gives a view of the text it wrote there; its
  own machinery never allocates, so the call allocates only if a value's
  `Display` does (`[EFF-1]`). An f-string lowers to a `StringBuilder` sized from its
  literal parts.

## XV.3 Text

* `[TXT-1]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `StrView` is a read-only view of bytes, a `Span[u8]`, known to be valid UTF-8; `String`
  owns a heap buffer with the same guarantee. Safe code may rely on the invariant (`[UNS-4]`).
* `[TXT-2]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Nothing becomes a `StrView` without validation: every conversion from bytes or foreign text
  returns `Result[StrView, Utf8Error]`, or a `_lossy` form that substitutes U+FFFD. An importer or
  binding that would hand foreign bytes to a `StrView` without validation is `E5063`.
* `[TXT-3]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `StrView` and `String` are a pointer and a length, not null-terminated, and may contain
  `\0`. A C boundary uses `CStrView`/`CString` (Part XVI); a `c"…"` literal containing a NUL is `E5064`.
* `[TXT-4]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* Slicing a string, `s[a..b]`, is by byte offset and panics in every
  profile when a bound is not on a character boundary; `s.get(a..b) -> Option[StrView]` is the total
  form. There is no indexing by character position, because it would be O(n).
* `[TXT-5]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `StrView` → `String` allocates and copies, and is written `String(s)`; `String` →
  `StrView` is free; `Span[u8]` → `StrView` validates in O(n) without allocating; `StrView` →
  `CString` is the fallible allocating `.to_cstring()` of `[FFI-15]` (ODR-081).
* `[TXT-6]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Across the C ABI a `StrView` is `{const uint8_t *ptr; size_t len}`.
* `[TXT-7]` Text is UTF-8 everywhere. `std.ffi.WideString` converts, explicitly, for APIs that need
  UTF-16.
* `[TXT-8]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `StrView` is a view, like every `Span`: it lives no longer than the text it points into,
  and a change that may reshape that text (replacing a `String`, `push_str`, `clear`) ends it.
  A `String` place reads as a `StrView` wherever one is expected.
* `[TXT-9]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **A string literal initialises a `String`.** Wherever a `String` is
  expected — an initialiser, an argument, a field, a collection element, a return value — a string
  literal produces a new `String` holding its text. The allocation happens at the literal and is
  reported there (`Alloc`); where a `StrView` is expected, a literal is a view of text written in the
  program and allocates nothing. A `StrView` *value* never converts implicitly: a `String` of your own
  is written `String(s)` (`s.to_string()` and `String.from(s)` mean the same).
* `[TXT-10]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **`StrView` operations.** `len()` is the length in bytes and
  `char_count()` in characters; `is_empty`, `chars`, `char_indices`, `bytes`, `as_bytes`, `lines`,
  `split(sep)`, `split_whitespace()` (Python's `split()` with no argument), `split_once(sep) ->
  Option[(StrView, StrView)]`, `partition(sep) -> (StrView, StrView, StrView)` (Python's), `trim`,
  `trim_start`, `trim_end`,
  `starts_with`, `ends_with`, `find(sub) -> Option[int]`, `rfind`, `count(sub)`, `replace(old, new)
  -> String`, `to_upper`, `to_lower`, `repeat(n)`, `parse[T]() -> Result[T, ParseError]`,
  `to_string`, `get(range)`, `is_char_boundary(i)`, and `x in s` (`[STD-8b]`). A method that gives
  text it did not make (`trim`, `split`, `lines`) gives views pointing into `s`; one returning several
  strings returns an iterator of such views. Case mapping and `char_count` are
  Unicode-aware; nothing depends on the locale. `char` has `is_alphabetic` (Unicode's Lu, Ll, Lt, Lm
  and Lo), `is_digit` (the digits of every script, and the superscripts), `is_alphanumeric`
  (alphabetic or numeric) and `is_whitespace` (what `split_whitespace` splits at), which mean what
  Python's `isalpha`, `isdigit`, `isalnum` and `isspace` do, and `is_ascii_alphabetic`,
  `is_ascii_digit`, `is_ascii_alphanumeric` and `is_ascii_whitespace`, the same restricted to ASCII.
  `parse[T]()` (ODR-029) reads the whole text as an
  integer type (the 256-bit counts included, over their whole range), a float type, `bool` or `char`,
  skipping no white space (`s.trim().parse[int]()`): an
  integer is an optional sign (`-` only for a signed type) and ASCII decimal digits, and must fit `T`;
  a float is an optional sign and `inf`, `infinity` or `nan` in any case, or decimal digits with an
  optional `.`, fraction and exponent (`e` or `E`, an optional sign, digits), rounded to the nearest
  `T`; a `bool` is `true` or `false`; a `char` is exactly one character. `ParseError`, in `std.string`,
  is a unit-only enum, `Empty`, `Invalid` or `Overflow`, naming the first problem from the left.
* `[TXT-11]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **`String` operations.** Everything `StrView` has (by read-through),
  plus `String()`, `String(s)` (a `String` of your own made from text), `with_capacity(n)`,
  `push(c: char)`, `push_str(s)`, `insert`, `remove`, `truncate`, `clear`, `capacity`, `reserve`, and
  `as_str` (a `StrView` of the whole text). `a + b` for `a: String, b: StrView` takes `a` over and
  returns it extended; `s += t` appends. `StrView + StrView` is `E2040` whose help is an f-string.
  ODR-098 defines the mutation and capacity methods: `String.with_capacity(n) -> String` makes an
  empty string with room for at least `n` bytes; zero allocates nothing. `capacity() -> int` reads
  the allocated byte capacity. `reserve(additional)` makes room for at least `len() + additional`
  bytes, without changing the text, and does nothing when that capacity already exists.
  `insert(i, c: char)` inserts one character at byte offset `i`, which must be in `0..=len()` and
  on a character boundary. `remove(i) -> char` removes and returns the character starting at byte
  offset `i`, which must be in `0..len()` and on a character boundary. Both close up or move the
  suffix as necessary; neither scans the prefix for a character position. `truncate(n)` retains
  the first `n` bytes when `n < len()` (then `n` must be a character boundary), and otherwise does
  nothing. `clear()` removes all text. `remove`, `truncate` and `clear` keep the capacity.
  These change the string, through a name that may change it, and return `void` unless a result is
  named above; each is a reshape, which ends every view into the text. Counts and
  offsets accept any integer type; a negative literal is `E2011`, and a negative run-time value or
  one not representable as a native length panics before conversion. An invalid offset or character
  boundary panics in every profile. Growth uses the checked allocation rules of `[HEAP-8]`.
  The arguments are evaluated before the string is changed, as for `Array`'s methods that change it.

## XV.4 Collections

* `[STD-15]` *(new in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **`Array[T]`** is a growable contiguous list (Python's `list`).
