# Annex B — Hot Reload (the Dynamic profile)

Hot reload turns a source edit into running behaviour in a live process, keeping existing objects,
statics and open resources. It is part of the Ember Dynamic conformance profile (`[CONF-5]`), is
available in `debug` and `development` builds; a `release` build ignores `[build] reload` (`[MAN-7]`).

* `[HR-1]` An edit to one function body in a 50k-line reloadable package MUST be running in the process
  within one second on the reference machine (`[BUD-1]`), with all live object state preserved: budget
  B2 (`[BUD-2]`) for the build, plus load, plan, prepare and commit, measured together over a live set
  of 10,000 instances (`[BEN-8]`).
* `[BEN-8]` The end-to-end reload benchmark times three edits — a function body, a field added with a
  default, and a field whose type changes through `migrate_from` — from save to the new code running.

## B.1 Model

The unit of reload is the package. A package built with reload enabled is a shared library whose
functions are reached through permanent thunks and whose types carry schemas. A reload proceeds in
phases: **plan** (compare schemas and the facts the compiler worked out; refuse here with a reason),
**prepare** (build every migrated instance; may fail, changes nothing), **commit** (publish; cannot
fail), **reclaim** (end what the old image owned).

* `[HR-2]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Reload is transactional.** A failure in plan or prepare leaves the process running the old
  image, with no instance changed, handed over or ended, and a report naming the cause. Commit performs
  only pointer stores into memory reserved in prepare: no allocation, check, callback or other fallible
  operation. A failure in reclaim is an ordinary panic after the reload has succeeded.
* `[HR-2a]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Plan reads schemas, the facts of `[HR-44]` and the registered set and runs no user code.
  Prepare allocates every new instance in the transaction arena (`[HR-37]`), runs every `migrate_from`
  against a read-only view of the old instance, and computes the old-to-new address map. Commit
  publishes the instances, patches type information, applies the map and repoints the thunks. Reclaim
  frees each migrated instance's old version field by field without the type's own `drop`, since the
  instance lives on in its new form, and ends removed fields, running their `drop`.
* `[HR-3]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* A reload is applied only inside `ember_reload_poll()`, and only when no
  registered thread is executing Ember code (each thread's Ember-depth counter is zero); otherwise the
  poll returns `EMBER_RELOAD_UNSAFE_POINT` and does nothing. The exception is `std.hot.checkpoint()`
  (`[HR-33]`), a poll the program makes itself, where its own thread's frames below the checkpoint stay
  live (`[HR-3b]`).
* `[HR-3a]` Every thread that can run Ember code is registered: host threads on attach (`[FFI-22]`),
  `thread.spawn` threads, and job workers. `debug` builds assert on entry to Ember code from an
  unregistered thread.
* `[HR-3b]` *(new in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* At a checkpoint the frames below it run their old code on after the swap.
  Each function of a reloadable image keeps a record of which of its calls it is in, and the image lists,
  for each call, the types whose layout the rest of the function depends on once the call returns: those
  its old code reads or writes fields of, builds, holds, passes or gets back by value, indexes or
  allocates, and those the functions it calls directly depend on (they run old code too; a call through
  a function value may reach any); and, beside the types, the functions the rest of the function may
  still call, whose facts `[HR-44]` compares. A layout change applies at the checkpoint when no frame
  below it depends on the changed type: the instances migrate as at a poll (`[HR-14]`), and one a
  frame's view points into keeps its address, which `[HR-15]` allows when its new size fits; one that
  must move is refused, since a frame's views are not counted (`[HR-15a]`). A change a frame depends
  on is refused, naming the function and the line of its call. A static's change still waits for a poll
  from the host.
* `[HR-44]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **The facts the compiler worked out are part of what a reload compares.** Every rule that
  decides when compiling whether a line is safe — a loop and a call that may change what it walks, a
  read-only view and a call that may change what it reads, a view argument and a callee that may end or
  move what it points into, a view of an object reached through a link and a call that may end the
  object, a lock this thread holds and a call that may take it, a parent link read with no header test,
  what a thread or a kept callback changes — rests on what each function may change, read and end,
  worked out from its body and from every function the program can put in a function value, behind an
  interface, `dyn` or virtual method, or in C's keeping (`[EFF-4]`). The image records these facts for
  every reloadable function, as a package's interface file does. Plan refuses a reload (`E9030`) whose
  new image changes such a fact of a function that code the reload does not rebuild was checked
  against: a frame below a checkpoint that may still call it (`[HR-3b]`), a suspended generator
  (`[HR-45]`), and another package compiled against this package's facts. The report names the
  function, the fact and the caller that relies on it ("`note` now adds to `LOG`, and `run`, still
  running below the checkpoint on line 10, walks `LOG` across its call of `note` on line 11; restart,
  or let `run` return before the reload"). Code the reload rebuilds is checked again when it compiles,
  so a change that only it relies on is no refusal. A change to a `@cached` method's body clears the
  result each instance of its type keeps: the kept result is migrated as a removed field and an added
  one with no value (`[HR-14]`), and is computed again on the next call. Nothing of this runs while the
  program runs.
* `[HR-42]` **Publication.** Entering Ember code increments the thread's depth counter with acquire
  ordering and leaving decrements it with release. Commit reads every counter with acquire, writes the
  new thunk targets and type information, and publishes them with one release store to a reload
  generation counter, which a thread entering Ember code next acquires.
* `[HR-42a]` The counter is not a lock: entering Ember code is one relaxed increment and one acquire
  fence whatever the number of threads; the reload side pays the scan over threads.
* `[HR-4]` Old images are never unloaded, so a stale return address or retired thunk target stays
  mapped.
* `[HR-4a]` Statics live in a runtime-owned table, never in image memory.
* `[HR-8]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Each image carries a reload manifest section listing every reloadable function by mangled
  name, every type schema, every static, the facts of `[HR-44]` and the protocol version; the runtime
  reads it rather than the platform's export table.

## B.2 Calls and function addresses

* `[HR-5]` A call to a reloadable function goes through its thunk.
* `[HR-6]` Each reloadable function gets one thunk, at a fixed address for the life of the process,
  that loads the current target from the runtime's call table and jumps to it; a reload rewrites the
  table, never the thunk. A reloadable function's address, wherever it can be observed, is its thunk's.
* `[HR-6a]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Hence function values (their code word), method tables, drop glue and `extern "C" fn`
  values stay ordinary code pointers; nothing else in the language changes.
* `[HR-7]` Call-table slots are identified by mangled name (`[MNG-1]`), never by index. A function
  removed by an edit keeps its thunk, now pointing at a stub that panics naming it; a reload that would
  leave such a thunk reachable is refused.
* `[HR-9]` A call through a thunk costs one load and one indirect jump; the measured overhead on the
  performance suite with reload enabled is reported with its configuration and must not exceed 3 %.
* `[HR-9a]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* A reloadable function is never inlined, devirtualised or placed in
  the inline header of `[CG-C-3]`, since an inlined body cannot be swapped; this holds over `@inline`
  (`[CG-C-3a]`). A `@noreload` function may be inlined (`[HR-10]`).
* `[HR-28]` `ember inspect --safety` reports the thunk indirection of each function beside its safety
  checks.
* `[HR-10]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `@noreload fn` is called directly and may be inlined; changing its body requires a restart
  (the reload is refused, naming it). Hot loops and `@no_alias_checks`, `@simd` and `@parallel` bodies
  should be `@noreload`.
* `[HR-10a]` A `@noreload` function may call reloadable functions, through their thunks.
* `[HR-21]` A foreign table of exported function pointers stays valid across every reload, because each
  exported function's address is its thunk. Adding, removing or changing the signature of an
  `@export` function changes the module protocol and is refused: that is a rebuild of the host.

## B.3 Types, schemas and migration

* `[HR-11]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Every type in a reloadable package has a **schema**: its kind, base, layout attributes, and
  the ordered list of fields (name, type schema hash, offset, size) or variants (name, discriminant,
  payload). A field's type schema includes the words its type is written with (`owns`, `shares`,
  `shares mut`, `thread_shared`, `weakref`, `sharedref mut`, `ref`, `ref mut`, `using A`), so a change
  of one is a change of the field's type.
* `[HR-11a]` Enum values are migrated by variant name, never by discriminant.
* `[HR-12]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* In a reloadable build, class instances are registered in a live-instance list, which adds
  16 bytes to the object header of `[OBJ-1]` (24 bytes instead of 8, and 28 instead of 12 for an object
  `weakref` links may reach); non-reloadable builds keep `[OBJ-1]`'s layout.
* `[HR-12a]` The header size is a whole-process property: every package in a process agrees on whether
  reload is enabled, enforced at link time (`E9035`).
* `[HR-13]` Value-typed data (structs in arrays, `SoA` columns, ECS storage, arena contents) is migrated
  through its container, which registers itself with its element type's schema.
* `[HR-13a]` Standard-library containers of a type from a reloadable package register themselves; the
  instantiating package emits the registration, so `std` needs no reload support.
* `[HR-13b]` Value data reachable only through raw pointers or foreign memory cannot be migrated; if its
  schema changed, the reload is refused.
* `[HR-14]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Migration is by name**, and this table is exhaustive:

  | Change | Behaviour |
  |---|---|
  | field added with a default | initialised to that default |
  | field added, its type is `Default` | initialised to `Default.default()` |
  | field added, neither | refused, naming the field and suggesting a default |
  | field removed | old value ended in reclaim |
  | field renamed with `@renamed_from("old")` | value carried over |
  | field renamed without it | a removal and an addition |
  | field type widened losslessly (`[TYP-5]`) | converted |
  | field type changed to a range type | refused unless every value passes `T.checked` |
  | field type changed otherwise, its words included (`[HR-11]`) | refused unless the type declares `migrate_from` |
  | field of a migrated type | migrated depth-first |
  | fields reordered, `let` changed | carried over by name |
  | methods added, removed or changed | no instance change, except as `[HR-44]` says for a `@cached` method |
  | base class changed | refused |
  | class removed while instances live | refused, naming the class and the count |
  | enum variant added, reordered or renamed with `@renamed_from` | discriminants rewritten |
  | enum variant removed while a value holds it | refused, naming the variant and the count |
  | enum variant payload changed | the field rows, applied to the payload |
  | layout or fields changed on a type used across FFI by value | refused |
  | a `gen fn`'s frame layout or states changed while a frame of it lives | refused (`[HR-45]`) |
  | a value made `using` an instance moved, or a memory manager's type changed while values made in it live | refused (`[HR-46]`) |
  | static's initialiser changed | refused unless the static is `@reinit_on_reload` (`[HR-17a]`, `[HR-47]`) |

* `[HR-15]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* Migration keeps an instance's address where the new size fits;
  otherwise commit rewrites every owner, link and view of it that the runtime can enumerate: the
  one-owner fields and elements that hold it (`T`, `owns T`), its `shares`, `shares mut` and
  `thread_shared` owners, its `weakref` links, and the kept views into it (`ref T`, `ref mut T`,
  `sharedref mut T`, `Span[T]`, `MutSpan[T]`, `StrView`), in live instances and registered containers,
  in statics, and inside tuples, `owns` blocks and function values' state held by any of these; and the
  instance address a value made `using` an instance keeps (`[HR-46]`), where that instance moves.
* `[HR-15a]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* An owner, link or view the runtime cannot enumerate — in foreign memory, behind a raw
  pointer, in an object handed to C (`[HR-20]`) — cannot be rewritten, and the reload is refused when
  what it names must move.
* `[HR-15b]` Every refusal is decided in plan, before prepare runs.
* `[HR-16]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `static fn migrate_from(old: OldSelf) -> Result[Self, ReloadError]` replaces field-wise
  migration for its type. `OldSelf` is the previous schema as a generated struct `Old<Name>`, visible
  only in that function; `old` is a read-only view of the old instance.
* `[HR-34]` Prepare cannot panic: every operation it performs is either free of panics or reported as
  a `ReloadError`.
* `[HR-35]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* `migrate_from` cannot abort the process. It may not contain an
  explicit panic (`panic`, `unwrap`, `expect`, `assert`: `E2225`, whose help names the fallible form);
  and every run-time check inside it — overflow, bounds, a cast, a count at its maximum, a stale
  handle — returns `Err(ReloadError.Migration(type_name, instance, message))` instead of stopping the
  program.
* `[HR-39]` A foreign call inside `migrate_from` returns its failure as `ReloadError.Foreign`; a call to
  a C++ function asserted `noexcept`, which could terminate the process, is rejected at compile time.
* `[HR-43]` `@allow_reload_terminate` on a `migrate_from` admits such calls and states that this
  migration may end the process rather than refuse; `ember tcb` lists every use.
* `[HR-36]` Allocation during prepare comes from the transaction arena; exhausting it fails the reload
  with `ReloadError.Allocation`, so construction inside `migrate_from` needs no special spelling.
* `[HR-37]` The transaction arena holds everything prepare allocates and is released whole if the
  reload fails.
* `[HR-38]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* `std.hot.ReloadError` is `SchemaRefused(type_name: String, reason:
  String)`, `Migration(type_name: String, instance: u64, message: String)`, `Allocation`,
  `Foreign(error: String)` or `Timeout`; `instance` counts the type's live instances from 0.
* `[HR-45]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **A suspended generator keeps its frame.** A `gen fn`'s frame (`[CORO-3]`) has a schema:
  its layout and its states, one per suspension point, each with what lives across it. The runtime
  finds the live frames of each reloadable `gen fn` among the values it can enumerate (`[HR-15]`). A
  body change that leaves the frame's layout and states as they were applies: a live frame resumes in
  the new code at the state it was suspended in, and a paused generator walking a list counts, for
  `[HR-44]`, as a frame that still calls what its body calls. A body change that changes them is
  refused in plan while a frame lives, naming the `gen fn` and the count; with no live frame it
  applies as any body change does. A frame the runtime cannot enumerate (in foreign memory, behind a
  raw pointer) is treated as live.
* `[HR-46]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Values made in a memory manager's instance.** A value made `using` an instance of a
  memory manager that may have several (`[ALC-1]`) came from that instance and goes back to it, through
  the instance address it keeps. Its migration keeps it in that instance's block: it is migrated in
  place where its new layout has the same size and alignment, so that its end hands the instance back
  the layout it was given; one that would have to move or change size is refused in plan, naming its
  type, the manager's type and the count. Where the instance itself moves (`[HR-15]`), commit rewrites
  the instance address every such value keeps; a value whose instance address the runtime cannot
  enumerate is refused as `[HR-15a]` says. A type that implements `Allocator` is changed only through its
  own methods while values made in one of its instances live, so a change of its schema while such
  values live is refused in plan, naming the type and the count; with none live it migrates as any
  type does.
* `[HR-17]` A static whose type and initialiser are unchanged keeps its value; one whose type changed
  migrates by `[HR-14]`; a new static is initialised normally.
* `[HR-17a]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* Editing a static's initialiser changes its schema: the reload is
  refused, naming the static, unless the static is `@reinit_on_reload`, which re-runs the initialiser
  and ends the old value. Keeping the old value silently is never an outcome.
* `[HR-47]` *(new in 0.9.15)* `@reinit_on_reload` ends the static's old value when the reload is applied, so nothing may
  still point into it: plan refuses it (naming both statics, or the static and the type) where a view, a `sharedref mut` link
  or the instance address of a value made `using` it, held by another static, a live instance or a
  registered container, may point into the static's value or what it owns, judged from the types that
  can hold one. `shares` owners of what it held keep their objects alive, and `weakref` links to them
  find them ended, as anywhere else.
* What the compiler works out from bodies (where each view is used, what each function changes, reads
  and ends) plays no part in schemas or migration; a change to it is judged by `[HR-44]`.

## B.4 Refusal, scope and cost

* `[HR-18]` A refusal returns a report naming each type and change that caused it; it is never a crash.
* `[HR-18a]` A refusal is never partial: nothing of the new image is live.
* `[HR-18b]` `ember build --reload --explain` predicts the outcome against the running process without
  applying anything.
* `[HR-41]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* **Failure matrix.**

  | What happened | Detected in | Outcome |
  |---|---|---|
  | source does not compile, or fails checking | before the poll | old image keeps running |
  | reload protocol mismatch | load | refused, `E9037` |
  | a C or C++ header changed | plan | refused (`[HR-23]`) |
  | schema change with no defined outcome | plan | refused (`[HR-14]`) |
  | `@noreload` body changed | plan | refused (`[HR-10]`) |
  | a worked-out fact changed that code not rebuilt relies on | plan | refused (`[HR-44]`) |
  | a live generator frame's layout or states changed | plan | refused (`[HR-45]`) |
  | a value made `using` an instance must move, or its manager's type changed while it lives | plan | refused (`[HR-46]`) |
  | `@reinit_on_reload` on a static something else may point into | plan | refused (`[HR-47]`) |
  | an owner, link or view that cannot be rewritten names what must move | plan | refused (`[HR-15a]`) |
  | allocation exhausted, `migrate_from` fails, or a foreign call fails | prepare | discarded; old image keeps running |
  | panic in `migrate_from`, or a failure in commit | cannot occur | forbidden by `[HR-35]` and `[HR-2]` |
  | panic in a `drop` during reclaim | reclaim | the reload has succeeded; the panic aborts as any panic does |

* `[HR-19]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `reload = "bodies"` admits only function-body changes and changes that need no instance
  migration; it needs no type schemas and no larger header, and is the first tier an implementation
  provides. It still records the facts of `[HR-44]` and the frame schemas of `[HR-45]`, and refuses as
  they say.
* `[HR-25]` `reload` is `"all"`, `"opt-in"`, `"bodies"` or `"none"` (`[MAN-7]`); `@reloadable` and
  `@noreload` apply to modules and items, item level winning.
* `[HR-20]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* An object C holds — handed to a foreign parameter
  whose contract keeps it, or given with `into_raw()` — and the state of a callback that C keeps
  registered are never moved: C holds their addresses, which the runtime cannot rewrite. If the new
  size of such an object or state does not fit, the reload is refused, naming it.
* `[HR-22]` Foreign objects owned by Ember are carried across unchanged.
* `[HR-23]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* A changed C or C++ header refuses the reload and names it (the host
  must be rebuilt): any change to the header or to a file it includes, a comment's too, since the
  host compiled the inline bodies it declares. A changed overlay does not, because overlay edits
  change only Ember code; where the header is unchanged the previous thunks are reused.
* `[HR-24]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* An object in use by an in-flight GPU frame is migrated in place when
  it fits; otherwise the reload waits at most `frames_in_flight + 1` polls and is then refused, naming
  the resource. This is detected in prepare, so the reload is discarded and the old image keeps
  running (`[HR-41]`).
* `[HR-27]` A `release` build is bit-identical whether or not the source uses any reload attribute.
* `[HR-29]` With reload enabled, one shared runtime serves every image in the process
  (`[build] runtime = "shared"`); a reloadable package that links its own runtime copy is `E9036`.
* `[HR-30]` **Host contract:** `ember_reload_init(&config)` once; `ember_reload_poll()` at a point where
  no Ember frame is live (between frames, for a game); `ember_reload_stats()` for timing;
  `ember_reload_shutdown()`.
* `[HR-31]` Polling never blocks; compilation runs in the background.
* `[HR-32]` `ember_reload_stats()` reports the last reload split into compile, load, plan, prepare,
  commit and reclaim, with the instances migrated and any refusal.
* `[HR-33]` `ember run --hot` is the toolchain's own host: it builds under `debug`, runs the program,
  watches the sources and polls at the point the program declares with `std.hot.checkpoint()`; a
  program that declares none is told so after ten seconds rather than appearing to hang.
---

# Annex C — C++ Interoperation (the Native profile, optional)

Calling C++ is a separate, optional conformance claim (`[CONF-4]`). An implementation provides Part
XVI (C) first; nothing in Parts I–XVIII depends on this annex.

* `[FFI-3]` Ember never links against C++ mangled symbols. The importer generates `extern "C"` thunks,
  compiled by the project's own C++ compiler with the project's flags, and Ember calls the thunks.
* `[FFI-17]` `import cpp "Header.hpp" with (project="engine", overlay="…", instantiate=[…])` parses the
  header with libclang in the configuration of the named `[cpp.<project>]` section and generates one
  thunk per imported function, method, constructor and destructor. Overlays for C++ use
  `overlay cpp "Header.hpp":` with the grammar of `[GRM-35]`.
* `[FFI-50]` *(new in 0.9.9)* The manifest section `[cpp.<project>]` names the C++ project: `compiler`
  (`msvc`, `clang-cl`, `clang`, `gcc`), `standard`, `defines`, `include_paths`, `flags`, and `cmake =
  { build_dir, target }` to read the flags from the CMake File API (`[BLD-FFI-2]`). `ember bind
  --emit-cpp` writes the thunk translation unit for inspection.
* `[FFI-17b]` Templates are available only as explicit instantiations listed in `instantiate=[…]`; an
  Ember generic cannot instantiate a C++ template (`E5055`).
* `[BLD-FFI-1b]` The MSVC runtime-library switch, `_DEBUG` and `_ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL` are inherited
  byte for byte from the C++ project, because they change the layout of standard-library types;
  translation units that disagree are `E9020`, and an undeterminable C++ runtime is `E9021`.
* `[BLD-FFI-4]` Ember's emitted C and the project's C++ are compiled by the same compiler, so the
  project's LTO setting inlines calls across the boundary like any other call.
* `[BLD-FFI-5]` `ember build --emit header` with `--cpp` also writes a C++ header whose declarations
  take `std::string_view` and `std::span` where the C header takes pointer-and-length pairs.
* `[BLD-FFI-5a]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* With the C++ header, an exported function may take or return a
  `thread_shared` value of a class, the one owning Ember value that crosses (`[FFI-31b]`): the header
  presents it as a copyable handle class of the same name with the class's `pub` methods, each copy
  one more owner on the value's away count (`[RC-4]`, `[RT-8]`) and each end one fewer, its limit checked as an
  Ember owner's is (`[RT-7]`). No other Ember value has a C++ handle, so C++ code never counts a
  one-thread value, from one thread or from two.

## C.1 What imports, and how

* `[FFI-44]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *Automatic* means no overlay is needed; *overlay* means a contract
  must be written; *native island* means it stays in C++ behind a hand-written boundary.

  | C++ construct | Import |
  |---|---|
  | `extern "C"` functions, POD structs | automatic (Part XVI) |
  | standard-layout, trivially copyable classes | automatic, by value (`[FFI-32]`) |
  | other classes | automatic, opaque behind a pointer; methods through thunks |
  | the standard-library types of `[FFI-17a]` | automatic |
  | explicit template instantiations | automatic (`[FFI-17b]`) |
  | other templates, metaprogramming, concepts, compiler extensions | native island |
  | function-like macros, `std::function` | overlay |
  | single inheritance from a C++ base | automatic, bounded (`[FFI-39]`) |
  | multiple or virtual inheritance | native island (`[FFI-48]`) |
  | exceptions | automatic, with a derived or declared policy (`[FFI-24]`) |
  | custom allocators | overlay or native island |
  | ownership the header does not state | unsafe until `adopt` or a contract (`[FFI-36]`) |

* `[FFI-17a]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)*

  | C++ | Ember |
  |---|---|
  | `std::span<T>`, `std::span<const T>` | `MutSpan[T]`, `Span[T]`, zero-copy; a result needs a lifetime word (`[FFI-11]`) |
  | `std::span<T, N>`, `std::span<const T, N>` (a fixed extent) | `ref mut [T; N]`, `ref [T; N]` |
  | `std::string_view` | `Span[u8]`; `.to_str()` is the fallible conversion to `StrView` (`[TXT-2]`) |
  | `std::string` | `CppString`; `.to_str() -> Result[StrView, Utf8Error]`; `String.from(c)` copies |
  | `std::vector<T>` | `CppVector[T]` with `.span()`, `.span_mut()`, `.to_array()`, `push_back`, `len` |
  | `std::unique_ptr<T>` | `owns T`, ended through the deleter; one whose deleter holds state is refused (`E5034`): an `owns T` holds one address |
  | `std::optional<T>` | `Option[T]` for a `T` that maps by value |
  | `std::shared_ptr<T>`, `std::weak_ptr<T>` | `CppShared[T]`, `CppWeak[T]` — never `shares`/`weakref` (`[WK-14]`, `E5065`) |
  | `std::variant<…>` | a generated enum, when every alternative maps and the overlay names each: `@ffi(variant=["A", "B"])` on a `type` entry naming the header's alias of the variant, the names in the alternatives' order |
  | `std::function<R(A…)>` | an opaque object Ember owns; with `@ffi(std_function)` on its overlay entry, a function value of type `fn(A…) -> R` (`[CLO-3]`), called as any other, which owns its target; never a parameter type (`E5030`) |

* `[FFI-17e]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* The bridge types `CppVector[T]`, `CppString` and `CppShared[T]` are
  declared in `std.ffi`; they are not `Copy`, `Send` or `ThreadShared`; the first two end through their
  C++ destructors; and a span or string obtained from one is a view into it, so it cannot outlive it.
* `[FFI-17f]` `ember inspect` reports each bridge operation that is a thunk call rather than an inlined
  one (`CppShared` clone and drop, `CppVector` `push_back`, `len` and drop, `CppString` drop).
* `[FFI-32]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A C++ class that is standard-layout and trivially copyable, all of
  whose members map, is imported as a `@layout(c) struct` with `@derive(Copy)` and the same field
  offsets; an opaque class cannot be constructed from Ember except through its imported constructors
  (`E5032`), and a parameter that maps to nothing is `E5031`. A function returning an opaque class by
  value gives an `owns T`, as a constructor does: the result is moved to an object of its own, ended
  by the class's destructor; an abstract class, or one without a public destructor, is refused
  (ODR-166).
* `[FFI-11f]` A result lifetime derived from `[[clang::lifetimebound]]` imports as an asserted fact:
  the attribute is not enforced by C++, so it never counts as checked.
* `[FFI-48]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* **Unsupported constructs** (`E5034`, naming the row):

  | Construct | Why not | Instead |
  |---|---|---|
  | multiple inheritance, virtual bases | the pointer adjustment is ABI-private and differs between MSVC and Itanium | a single-inheritance facade in C++ |
  | C++20 modules | no stable AST for a compiled module interface | parse the headers |
  | C++ coroutines | promise and frame layout are implementation-defined | a callback or completion handle |
  | overloads differing only in return type | Ember has no return-type overloading | rename one in the overlay |
  | casts across a hierarchy the importer did not model | no Ember equivalent of `dynamic_cast` there | cast in C++ and export the result |
  | non-type template parameters of class type | mangling differs between compilers | instantiate in C++ and export a typedef |
  | allocator-parameterised containers | the allocator is part of the type and opaque | expose a span, or keep it native |

## C.2 Exceptions

* `[FFI-24]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* **Every imported C++ function has an exception policy, with a
  default.** The policy is derived: a function whose declaration is non-throwing (`noexcept`, a
  `noexcept(expr)` that evaluates true, a destructor, a defaulted special member) is called directly
  and returns `T`. Every other function returns `Result[T, CppError]`: its thunk catches every
  exception and returns it as a `CppError` holding the type name and `what()`.
* `[FFI-24b]` An overlay may assert `@ffi(noexcept)` for a function the header leaves throwing; its
  thunk still catches, and a throw then panics naming the declaration — never an unexplained
  `std::terminate`.
* `[FFI-24c]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* `ember inspect --cost`, which reads the built program, reports each
  C++ call's mode (`noexcept (derived)`, `noexcept (asserted)`, `catching`) and lists the catching
  calls on `@noalloc` or main-thread paths; `ember bind --report` reads a header and lists none.
* `[FFI-24d]` A header that adds or removes `noexcept` changes the Ember signature; the diagnostic in
  dependent code names the header, the declaration and the change as the cause, and `ember bind
  --report` lists it under API changes.
* `[FFI-43]` An overlay that marks a function both `noexcept` and throwing, or two composed overlays
  that disagree, is `E5062`; a function whose policy cannot be derived and is not declared is `E5061`.
* `[FFI-39e]` A C++ exception never crosses into Ember code, and an Ember panic never crosses into C++:
  both abort at the boundary if they would.

## C.3 Classes and inheritance

* `[FFI-36]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A C++ function returning a raw pointer with no ownership contract
  yields `*mut T`; `ffi.adopt[T](p)` (`unsafe`) turns it into an `owns T` ended through the contract's
  destructor.
* `[FFI-39]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* An Ember class may derive from a C++ class with no overlay entry
  (`[FFI-44]`), which makes the base open and sized; the importer generates a C++ subclass, the
  trampoline, which passes on to the Ember class exactly the virtual methods it overrides (`override
  fn`), read from the class. Its constructor is an ordinary `fn init(…)` calling `super.init(…)`
  exactly once.
* `[FFI-39a]` The trampoline calls the overrides through their permanent thunks, so overrides survive
  hot reload (`[HR-6]`).
* `[FFI-39b]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* `super.init(…)` selects the C++ base constructor by arity and
  argument types and runs it at `super.init(…)` (`[CLS-11]`); a base with no default constructor and
  no declared `init` is `E5058`.
* `[FFI-39c]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* A C++ parameter that keeps the pointer it is
  given (contracted `owns` in the overlay) takes the object over: its class is declared
  `@ffi(trampoline, owner="foreign")` (`[FFI-17d]`), the argument is handed over
  (`panel.add_child(b)`: `b` ends, upcast to the C++ base), and C++'s `delete` ends the object later.
  For a C++ function whose declaration cannot say so (a raw pointer it keeps), `b.into_raw()` inside
  `unsafe:` gives C++ the object's address (`[FFI-54]`). An object of an `owner="ember"` class given to
  a parameter that keeps it is `E5060`, whose message gives both lines (declare the class
  `owner="foreign"` and hand the object over, or give `into_raw()` inside `unsafe:`); a parameter
  borrowed for the call alone takes the object, or `this`, as any plain parameter, upcast to the C++
  base (ODR-156).
* `[FFI-17c]` Destruction of an Ember class derived from a C++ class is derived-first, as `[CLS-6]`
  says for every class: the Ember `drop`, then the Ember fields, and only then the C++ base destructor.
* `[FFI-17d]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `@ffi(trampoline, owner="ember")`, the default, makes Ember's owner
  own the object, which ends when its last Ember owner does; `owner="foreign"` makes a foreign `delete`
  end it, once it has been handed to C++ (`[FFI-39c]`). A trampoline base without a virtual destructor
  is `E5059`.
* `[FFI-39d]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* *(changed in 0.9.15)* Re-entrant calls from C++ into an Ember object
  are expected, and are checked when compiling: a call into C++ not marked `@ffi(no_callbacks)` counts
  as possibly running every override of an Ember class derived from a C++ class whose objects C++ may
  hold (`[FFI-52]`), and makes every change those overrides make. So a walk, a read-only name or a
  `ref mut` name the caller holds across the call is refused where an override may change what it
  views (`E3020`, `E3021`, `E3022`, `E3060`): "`cpp.dispatch_all()` (line 14) may run `on_event`, an
  override of `Button` whose objects C++ may hold (line 6), which pushes to a `Button`'s `codes`, and
  this loop walks `b.codes` (line 13); call `cpp.dispatch_all()` after the loop: move line 14 below the
  loop". Nothing is checked while the program runs.
* `[FFI-40]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A method imported from C++ is a method of the imported class: its
  object is `this`, and it lists no receiver. C++'s body is not read as Ember's is, so whether a method
  may change its object is taken from its declaration: a `const` method only reads its object when
  `[FFI-40a]` finds so, and every other method may change it, so it is not called through a name that
  only reads the object (`E3023`) and a call of it is a change of the object for the loop and view
  rules. `&&`-qualified members are skipped (`W5033`). A `T&` parameter imports as `ref mut x: T`,
  `const T&` as a plain parameter `x: T`, and `T&&` as `owns x: T` where the type is movable; a `T&`
  result is a `ref mut T` view into the object and a `const T&` result a `ref T` one (`[LT-1]`).
* `[FFI-40a]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `const` is not an aliasing guarantee in C++: a `const` method of a
  class with a `mutable` member, its own or a base's, may change its object. The importer reads the
  method's body, which the header has: it imports the method as only reading its object only when the
  body changes no field — it assigns none (`=`, a compound assignment, `++`, `--`), takes no field's
  address, binds no non-`const` reference or pointer to one, calls no non-`const` method of one, hands
  neither the object nor a field to a function by non-`const` reference or pointer, and calls no method
  of the object that may change it, nor anything it cannot follow — and as changing it otherwise, or
  when the header does not have the body (ODR-160). An overlay's `class C:` section restates a method
  as an Ember method line (`fn lookups() -> c_int`); `@ffi(const)` above the line asserts that the
  method only reads its object, an asserted fact, which `ember tcb` lists, and a line without it
  imports the method as changing its object. A line whose name, parameters or result differ from the
  import's method is `E5010`.
* `[FFI-41]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Static member functions import as functions of the type with no
  object, as a `static fn` is (`[FN-4]`). A static data member, and a
  variable of a namespace, imports as a foreign static (`[FFI-10]`), read and written as a global
  (`cpp.engine.Grid.made += 1`), in `unsafe` unless it is `const` and holds no pointer, each use going
  through a thunk that gives its address, since its symbol is mangled or, for an `inline` one, emitted
  only where C++ uses it (`[FFI-3]`, ODR-161). One holding a pointer imports like any other: it is read
  and written in `unsafe`, so `[STA-1]` does not ask it to be `ThreadShared` (ODR-163). Nested types sit
  under their outer type's name; namespaces become module paths, an inline one adding nothing to a name,
  as in C++ (`nlohmann::json_abi_v3_11_3::json` is `cpp.nlohmann.json`, ODR-165); entities in anonymous
  namespaces are skipped (`W5034`).
* `[FFI-42]` *(changed in 0.9.10)* Overloaded operators map to Ember operator interfaces where one exists (`operator[]` to
  `Index`/`IndexMut`, `operator*`/`->` on a smart-pointer-like type to read-through: such a class
  imports `get()`, and `get_mut()` where the operator is not `const`, through which `->` is reached);
  C++ iterators with `begin`/`end` become `Iterable`.
* `[FFI-42a]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* A `for` loop over an imported C++ container walks it, so nothing
  changes the container while the loop walks it: a call of any method imported as changing its object
  (`[FFI-40]`), the `const` ones `[FFI-40a]` imports so included, is refused inside the loop (`E3020`),
  since it could invalidate C++'s iterators.

## C.4 Trust and evidence

* `[TCB-1]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* Every fact an overlay states about foreign code carries a grade:
  **asserted** (someone wrote it; the default), **instrumented** (a test run observed no
  counterexample on the paths exercised), **checked** (verified against the header) or **proven**.
  The grade is written as an attribute on the overlay item, `@grade(instrumented)`. `ember tcb
  [--module m]` prints every assumption the program's safety rests on, grouped by module. A claimed
  grade whose evidence is missing or stale is `W5050`, and `E5050` under `ember build
  --require-evidence` or `ember tcb --require`. Evidence records live under `[ffi] evidence` (default
  `.ember/ffi-evidence`).
* `[TCB-2]` The report separates what the language guarantees from what external components supply,
  and writing a grade never raises it: no fact above asserted comes from declaration alone.
* `[TCB-3]` Every assumption a guarantee relies on appears in the report with its source and grade.
* `[TCB-4]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Entries are categorised — language, compiler, runtime, standard
  library, unsafe, C FFI, C++ bridge, external library, driver, hardware — and the compiler is in the
  list, with its version and known-defect list. The unsafe section lists each `unsafe:` block,
  `unsafe fn`, `unsafe import c` (`[FFI-51]`) and `@unsafe(export(…))` or `@unsafe(export_table(…))`
  (`[FFI-26]`) with its note; the C FFI section lists each `safe fn`, `@ffi(no_callbacks)`
  (`[FFI-52]`), `@ffi(safe)` (`[FFI-56]`) and thread contract, and the C++ bridge section each
  `@ffi(const)` (`[FFI-40a]`).
* `[TCB-5]` An instrumented fact is valid only for the foreign library, header, overlay, toolchain and
  test binary it was measured against; its evidence record stores their identities and hashes.
* `[TCB-6]` A change to any identity input makes the record stale; a change to an environment input
  (machine, timing) is reported but does not.
* `[FFI-37]` `ember test --instrument-ffi` runs the tests with the allocation, lock, wait and I/O entry
  points intercepted, to grade declared effect facts as `instrumented`.
* `[FFI-37a]` The intercepted set is published and recorded in the evidence; an allocation through a
  mechanism outside it (a custom pool, a driver) is reported as structurally unobservable, never as
  evidence.
* `[FFI-37b]` The evidence records how often each foreign function was called and from how many call
  sites; a fact never exercised is reported `unexercised` (`W5054`) and does not count.
* `[FFI-37c]` `instrumented` means "no counterexample was observed on the paths exercised", is shown as
  partial when not every call site ran, and is never shown as "holds"; a contradicted fact is `E5053`.
* `[FFI-37d]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* Only effect facts (`Alloc`, `Block`, `Lock`, `Io`) can be
  `instrumented`; ownership, nullability, lifetime, aliasing, exception, thread and callback
  (`no_callbacks`) facts stay asserted unless checked or proven.
* `[CXX-1]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* The conformance suite for this annex includes a corpus of real headers
  and at least one third-party header-only library, each with its expected outcome recorded (by value,
  opaque, behind an overlay, or refused with a named diagnostic) and its generated thunks committed and
  diffed; it runs under MSVC and Clang, with debug and release runtimes and RTTI on and off, and two
  configurations that disagree must fail with `E9020`, never bind differently.
---

# Annex D — GPU Host Model (`std.gpu`)

`std.gpu` is a library for driving a GPU from Ember — handles, frames, command recording, deferred
destruction and shader interfaces — over an abstract device that a host renderer implements through
the FFI, or that an Ember backend implements directly. It adds nothing to the language. Ember does not
compile shaders in this version.

```ember,fragment
type TextureHandle = Handle[gpu.Texture]
type BufferHandle = Handle[gpu.Buffer]

interface Device:
    fn begin_frame() -> Option[Frame]                   # None: skip this frame; no end_frame
    fn end_frame(owns frame: Frame)
    fn create_texture(desc: TextureDesc) -> Result[TextureHandle, GpuError]
    fn create_buffer(desc: BufferDesc) -> Result[BufferHandle, GpuError]
    fn destroy(h: TextureHandle)                        # physical destruction is deferred
    fn frames_in_flight() -> int
```

* `[GPU-1]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* GPU objects are named by generational handles (`[HND-1]`), which are
  `Copy` and `Send`. A stale handle is detected by its generation **in every profile**
  (`panic: stale TextureHandle (generation 7, current 9)`); there is no setting that removes the
  check.
* `[GPU-2]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `device.begin_frame() -> Option[Frame]`; `None` is normal (a minimised window). A `Frame` has
  one owner and is not `Copy`, and `end_frame(owns frame: Frame)` takes it over (`device.end_frame(frame)`
  ends the name `frame`), so ending a frame that never began, or ending one twice, is refused when
  compiling.
* `[GPU-3]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `frame.arena()` is the frame's transient memory manager, an instance that lives as long as
  the `Frame`: a value made `using` it (`[ALC-1]`) lives no longer than the frame (`E3063`), so nothing
  made in it outlives `end_frame`.

## D.1 Recording and access states

```ember,fragment
fn draw(ref mut frame: Frame, pipeline: PipelineHandle, vbo: BufferHandle, ibo: BufferHandle, index_count: int):
    with cmd = frame.command_list():
        cmd.begin_render_pass(RenderPassBegin(target=None))    # None: the swapchain
        cmd.bind_pipeline(pipeline)
        cmd.bind_vertex_buffer(0, vbo)
        cmd.bind_index_buffer(ibo)
        cmd.draw_indexed(index_count)                          # checked against `ibo` (`[GPU-12]`)
        cmd.end_render_pass()
```

Each resource has an access state the device tracks: owned by the CPU; recorded in frame N; in
flight in frame N until that frame's fence is observed; retired (destroyed while in flight, freed
later).

* `[GPU-4]` *(changed in 0.9.9)* Writing or mapping a resource that the GPU may still be reading is a
  panic in every profile (`buffer is in flight (frame 42); use a per-frame ring or wait`).
  `Ring[T, N]` holds one resource per frame in flight (`ring.current(frame)`).
* `[GPU-5]` Binding a resource declares its access; `cmd.read(h)`/`cmd.write(h)` declare it
  explicitly; barriers are derived from the declarations; `cmd.barrier(…)` remains available.
  `unsafe: cmd.native()` exposes the backend's command buffer.
* `[GPU-12]` *(new in 0.9.15)* **Every draw and dispatch is checked against what is bound, in every profile.** The
  command list keeps, for each bound vertex, instance and index buffer, how many elements it holds (its
  size over its stride or index width), and before recording a draw compares the ranges the draw reads
  with them: `draw(vertex_count, first_vertex, instance_count, first_instance)` against every bound
  vertex buffer and every instance-rate buffer, `draw_indexed(index_count, first_index, …)` against the
  bound index buffer, and `dispatch(x, y, z)` against the device's group-count limits. One compare per
  range per draw; a range outside stops the program, naming the call, the numbers and the buffer
  (`panic: cmd.draw_indexed(1000000) reads indices 0 to 999999, but the index buffer bound (ibo)
  holds 3`). What these compares cannot see — the vertex numbers stored in an index buffer, an
  indirect draw's arguments in GPU memory, a shader's own reads — is covered by robust buffer access,
  which the device turns on wherever the backend offers it, so such a read past a buffer yields zero
  or nothing instead of other memory. A device whose backend cannot offer it says so
  (`device.robust_access()` is `false`), and its use is an asserted fact that `ember tcb` lists
  (`[TCB-1]`). `unsafe: cmd.native()` records without these compares.
* `[GPU-6]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `device.destroy(h)` invalidates the handle at once and destroys the object after the GPU
  has finished the frames that may use it. Ending the device waits for the GPU and flushes every
  retirement list.
* `[GPU-7]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* In `debug`, ending a device while handles are still live reports each leaked handle
  with the place it was created.
* `[GPU-8]` `History[T]` owns the per-frame copies of a temporal resource
  (`gpu.History[TextureHandle].new(device, desc, count=2)`) and gives `(prev, cur)` each frame,
  forbidding reads of `cur` and writes of `prev` within a frame.
* `[GPU-9]` *(changed in 0.9.15)* `std.gpu.graph` is an optional render-graph layer over `CommandList`: passes declare reads
  and writes, `graph.compile()` orders them, aliases transient resources with disjoint lifetimes and
  inserts transitions, and `pass.native(fn(ref mut cmd) => …)` records directly inside a graph.

## D.2 Shader interfaces

* `[GPU-10]` `ember shader-bind <reflection.json>`, reading the reflection a SPIR-V toolchain produces,
  generates a module with a `@gpu_layout(std140 | std430)` struct per uniform or storage block, with
  compile-time layout assertions (`E8001` on a mismatch), a typed binding interface, the push-constant
  struct and the vertex-input layout; binding a resource set built for another interface is a type
  error.
* `[GPU-11]` Ember assumes no shader language: anything that produces SPIR-V and reflection works.
* A kernel language (`@gpu fn`) is reserved for a later version; `@gpu` and `std.gpu.kernel` are
  reserved names.
---

# Appendix E — Coming from Python *(non-normative)*

Ember reads like Python and runs like C. Most Python habits carry over unchanged; the ones that do not
are rejected with a fix-it (`[DIA-21]`) rather than given a different meaning (`[PHIL-14]`).

## E.1 What carries over

| Python | Ember | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| indentation, `:` blocks, `#` comments | same | spaces only (`[LEX-4]`) |
| `x = 1` declares | same | a name assigned in every branch is declared after the `if` (`[CTL-10]`) |
| `a, b = b, a`; `return a, b` | same | tuples (`[GRM-29]`) |
| `[1, 2]`, `{"k": v}`, `{1, 2}` | same | `Array`, `Map` (insertion-ordered like `dict`), `Set` |
| `[x * x for x in xs if x > 0]` | same | also map and set comprehensions |
| `for x in xs:` … `else:` | same | |
| `for i, x in enumerate(xs):` | same | also `xs.enumerate()` |
| `len(xs)`, `range(n)`, `sum`, `sorted`, `zip`, `reversed`, `any`, `all` | same | Python's meaning (`[STD-26]`); `len` of a string is rejected, because Ember's counts bytes |
| `for k in d:`, `for k, v in d.items():` | same | a `Map` iterates its keys; `m.values()` its values |
| `x in xs`, `x not in xs` | same | cost reported by `ember inspect --cost` |
| `a < b < c` | same | `b` evaluated once |
| `x is None` | same | on `Option` |
| `7 // 2`, `-7 // 2 == -4`, `-7 % 2 == 1` | same | floor semantics |
| `7 / 2` on ints | `7 // 2` or `7 as float / 2` | integer `/` is rejected (`[TYP-28]`) |
| `2 ** 10` | same | overflow panics instead of growing |
| f-strings with `=`, `!r`, format specs | same | |
| `print(a, b, sep=", ", end="")` | same | |
| `input("> ")` | same | panics at end of input (`[STD-10]`) |
| keyword arguments, defaults | same | |
| `lambda x: x + 1` | `fn(x) => x + 1` | |
| generators, `yield` | `gen fn f() -> Generator[T]:` | |
| `with open(p) as f:` | `with f = fs.File.open(p)?:` | the file closes at the end of the block, or whenever it is dropped |
| `try` / `except` / `raise` | `Result`, `?`, `match`, `return Err(e)` | Part XIII |
| classes, inheritance, `super()` | `class`, `open class`, `super.init(…)` | an object has one owner; `shares` for a second owner, `weakref` for a back link the program sets |
| `nonlocal x`, `global x` | not written | a lambda changes the real variable it uses (`fn(): score += 1`); a function changes a module variable (`static mut`) by its name |
| `@dataclass` | `struct` | equality, debug printing and cloning are automatic |
| `list.sort()`, `sorted(xs)` | same, or `xs.sorted()` | stable |
| `dict.get(k, d)` | `m.get_or(k, d)` | `m.get(k)` returns an `Option` |
| `d[k] = v`, `d[k]` | same | a missing key panics like `KeyError` |

## E.2 Names that differ (`[STD-13]`)

| Python | Ember |
|---|---|
| `len(s)` for a string | `s.char_count()` (characters, Python's count) or `s.len()` (bytes) |
| `str(x)`, `repr(x)` | `x.to_string()` or `f"{x}"`; `f"{x!r}"` |
| `"%d" % n`, `"{}".format(n)` | `f"{n}"` |
| `int(s)`, `float(s)` | `s.parse[int]()`, `s.parse[float]()` (a `Result`) |
| `int(x)` for a float | `x as int` (saturates; NaN is 0) |
| `range(a, b)` in a loop | `a..b` is the usual spelling; `range` also works |
| `xs.append(x)`, `xs.extend(ys)` | `xs.push(x)`, `xs.extend(ys)` |
| `xs.pop()` | `xs.pop()` returns an `Option` |
| `xs.index(x)` | `xs.index_of(x)` (an `Option`) |
| `xs.sort(key=f)` | `xs.sort_by_key(f)` |
| `xs[-1]` | `xs.last()` or `xs[xs.len() - 1]` (negative indices panic) |
| `xs[a:b]` | `xs[a..b]` |
| `s * n`, `[x] * n` | `s.repeat(n)`, `[x for _ in 0..n]` |
| `s.strip()`, `s.lstrip()`, `s.rstrip()` | `s.trim()`, `s.trim_start()`, `s.trim_end()` |
| `s.split()` | `s.split_whitespace()` |
| `s.splitlines()` | `s.lines()` |
| `s.startswith(p)`, `s.endswith(p)` | `s.starts_with(p)`, `s.ends_with(p)` |
| `s.upper()`, `s.lower()` | `s.to_upper()`, `s.to_lower()` |
| `c.isdigit()`, `c.isalpha()`, `c.isalnum()`, `c.isspace()` | `c.is_digit()`, `c.is_alphabetic()`, `c.is_alphanumeric()`, `c.is_whitespace()`; `c.is_ascii_digit()` and the like for ASCII only |
| `s.find(t)` (returns -1) | `s.find(t)` (returns `Option[int]`) |
| `", ".join(xs)` | `xs.join(", ")` |
| `True`, `False`, `None` | `true`, `false`, `None` (only as an `Option`) |
| `def f():` | `fn f():` |
| `if xs:` | `if not xs.is_empty():` |
| `abs`, `min`, `max`, `round` | `abs`, `min`, `max`; `x.round()` rounds half to even, as Python's does |

## E.3 What is new

* **Types are checked before the program runs.** Most are inferred; function parameters and struct
  fields are written.
* **Values have one owner.** `b = a` hands a list over: `a` cannot be used again, and the error says
  where it went and offers `b = copy of a` (a copy of your own) or `b = shares a` (two owners of one
  list). A plain parameter reads the caller's value; a function that changes it says `ref mut` on the
  parameter and at the call (`fn bump(ref mut c: Counter):`, `bump(ref mut a)`); `owns` on a parameter
  takes the value over.
* **Objects are freed when their last owner ends**, at a predictable point, not by a collector. A
  loop of `shares` owners that nothing opens again would never be freed, so it is refused when
  compiling, with the link to make `weakref`.
* **A list does not change while a loop walks it.** `for x in xs: xs.push(x)` is refused; the loop's
  own handle may change the item it is on (`for ref mut x in xs: x = 0`), and anything else is added or
  removed after the loop.
* **What each name may do is written on it.** A plain name reads; `ref mut` may change someone else's
  value; `copy of` makes a copy of your own; a lambda keeps a copy only where its first line says so
  (`fn() copy of score:`). The compiler works out what each function changes from its code, so no first
  line lists it.
* **Integers are 64-bit and overflow panics.** `@overflow(wrap)` or `wrapping_add` when wrapping is
  wanted.
* **Threads run in parallel.** There is no global lock; the compiler rejects data races instead
  (Part XI).

## E.4 One program, side by side

A dice game in Python:

```python
import random

class Player:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.hp = 10
        self.inventory = []

def roll(rng):
    return rng.randint(1, 6)

rng = random.Random(42)
player = Player("Ada")
counts = {}
for turn in range(5):
    r = roll(rng)
    counts[r] = counts.get(r, 0) + 1
    if r == 6:
        player.inventory.append("gem")
    else:
        player.hp -= r // 2
print(f"{player.name}: hp={player.hp}, items={len(player.inventory)}")
for face in sorted(counts):
    print(face, counts[face])
```

The same game in Ember:

```ember
import random

class Player:
    name: String
    hp: int = 10
    inventory: Array[String] = []

fn roll(ref mut rng: random.Rng) -> int:
    return rng.int_in(1..7)

rng = random.Rng.seeded(42)
player = Player("Ada")
counts: Map[int, int] = {}
for turn in range(5):
    r = roll(ref mut rng)
    counts[r] = counts.get_or(r, 0) + 1
    if r == 6:
        player.inventory.push("gem")
    else:
        player.hp -= r // 2
println(f"{player.name}: hp={player.hp}, items={len(player.inventory)}")
for face in sorted(counts):
    println(face, counts[face])
```

What changed: fields are declared, with types, in the class body; `roll` says it changes the caller's
`rng`, with `ref mut` on its parameter and at the call; `append` is `push` and `dict.get(k, d)` is `get_or`; the generator is seeded explicitly and
draws from a half-open range; `print` with a newline is `println`. Everything else — the script at
the top level, `range`, `len`, `sorted`, iterating a map's keys, f-strings, `//` — reads as in Python.
The two programs print different numbers only because their generators differ.
---

# Appendix F — Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **access state** | a GPU resource's lifecycle: owned by the CPU, recorded, in flight, retired (Annex D) |
| **arena** | a memory manager that hands out memory by bumping a pointer and frees it all at once; named with `using` (§IX) |
| **capture** | a name a lambda uses from the function that made it: the real variable unless the lambda's first line names it with a word after its brackets (`fn() copy of score:`, `fn() owns n:`), which makes it part of the function value's own state |
| **class** | a type whose objects live each in a heap block of their own, with identity (`is`) and subclasses; an object has one owner unless a line says `shares`, and an 8-byte header (Part VIII) |
| **contract** | an attribute stating an effect a function must not have (`@noalloc`), checked over the call graph (§X.2); for FFI, the facts about a foreign pointer that a header does not state (§XVI.4) |
| **`Copy` type** | a type whose `=` copies a value bit for bit, the two copies independent: numbers, `bool`, `ref T`, `Span[T]`, `StrView`, and structs made only of these; class objects, `shares` values, links, `ref mut` views and `MutSpan`s are not `Copy` |
| **copy of** | a new value equal to the old one, made by its type's `Clone`, on which nothing done to the other is seen; before a link it copies the target, never the link |
| **count, weak count** | the number of owners in the header of a value with several owners, and the number of `weakref` links to an object, which keeps its memory block (not the object) until the last link ends; each is compared with its limit before every +1 (its maximum for a one-thread count; half its range for a `thread_shared` count, which threads add to at once, `[RC-4]`), and the program stops there |
| **deferred-drop region** | a walk during which an object whose last owner ends is set aside whole, with everything it owns, marked ended at once and freed when the walk ends |
| **effect** | a kind of thing a function may do — allocate, block, lock, perform I/O, panic, run a run-time check — inferred by the compiler (§X.1) |
| **`.embind`** | the cached, content-addressed result of importing a header with its flags and overlay (`[FFI-14]`) |
| **ended** | the state of an object from the moment its last owner lets it go, before its `drop` runs; a `weakref` link to it then finds nothing. Ending an object counts as a call of its `drop` |
| **enforcement ladder** | prove a property when compiling; a check runs while the program runs only where the property is data the program computes as it runs (an index, an overflow, a `weakref` link's target); what can be proved neither way is refused with the line to write, or allowed only inside `unsafe` (`[PHIL-8]`) |
| **exclusivity** | the rule that while a `ref mut` name is used, its place is read or changed through no other name; checked when compiling, never while the program runs |
| **`exists as`** | the opening of an `Option` or a `weakref` link: `if cam.target exists as p:` runs its block when there is something, and names it `p` |
| **first line** | a function's signature: its parameters, each with the word in front of its name, `owns this`, the result type and `from`; it says nothing about what the function changes or reads |
| **fix-it** | a suggested edit attached to a diagnostic that tools can apply mechanically |
| **function value** | a function or lambda kept in a variable, a list or a field: two words, its code and its state (what it captured with a word); its type says its parameters, its result and whether any thread may run it (`thread_shared fn()`) |
| **generator frame** | a `gen fn`'s suspended state as a sized value; resuming runs the body to the next `yield` (`[CORO-1]`) |
| **hand-over** | the giver's name ends and the receiver becomes the owner, for every type, numbers included: `b = a`, an argument for an `owns` parameter, a capture `owns x` |
| **handle** | a token that names something elsewhere: `Handle[T]`, a generational index into a `Pool` (`[HND-1]`), a `JoinHandle`, a C object's `@ffi(handle)`; never a class object |
| **interior mutability** | a change through a name that only reads, which only the types made to be shared between threads allow, by their own operations: `Atomic`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, channel ends, and `guarded by` fields under their lock |
| **kept callback** | a function value C keeps after the call that hands it over (`callback(retained)` or `callback(once)`) and runs during later foreign calls |
| **kept view** | a view stored in a struct or a list; the value that holds it lives no longer than what it points into |
| **kind test** | `x is T`, which asks whether a value of an interface or base-class type is a `T`; `if s is Circle as c:` names it |
| **link** | a field or value that names an object it does not own alone: `weakref T`, `shares T`, `shares mut T`, `thread_shared T`, `sharedref mut T` |
| **memory manager** | where a value's heap memory comes from: the built-in one, or one named with `using` (its kind in a type, its instance on the line that makes the value) (§IX) |
| **mode** | the word in front of a parameter's name, which sets what the function may do with it, for every type: none (reads the caller's value), `ref mut` (changes the caller's place), `const ref mut` (changes it and is never given another ref), `owns` (takes the value over) (`[FN-2]`) |
| **native island** | a subsystem kept in C or C++ behind a typed boundary rather than imported (Annex C) |
| **niche** | an invalid bit pattern of a type that `Option` uses for `None`, so `Option[T]` costs no space |
| **noalias** | C's `restrict`: the promise to the C compiler that two pointers never point at the same memory; every `ref mut` parameter is compiled with it, `this` never |
| **`Nondet`** | the effect of an operation whose result may differ between runs or machines (`[DET-2]`) |
| **overlay** | an Ember file that states contracts, renames and wrappers for an imported header (§XVI.4) |
| **owner** | the one place (a local, a field, a list element) that ends a value when it ends; a value made shared has several |
| **panic** | a failure that means the program is wrong; it prints a message and aborts the process (`[PAN-1]`) |
| **parent link** | a `weakref` field naming the object that owns its holder (`parent: weakref Node`), set by the program (`child.parent = weakref this`); read with no test where the compiler proves its target lives |
| **permanent thunk** | the fixed address standing for a reloadable function; a reload changes its target, never its address (`[HR-6]`) |
| **place** | where a value lives: a local, a field, a list element, an enum variant's payload, or what a `ref mut` name stands for |
| **position** | a name for a list element made by indexing, which finds the element again at each use; the list may grow while it is used, and a removal, reorder or clear ends it |
| **profile** | `debug`, `development` or `release`: optimisation and diagnostic settings that never change meaning (`[PRF-1]`) |
| **proven fact** | a fact a verifying operation establishes for two names (`assert_disjoint` after its call, `check_disjoint` inside its `Ok` branch), dropped when either name is given another value (`[DSJ-2]`) |
| **read-only view** | every view except `ref mut T`, `sharedref mut T` and a `MutSpan` held by a `ref mut` name; it promises that what it reads does not change while it is used |
| **real variable** | the very variable a lambda uses without a word, not a copy: `b.on_click(fn(): score += 1)` changes the caller's `score` |
| **reason code** | why a run-time check exists (`[EFF-11]`) |
| **reduction** | a combining change (`total += e`, `max`, `push`) made by scoped tasks to one place: each task keeps a private accumulator, combined at the join in spawn order |
| **reload manifest, reload transaction, safe point** | the image section listing what can be reloaded (`[HR-8]`); the plan and prepare phases that may fail without effect (`[HR-2]`); the poll at which no thread runs Ember code (`[HR-3]`) |
| **reshape** | a change that can free or move memory: replacing a value that owns memory, adding to or removing from a collection, changing an enum's variant, ending an object's last owner; writing a number is not one |
| **Safe Ember** | code outside `unsafe:` blocks, an `unsafe fn` body's included (each of its unsafe operations sits in an `unsafe:` block of its own); the memory-safety guarantee covers it (`[PHIL-10]`) |
| **`Send`, `ThreadShared`** | may be handed to another thread; several threads may hold and read one value at once; both inferred from the words a value is written with (§XI.1) |
| **shape** | a category of error with a required help text (§XVII.6) |
| **shareable generic** | one whose type parameter is used only to call its bounds' methods, so one shared body can serve every instance (`[MONO-5]`) |
| **`shares`, `shares mut`** | one more owner of a value on this thread, counted: a `shares` owner reads it, a `shares mut` owner may also change it |
| **`sharedref mut`** | a link that may change its target and that several holders, and the owner, may share; on two threads it is changed only under a lock, through `Atomic`, or by a reduction |
| **SoA** | structure of arrays: one array per field (`SoA[T]`, §XII.1) |
| **source parameter** | a parameter a returned view may point into without `from`: every view argument, or the one named by `from` (`[LT-1]`) |
| **static** | a program-wide value with a fixed address that never changes; `static mut` is a module variable that may, reached only by the main thread and its scoped tasks unless `guarded by` a `static` lock |
| **`static fn`** | a function in a type body that has no object (`this`), called on the type: `Counter.starting_at(5)` |
| **summary** | what the compiler works out from a function's code, with no word written: what it may change, read and end, through which chain of calls, which locks it may take, and which view parameters it uses after a line that may end what they view; kept in a package's interface file |
| **`this`** | inside a method, the object the method was called on; a method does not list it among its parameters |
| **`thread_shared`** | a value with several owners on any threads, counted in two numbers (its making thread's owners, and the other threads' with atomic instructions, `[RC-4]`), changed only through `Atomic`, a lock, a channel or `guarded by` fields; `thread_shared fn()` is a function type whose functions any thread may run |
| **trampoline subclass** | the generated C++ subclass through which an Ember class extends a C++ base (`[FFI-39]`) |
| **unseen code** | code whose body the compiler cannot read, which is only a foreign (C) function: a call of one counts as possibly running every callback C keeps, unless its declaration says `@ffi(no_callbacks)` |
| **view** | a name or value that points into a place someone else owns and may not outlive it: `ref T`, `ref mut T`, `sharedref mut T`, `Span[T]`, `MutSpan[T]`, `StrView`, a plain parameter, loop or pattern name, a name opened with `exists as` or named by a kind test, a name for a part (`[TYP-34]`) |
| **`weakref`** | a link that does not keep its target alive; it is read by opening it (`exists as`), which finds nothing once the target has ended |
| **zero-cost** | for a use whose checks are all discharged, emitted code with nothing equivalent C would not contain (`[COST-1]`) |
---

# Appendix G — Resolution of Findings F-001–F-214

Every finding of the 2026-09-23 research pass (`tasks/audit/FINDINGS.md`) and how this revision
resolves it. **SPEC**: the language text changed or gained a rule. **IMPL**: the rule stands or was
clarified and the implementation must meet it. **GATE**: a test or CI obligation now in the text.
**OUT**: outside a language specification, with the reason. **WDN**: withdrawn.

| Finding | Kind | Resolution | Rules |
|---|---|---|---|
| F-001 — `tasks/audit/TASKS.md` is cited by every reproducer and exists on no branch | OUT | Audit bookkeeping, not language text; `FINDINGS.md` Part D rebuilt the missing index. | — |
| F-002 — `()` is not accepted as a value of type `void` | IMPL | `()` is the value of `void`; `Ok(())` is the success value of `Result[void, E]`. | `[TYP-27]` |
| F-003 — `import a.b.c` does not bind `c` | IMPL | `import a.b.c` binds `c`; unknown modules are `E1060`. | `[MOD-3]` |
| F-004 — importing a module that does not exist is silently accepted | SPEC | An import of a missing module is `E1060`; nothing is accepted silently. | `[MOD-3]`, `[PHIL-12]` |
| F-005 — every E2020 type mismatch carries a note about numeric conversion | SPEC | The numeric-conversion note appears only when both operands are numeric. | `[TYP-4]` |
| F-006 — N1 suggestion quality | SPEC | Suggestion threshold scales with name length and kind. | `[DIA-24]` |
| F-007 — the showcase program passes a `str` literal where a `String` is required | SPEC | A string literal initialises a `String` where one is expected. | `[TXT-9]` |
| F-008 — one bad character reports once per byte | SPEC | A run of invalid characters is one diagnostic. | `[DIA-20]` |
| F-009 — "not implemented in this phase" reuses `E1010` | SPEC | Unimplemented constructs are `E0900`, never a name-resolution code. | `[PHIL-12]`, `[CLI-19]` |
| F-010 — cascades after a failed import | SPEC | Names bound to a failed import produce no further errors. | `[DIA-14]` |
| F-011 — cascade after a private constructor | SPEC | One error per failed construction; privacy has its own code. | `[DIA-14]`, `[MOD-2]` |
| F-012 — `println` of any `String`, including every f-string, emits C that does not compile | IMPL | `print`/`println` are specified; an accepted program that yields bad C is a compiler defect, caught by the C gate. | `[STD-9]`, `[CG-C-2]`, `[TST-27]` |
| F-013 — "accepted by Ember, rejected by the C compiler" is a whole defect class with no gate | GATE | Every accepted test program is compiled by each host C compiler with warnings as errors. | `[TST-27]`, `[CG-C-2]` |
| F-014 — a name assigned in every branch of an `if`/`else` is not visible after it | SPEC | A name assigned in every branch at one type is declared after the branch. | `[CTL-10]` |
| F-015 — `if x = 5:` (a `==` typo) gets a misleading fix | SPEC | `if x = 5:` gets the `==` fix-it. | `[DIA-21]` |
| F-016 — the 0.8.2c change log says there is no if-let; the grammar has one | SPEC | Pattern conditions are in the grammar; 0.9.9 carries no stale change log. | `[GRM-19]` |
| F-017 — the EBNF still contains what `[GRM-16]` and `[GRM-11]` delete | SPEC | Part III is a complete grammar with no deleted productions. | `[GRM-11]`, `[GRM-16]` |
| F-018 — two path separators, `.` and `::` | SPEC | One path separator, `.`; `::` is not a token. | `[GRM-24]`, `[LEX-21]` |
| F-019 — `as` binds tighter than unary minus | SPEC | Prefix `-`/`~` bind tighter than `as`. | `[TYP-6]` |
| F-020 — `@deprecated` has two signatures | SPEC | `@deprecated(since, note)` is the one form. | `[VER-3]` |
| F-021 — `@nopanic` is listed as v2 in the attribute table, while the 0.8.4_Hardened_1 change log calls `@nopanic(explicit)` one of Ember's current c | SPEC | `@nopanic(explicit)` is a current contract; bare `@nopanic` is `E0104`. | `[EFF-17]` |
| F-022 — a pasted editorial instruction inside `[BLD-11]` | SPEC | Rule rewritten; no editorial instructions remain in rule text (end check). | `[BLD-11]` |
| F-023 — `E1020` means two things in the compiler | SPEC | `E1020` means only a duplicate declaration; visibility errors are `E1052`. | `[GRM-4]`, `[MOD-2]` |
| F-024 — `[GRM-14]` adds a third kind of generic parameter (`access P`) for one library type, `std.ecs.Query` | SPEC | `Query` uses the ordinary marker type `Mut[T]`; no access-mode generic kind. | `[ECS-3]` |
| F-025 — `[LEX-22]` reserves `'a` for "v2 named lifetimes" | SPEC | Ember has no lifetime syntax, now or later. | `[LEX-22]` |
| F-026 — `[LEX-2]`: the formatter writes the platform's line ending by default | SPEC | The formatter writes LF everywhere. | `[FMT-1]` |
| F-027 — `[LEX-15]` still says "The reserved set therefore has 48 entries" | SPEC | The reserved-word count is stated once, correctly. | `[LEX-15]` |
| F-028 — the Part I.4 table still promises "~2 ns per access pair" | SPEC | The I.4 table states check mechanisms, not nanosecond promises. | `[PHIL-15]` |
| F-029 — `xs = Array[i32]()` is rejected: the explicit type argument is ignored | IMPL | Explicit constructor type arguments fix the type. | `[TYP-18]` |
| F-030 — `min`, `max` and `clamp` are used as free functions and declared nowhere | SPEC | `min`, `max`, `abs`, `clamp` are prelude functions. | `[MOD-5]` |
| F-031 — strings are the biggest Python-ergonomics gap | SPEC | Literal-to-`String` coercion, `String + str`, `+=`, `to_string`. | `[TXT-9]`, `[TXT-11]` |
| F-032 — `[TYP-15]` and `[TYP-15a]` disagree about containers of static views | SPEC | One rule for where views may be stored; containers of static `str` are legal. | `[TYP-15]` |
| F-033 — `<<` overflow is undefined by the text | SPEC | Shift amount checked; bits shifted out are not overflow; `>>` arithmetic on signed. | `[TYP-10]` |
| F-034 — `[TYP-13]` guarantees a niche for `*fn` | SPEC | The niche list names `extern fn`, which exists. | `[TYP-13]` |
| F-035 — `as?` / `as!` are used in IV.6 and absent from the grammar | SPEC | `as?` and `as!` are single tokens in the grammar. | `[GRM-30]`, `[LEX-21]` |
| F-036 — `@view` is required on a struct the compiler already knows is a view | SPEC | View-ness is inferred; `@view` is optional documentation. | `[TYP-34]` |
| F-037 — the default integer is `i32` | SPEC | `int` is `i64`, `float` is `f64`; literals default to them after context. | `[TYP-1]`, `[LEX-16]` |

| F-186 — the runtime exclusivity panic names a C symbol, not the Ember object | SPEC | Panics name Ember entities. | `[DIA-23]`, `[COST-6]` |
| F-187 — `L3011` fires on calls that cannot re-enter the cell | OUT | `L3011` is gone with `RefCell` (0.9.15): what a call may change is worked out when compiling. | `[BRW-21]` |
| F-188 — a view escaping its source gets two errors, the first wrong | SPEC | Storage end with a live loan is one diagnostic, shape B7. | `[BCK-4]`, `[DIA-7]` |
| F-189 — `Array.iter()` does not exist | IMPL | `Array.iter()` is specified. | `[STD-15]` |
| F-190 — growable-buffer arithmetic is unchecked | SPEC | Capacity arithmetic is checked. | `[HEAP-8]` |
| F-191 — `Array[T]` storage is aligned to 16 bytes whatever `T` needs | SPEC | Heap storage honours element alignment. | `[HEAP-9]` |
| F-192 — `@align(N)` is silently ignored | SPEC | Layout attributes are honoured or rejected. | `[LAY-2]`, `[PHIL-12]` |
| F-193 — every reference-count operation is an out-of-line call, and a `Sync` retain is a CAS loop | SPEC | Count fast paths are inline; a `@sync` retain is one `fetch_add`. | `[RT-10]` |
| F-194 — every allocation goes through `_aligned_malloc` (MSVC) / `aligned_alloc`, and `ember_realloc` always allocates-copies-frees | SPEC | System allocator for ordinary alignment; per-thread statistics. | `[RT-1]`, `[RT-11]` |
| F-195 — reference-count overflow reports the wrong reason | SPEC | Count overflow panics with its own message. | `[RT-7]` |
| F-196 — redeclaring a name in the same block is accepted | IMPL | Redeclaring in one block is `E1020`. | `[GRM-4]` |
| F-197 — raw strings, byte strings and f-string format specs are not implemented | IMPL | Raw strings and format specs are specified. | `[LEX-19]`, `[LEX-25]` |
| F-198 — the ten most common Python habits get no help at all | SPEC | A table of Python habits with fix-its. | `[DIA-21]`, `[STD-13]` |
| F-199 — the ledgers say "none open" while ~80 defects reproduce | OUT | Defect ledgers are project process; Appendix G lists every open finding with its resolution. | — |
| F-200 — specification churn far outpaces the compiler | OUT | Process: 0.9.9 consolidates to one revision and a smaller document. | — |
| F-201 — `docs/HANDOFF.md` is 10,698 lines | OUT | Repository handoff size is not language text. | — |
| F-202 — `examples/` has only `hello.em` | GATE | Documentation samples are compiled and run. | `[DOC-2]` |
| F-203 — a generic struct's methods cannot name their own type | SPEC | `Self` and the type's own name work inside its declaration. | `[STR-7]` |
| F-204 — the textbook recursive enum cannot be traversed | SPEC | `Box[T]` reads through like a reference. | `[TYP-14]` |
| F-205 — calling a parameter whose type is a generic bounded by `Callable` fails | SPEC | Callable bounds are written `F: fn(A) -> R`; `Callable[…]` is not source. | `[CLO-14]` |
| F-206 — 32 error pages for 210 registered codes | GATE | Every code has an error page; a missing page fails CI. | `[DIA-6]` |
| F-207 — the six "green" gates are green because their baselines absorb almost everything | GATE | Baselines are reported and a heavily baselined gate is not called green. | `[TST-29]` |
| F-208 — range slicing `xs[a..b]` is not implemented | IMPL | Slicing is specified; its failure must not cascade. | `[DIA-14]` |

| F-210 — interfaces are nominal only | SPEC | Interfaces stay nominal, with the reason stated. | `[TYP-40]` |

| F-212 — two errata are marked open that the grammar already fixed | OUT | The errata ledger is outside the document. | — |
| F-213 — `i32.MIN % -1` | SPEC | `MIN % -1 == 0`; `MIN // -1` panics as overflow, naming the right operator. | `[TYP-28]` |
